case20v1-exp.qual.quant.loop:
Jenmam Health: The Ticked Box

A case on pairing a metric movement with a reason from users

1. Opening

Thursday 8 October 2026, Kochi. Sreejith Chirayath, head of product at Jenmam Health, had until 5 pm on Friday 16 October to tell the platform engineers in Bengaluru and Pune what the Diwali build would contain. Their code freeze began on Monday 2 November, and Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November. One line of the build was undecided: whether the checkout box offering automatic monthly refills, ticked by default in a test since August, should be ticked for every customer from Monday 26 October.

The test had produced a headline that Suresh Chelakkat, the chief growth officer, had already shown the executive committee on Tuesday 6 October: more customers reordered. It had also produced a stack of refused parcels and nine customer interviews that did not sit easily beside the headline. Sreejith had eight days to decide what the numbers meant.

2. Company background

Founded in Kochi in 2019, Jenmam Health sells 30-day supplies of medicine for long-term conditions, mainly diabetes, hypertension and thyroid disease, to patients and to the adult children who order for them. Licensed partner pharmacies in Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu fill each order after a pharmacist checks it against the prescription on file. Customers pay cash on delivery or by UPI. In September 2026 the company had 1.9 lakh active customers and an average basket of ₹1,150, bought at about ₹920.

Its rivals are Tata 1mg, PharmEasy, Netmeds (part of Reliance Retail), Apollo Pharmacy's app, and the neighbourhood chemist who knows the family. Government Jan Aushadhi stores sell low-priced generics. A customer who reorders monthly is worth far more than one who orders once, so the refill rate is the number product, growth and finance all quote. Engineering sits in Bengaluru and Pune, data science in Toronto, and the customer-success team that serves Gulf-based families ordering for parents in Kerala in Singapore.

3. The situation

In July the growth team proposed auto-refill: a box at checkout that, once ticked, makes Jenmam create the next order on day 30. It had always been unticked. Between Monday 17 and Sunday 23 August, the 12,000 Kerala customers who placed an eligible 30-day order were split at random, 6,000 to each arm. Control saw the unticked box; treatment saw it ticked. Each customer was followed for 35 days (a 30-day supply plus five days' grace), and the last window closed on Sunday 27 September.

Exhibit 1 sets out the result. Enrolment rose from 9.0 to 41.0 per cent. Sreelekha Chandy, the data scientist in Toronto, reported on Thursday 1 October that a second order was created within 35 days for 57.0 per cent of treatment customers and 54.0 per cent of control, a difference of 3.0 points with a 95 per cent interval of 1.2 to 4.8 points. Suresh took that to the executive committee.

The operations dashboard in Kochi had shown something else since 18 September. Auto-created orders were coming back from the doorstep: 301 of 2,150 in treatment against 15 of 500 in control. A refused parcel cannot be resold, so each costs Jenmam ₹1,050. Sreelekha had therefore added a row to Exhibit 1 that counts only second orders not refused.

Sajitha Cheruvathur's Singapore team phoned 60 of the 301 customers who had refused, and nine agreed to talk between 25 September and 2 October (Exhibit 2). At 6 pm Singapore time on Friday 2 October, 3.30 pm in Kochi, she told Sreejith the reasons did not sound like one thing. Sreelekha read her notes at 9.30 pm Toronto time on Sunday 4 October, 7.00 am Monday in Kochi, and asked the logs one question the calls had raised: had the customer uploaded a new prescription between enrolment and the auto-order? Exhibit 3 holds her answer, which reached Kochi on Monday 5 October.

4. The people

Sreejith Chirayath, head of product in Kochi, joined in 2022. He owns the roadmap and wants a decision he can defend after Diwali whichever way the numbers move.

Suresh Chelakkat, chief growth officer in Kochi, carries a target of 40 per cent auto-refill enrolment among eligible customers by 31 December. He reads the created-order result as proof the feature works and wants it switched on for everyone.

Sreelekha Chandy, data scientist in Toronto since 2024, wants the decision tied to orders customers actually kept. She is wary of reading more into nine calls than nine calls can carry.

Sajitha Cheruvathur, customer-success lead in Singapore, takes the calls from parents in Kerala and their children in the Gulf. She wants no customer surprised by a parcel they did not expect.

6. The options

Option A: tick the box for everyone. From Monday 26 October every eligible customer sees the box ticked, as in the test. It takes a configuration change only and moves enrolment toward the 41.0 per cent measured in Kerala. It leaves the refusal pattern of Exhibit 1 in place, at ₹1,050 for each parcel refused.

Option B: return to the unticked box. The box is unticked again for all customers and the existing reminder messages continue. It needs no engineering, adds no refused parcels beyond the control pattern, and leaves enrolment near the control level of 9.0 per cent and the 40 per cent target out of reach.

Option C: confirm before dispatch, and test it. The box stays unticked for customers outside the test. Pune builds a message sent 72 hours before dispatch, "Same medicines? Reply YES or edit", and an unanswered message holds the order for a pharmacist's call. The build takes ten working days, merged by Friday 30 October and switched on for a new 12,000-customer test enrolling 2 to 8 November, 6,000 customers with the box unticked and 6,000 with it ticked plus the confirm step. The last window closes on Sunday 13 December. Every pharmacist call adds handling cost.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Exhibit 1 reports a second order created and a second order created and not refused. For each measure, how large a difference between the arms would you treat as more than noise, and what is your evidence?

2. Sajitha's nine interviews were recruited as the note to Exhibit 2 describes. Which statements about Jenmam's customers could Sreejith defensibly make from them, and which could he not?

3. What did Sreelekha's cut in Exhibit 3 add to what the interviews had suggested, and what question does it leave open?

4. Which option would you take to the meeting on Friday 16 October, and what result in the following weeks would make you reverse it?

8. A note for the learner

Every metric movement needs a why from users, and the why needs a size. The loop here ran in three steps: the test said what moved, nine calls proposed reasons, and the logs measured one of them.

The first step, read carefully, supports less than the headline. The created-order gap of 3.0 points sits 3.3 standard errors from zero (the standard error is about 0.9 points), but it counts refused parcels as reorders. Orders created and not refused give 51.98 per cent against 53.75, a gap of minus 1.77 points with an interval of about minus 3.6 to 0.0. It is neither a proven loss nor a win.

The second step gives kinds of reason and no frequencies: nine volunteers out of 60 phoned, all of them refusers. The third sizes one reason. Had the 410 flagged treatment orders been refused at the 7.9 per cent of the unflagged ones (137 of 1,740), about 32 would have been, not 164. So about 132 of the 301 refusals, 44 per cent, trace to the prescription change, against a baseline that already includes the box's effect. The control rate of 3.0 per cent implies roughly 65 of the 301 (2,150 × 0.03 = 64.5) would have been refused anyway, leaving about 105 unexplained.

One defensible path is Option C. It targets the measured cause, keeps the enrolment gain available, and treats kept orders as the outcome. With 6,000 per arm the test can detect about 2.5 points (two-sided 5 per cent, 80 per cent power: 2.8 times a standard error of 0.91), so the decision rule should be written before launch: ship the confirm step if the kept-order gap is not negative, and say in advance what a result inside the noise means.
exp20v2-exp.qual.quant.loop:
Qual + quant feedback loop

1. A five-point drop with no explanation

On Monday 31 August 2026, Aneesh Hansaria, head of product at Nilkanth Meals, an Ahmedabad service delivering home-style weekday lunches, opened the weekly cohort report and stopped at one line. Nilkanth sells a five-lunch trial week for ₹350. A customer has renewed if they buy a first paid five-lunch pack, ₹600, within 28 days of the trial's first Monday. Abhay Hurkat, the analyst, grouped trial starters into four-week cohorts. Cohort A, 6,000 customers whose trials began on Mondays 8, 15, 22 and 29 June, renewed at 42.0% (2,520). Cohort B, 6,200 customers beginning 6, 13, 20 and 27 July, renewed at 37.0% (2,294). The last B window had closed on 24 August, so the gap surfaced only now.

Five points on 6,200 starters is 310 customers, or ₹1.86 lakh of first packs, per cohort. Aneesh asked first whether it was noise. The standard error of the gap is 0.88 points, so the gap is 5.7 standard errors wide: real. What he lacked was a cause. Marketing blamed July's cheaper ad creative; the app team suspected a new checkout screen. Each theory implied a different fix, and a wrong fix costs a quarter. He had a decision in front of him, not a curiosity. Nilkanth was about to commit its September marketing budget to one of the two stories, and the two stories pointed in opposite directions: one meant changing the advertising, the other meant changing the product. He asked Ameeta Hindocha, the research lead, for eight interviews by Friday 11 September, and asked Abhay to hold any further cuts of the data until the interviews had said what to cut by. The order mattered to him. A dashboard can be sliced a hundred ways, and a team that slices before it has a hypothesis will find a pattern in at least one of them.

2. The idea

A qual + quant feedback loop pairs every metric movement with a reason drawn from users, then turns the reason into a prediction a measurement can confirm or kill. Quantitative data (counts, rates, experiments) says what happened and how much. Qualitative data (interviews, observation) says why, but not how often. Each alone fails: a dashboard shows movement without cause, and interviews produce vivid stories without size. The loop exists because the two failures are complementary, so each method can be pointed at the other's blind spot. Social scientists formalised the pairing as mixed-methods research from the 1980s onward; product teams absorbed it through Eric Ries's build-measure-learn cycle (2011) and Teresa Torres's continuous discovery (2021).

The sentence Aneesh could repeat in a meeting: the metric tells us where to look, the interviews tell us what to guess, and the experiment tells us whether the guess was right and by how much.

3. How it works

Step 1 defines the movement precisely, with its denominator and window, and tests it against noise, as above. Step 2, which practitioners leave implicit, is choosing whom to ask. Ameeta invited 41 lapsed cohort-B customers; 8 agreed, 19.5%. Step 3 asks about recent specific behaviour ("walk me through your last lunch") and records which topics people raised unprompted. Step 4 checks each theme against behavioural data, since people misremember. Step 5, the other implicit step, converts the theme into a hypothesis with a predicted size and a decision rule written before any data arrives. Step 6 tests it. Step 7 returns to users, because a result without a reason restarts the problem. The loop is a cycle for a practical reason: the experiment's answer, whether yes or no, is itself a new metric movement that needs its own why. Teams that treat step 6 as the end have built an A/B testing habit, not a learning habit. Notice also that the quantitative and qualitative steps alternate: numbers choose the question, people suggest the answer, numbers judge it.

4. A worked example

Interviews ran on 3, 4, 7 and 8 September. Six of the eight, among them Anshul and Ajeet, raised lunch timing unprompted: the tiffin "came after my half hour was over". On Wednesday 9 September Abhay pulled arrival timestamps the delivery partner's app has recorded since launch. Aarti Hakani, head of kitchen operations, confirmed that dispatch routing changed on Monday 6 July. He defined a late-heavy starter as one with at least two of five trial lunches arriving after 1:00 pm, the end of the lunch window customers described. He had not cut the data this way before the interviews because the dashboard carried no delivery-time dimension; the interviews supplied the cut. Each rate below is renewed customers divided by starters in that cohort and segment, so the denominators are the starters, not the interviewees.

Cohort and segmentStartersRenewedRate

A, other5,4002,32243.0%
A, all (pooled)6,0002,52042.0%

The late-heavy share rose from 10.0% to 30.0%. Had B kept its own segment rates but A's mix, it would have renewed at 0.10 × 30.0 + 0.90 × 40.0 = 39.0%. Composition therefore explains 2.0 of the 5.0 points; the other 3.0 are lower rates inside each segment (0.10 × 3 + 0.90 × 3 = 3.0). This split is a standard decomposition: change the mix while holding rates fixed, and the remainder is the change in rates. Both parts add to the 5.0-point gap, as they must.

If lateness is the cause, a delivery-window feature that returns the late share to 10.0% should lift renewal by 2.0 points, 37.0% to 39.0%. Sizing uses a two-sided 5% test, 80% power and unpooled variances: each arm needs n = 7.85 × [p1(1 − p1) + p2(1 − p2)] ÷ (p2 − p1)², where 7.85 is (1.960 + 0.842)². For 37.0% against 40.0% that is 7.85 × 0.4731 ÷ 0.0009, or 4,126 per arm. Starts arrive at 1,550 a week (6,200 across four weeks), so total sample divided by 1,550 gives the weeks.

5. Nuances

Saturation is not a confidence interval.

By the sixth interview no new theme appeared, which means the list of themes was probably complete. It says nothing about how common any theme is. Six of eight is 75% in the sample, but the exact 95% interval for the underlying share runs from about 35% to 97%. Treat the six as suggestive: enough to name a hypothesis, nowhere near enough to size one. The renewal rate, measured on thousands, is the narrow interval in Figure 4; the interviews are the wide one, and the figure puts them on one axis so that the contrast in what each can claim is visible.

Prevalence among whom.

Ameeta spoke only to lapsed B customers who answered an invitation. No A customers were asked, and renewers were not asked. Eight of 41 agreeing may mean the aggrieved were over-represented. The cure is not more interviews of the same kind but a different frame, such as a handful of renewers, and the logs, which cover everyone.

A segment contrast is not an experiment.

Late-heavy customers renewed 10 points less, but late deliveries may cluster in outlying neighbourhoods where customers differ anyway. The 2.0-point prediction treats the contrast as causal, so it is an optimistic assumption, not a measurement. If the true lift is smaller, the test needs more people, which is why the design commits to the optimistic figure and no larger.

Behaviour outranks recall.

Of the six who raised timing, logs showed at least two late lunches for four. Two had at most one. One participant with at least two late lunches never mentioned timing. Interviews generate hypotheses; logs test whether a story matches what happened. A mismatch is not a lie: people remember a bad week as a bad month.

A theme present in both cohorts cannot explain a change.

Three of eight called the jump from ₹70 to ₹120 a lunch abrupt. That step existed for cohort A too, so it can explain why many never renew, not why more stopped in July. Qualitative themes earn their keep only when they differ between the periods being compared.

Explained share is computable.

Timing explains 2.0 of 5.0 points through mix. The remaining 3.0 have no interview theme attached yet, and the write-up should say so rather than letting the timing story absorb the whole gap. Computing the explained share keeps a satisfying narrative from claiming more than it earned.

What the loop cannot tell you.

It cannot size an effect from interviews, and a null result does not say whether the theme was wrong or the fix was weak. It also cannot reach customers who never trialled at all.

6. Across products and stages

SettingQuant armQual arm
ConsumerThousands per week; experiments feasibleEight to twelve users per round
B2BFew accounts; usage trends, rarely testsDominant; buyer and user differ
MarketplaceTwo sides; test interferenceInterview both sides

Early-stage companies lean on qualitative evidence because traffic cannot power tests. Large ones can test everything, which tempts them to skip the why and ship whichever variant won, without knowing what to try next. In every setting, the rule is the same: use the method that matches the sample available, and say which question each can answer.

7. Common mistakes

Reporting a count as a rate. A slide says "75% of users". The misunderstanding: saturation as precision. Cheapest diagnostic: write the exact interval beside the count; if it spans most of the scale, say so on the slide.

A hypothesis with no size. A test is planned for 3.0 points that the fix cannot plausibly deliver. Misunderstanding: that a theme implies a magnitude. Diagnostic: compute the lift from the segment table, then the power at that lift.

Finding the theme you already held. The winning explanation matches the loudest team's prior view. Misunderstanding: coding after hearing. Diagnostic: list candidate themes, in writing, before pulling logs, and see whether the logs could have contradicted any of them.

8. What good looks like

Within eleven days of the movement, a named owner holds a short document: the sized gap, eight interviews with the sampling frame stated, one hypothesis checked against logs, a predicted lift of 2.0 points, a test sized to detect it, and a decision rule fixed in advance. Nothing in it converts eight people into a percentage. It also names what is unexplained: 3.0 of the 5.0 points. A reader can tell at a glance which claims rest on thousands of customers and which on eight conversations.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

On Friday 11 September Aneesh chose the 2.0-point design. Enrolment would run twelve Mondays from 21 September to 7 December, 1,550 starts a week, 9,300 per arm after rounding up, which detects 1.99 points. The window feature was built 14 to 18 September. The rule: ship if the treatment renews above control with the 95% interval excluding zero; no mid-test stopping on a win. Concurrent control absorbs the early-November festive season that a before-and-after comparison would not. A second interview round, in both arms, waits for the 11 January readout. His reasoning: a 3.0-point test would have missed a real 2.0-point lift 54% of the time, and an ambiguous answer after five weeks is the costliest kind, because it looks like permission to argue again. Aarti would route kitchen capacity to the window slots meanwhile.

Learn next the power calculation itself, then interview technique. Two questions: what would you conclude if six of eight non-renewers had named price instead, and what test would you run? And if the test returns 38.0% against 37.0%, what do the interviews let you say about why?
exp40v2-exp.qual.quant.loop:
When the metric moves, do you know why?

The qualitative–quantitative feedback loop, as practised by people who have to defend the answer — near-expert depth.

1Two readouts, two months apart

On Thursday 5 March 2026, in a meeting room above Baner Road in Pune, Bhavisha Indorewala had the cleanest experimental result of her two years as Director of Product at Pravara Money. Her team had replaced the blank amount field in the first-deposit screen with a pre- filled suggestion of ₹500. Over the four weeks from Monday 2 February to Sunday 1 March the test ran on 36,800 newly verified users, 18,400 per arm. First-deposit rate went from 11.00 to 12.00 per cent: a one-point lift, three standard errors wide, the kind of result that ends a conversation.

Bharatsinh Indrodia, the staff data scientist who built the readout, had carried the guardrail row the January brief required. Mean first deposit had fallen from ₹1,840 to ₹1,505. Multiplied out, the treatment arm banked ₹4.01 lakh less than control from 184 more depositors. The lift was real and the product was worse. Nobody could say why, and the quarterly roadmap review was set for 2 April.

Two months later, on Thursday 7 May, Bhadresh Ijardar faced the opposite problem in Ahmedabad. Pinaak Systems sells warehouse-execution software and the rugged handhelds that run it, across 41 live customer sites. Release 9 reached 17 of them in the week of Monday 30 March. Over the four weeks that followed, picks per operator-hour at those sites rose from 116.2 to 124.6, while the 24 still on release 8 rose from 119.8 to 121.1. The difference of the differences was 7.1 picks per operator-hour — the largest productivity claim Pinaak had ever made, with renewal pricing for the 24 remaining sites due on 25 June.

Ijardar could not randomise: 41 customers is not a population and a warehouse cannot be half-upgraded. He had a staggered rollout, a number, and no account of where it came from. Both stood at the same place in the same loop, from opposite directions.

2The idea, and who disagrees about it

A qualitative–quantitative feedback loop is a standing arrangement with three obligations. A quantitative movement, defined in advance, triggers a qualitative inquiry. That inquiry's deliverable is not a conclusion but a mechanism stated as a countable claim. That claim is then re-measured on the quantitative instrument, ideally the one that raised the alarm. Drop the third and you have storytelling; drop the second, an unfalsifiable interview deck; drop the first, research that arrives after the decision.

The lineage is older than software. Campbell and Fiske's 1959 multitrait–multimethod matrix argued that a construct is credible only when methods that fail differently agree. Denzin generalised it to triangulation in 1970. Greene, Caracelli and Graham's 1989 taxonomy separated five reasons to mix methods — triangulation, complementarity, development, initiation and expansion — and that separation is still where practitioners talk past each other. Glaser and Strauss gave the field saturation in 1967; Guest, Bunce and Johnson put a number on it in 2006, finding twelve interviews exhausted new themes in a homogeneous sample. Nielsen and Landauer's 1993 detection model supplied the arithmetic of how much a small round can see; controlled online experimentation contributed the trigger.

Three schools now disagree, substantively rather than terminologically. The triangulation school will sign that convergence between independent methods raises credibility; it will not sign that a qualitative round establishes a magnitude. The development school — the mechanism school — will sign that the qualitative round's only legitimate output is a hypothesis with a pre-specified quantitative test; it will not sign that convergence is itself evidence, because two methods drawing on the same recruited users share a bias and converge on it. The complementarity school will sign that qualitative work exists to change the question rather than confirm the answer, and will not sign that a finding which cannot be instrumented does not count.

3Mechanics: six steps, two of them usually skipped

Expert practice begins before anyone is interviewed. Step one is a pre-committed trigger. Pravara's January experiment brief said that any arm shipping on first-deposit rate must also hold value per assigned user flat. Without that rule the March meeting is an argument about whether to look.

Step two is to decompose the movement arithmetically before talking to anyone. Value per assigned user is a rate times an amount, so its change splits exactly into three terms: the rate effect at the old amount, the amount effect at the old rate, and the interaction. They must sum to the whole, and they do.

Design: 18,400 per arm, an 11.00 per cent baseline, 80 per cent power and α = 0.05 two-sided give a minimum detectable effect of 0.93 pp, 8.46 per cent relative, computed with the unpooled variance at the alternative; the observed 1.00 pp clears it, but only just.

Step three is to sample on the decomposition rather than the product. Bhairvee Ishwarani, Pravara's researcher, did not recruit "recent users": between Monday 9 and Friday 20 March she interviewed eleven treatment-arm depositors, stratified by deposit size, each narrating the screen from memory before seeing it. Seven of the eleven raised the pre-filled ₹500 unprompted. Step four is to resist converting that into a rate: the exact Clopper–Pearson 95 per cent interval on seven of eleven runs from 30.8 to 89.1 per cent, and the normal approximation has no business there. Saturation is not a confidence interval.

Step five is what makes it a loop: turn the mechanism into a counting question the existing instrument can answer. If the pre-fill anchors people, deposits should pile up at exactly ₹500. They did: 1,104 of the 2,208 treatment deposits, 50.0 per cent, against 324 of the 2,024 control deposits, 16.0 per cent. That 34.0-point gap carries a standard error of 1.34 points — a z of 25.4. Eleven interviews could never have established 34 points; they established where to look, and an afternoon's query established the size.

Step six is to compute what the round could not have seen. Under Nielsen and Landauer's model, a problem present in a proportion L of users appears at least once in n sessions with probability 1 − (1 − L)n.

4Three conditions, stated so they can fail

The conditions are testable rather than rhetorical. First: the moved metric must decompose into parts that are separately observable. Pravara passes — rate and amount are both logged per user. Pinaak passes in principle — picks over hours, both counted — but the decomposition that mattered, whether a site had reslotted in the same week, was not in the data at all. Second: the mechanism, once named, must be instrumentable inside the decision window. Pravara passes; the ₹500 question was answerable from an existing store on 24 March, before the roadmap review. Pinaak fails for the wave-one question: Bhuvi Isarwal's site visits on 11–14 May produced the slotting hypothesis, the slot-map-version field shipped on Friday 15 May, and it says nothing of March or April because it did not exist then.

Third: there must be people whose behaviour changed and who can be reached. Both pass, but Pinaak's changed behaviour belongs to shift supervisors while the renewal is signed by a procurement head who has never held the handheld.

The loop is actively misleading when the movement is mechanical. A tracking release, a price change or a bot filter moves a metric for reasons no user can report, and users asked why supply a fluent, plausible, invented account. Rule out the mechanical explanation before spending a research round on a human one.

5Hard edges: platforms, regulation, hardware, models

On a two-sided marketplace the metric moves on one side for reasons living on the other: supply-side churn shows up first as a buyer-side conversion dip, and buyer interviews will produce an articulate account of a product problem that does not exist. The trigger on either side must dispatch research to both.

Regulated products constrain the qualitative half more than the quantitative. A flow governed by RBI conduct rules and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's consent requirements limits what may be recorded, who may be approached and which screens replayed. Ishwarani could not screen-record a live KYC step; the prototype she rebuilt it in is a different instrument and should be reported as one.

In hardware-plus-software, as at Pinaak, the mechanism is often physical — slotting, aisle congestion, a battery that dies at hour six — and telemetry built around the software never sees it. AI-native products invert the problem: the mechanism sits inside the model, the user genuinely cannot report it, and the qualitative round must run against outputs, as a labelled evaluation set, not against opinions.

At the organisational seam the loop breaks because research reports into design and experimentation into data, so no manager owns both halves. Mature companies say they have a unified insights function. What they mostly have is a weekly forum where an experiment owner must name a mechanism and a researcher a counting test, and the minutes record which was skipped.

6Eight things experts do that competent practitioners do not

They decompose before they interview. The tell is an interview guide written from a decomposition table rather than a dashboard. The obvious reading — talk to users, then look at the data — wastes the round, because without the decomposition nobody knows whom to recruit.

They treat saturation and precision as different currencies. The tell is someone saying "eleven interviews, so we know where to look" and refusing, in the same breath, to name a share of users. Seven of eleven supports a hypothesis, not a forecast.

They sample on the arm, not the product. Pravara interviewed treatment depositors only. The obvious reading — both arms, for balance — is wrong when the question is what the treatment did: control users cannot describe a screen they never saw.

They compute the direction of their recruitment bias rather than apologising for it. Pravara's eleven interviewees averaged ₹1,980 against the arm's ₹1,505, leaving the other 2,197 depositors at ₹1,502.62. The interviewed group over-indexed on large deposits by 31.6 per cent, so they are the depositors least likely to have been held at the ₹500 floor, and seven still named the pre-fill. Because the sample was stratified by deposit size, part of that 31.6 is a design artefact rather than self-selection — but either reading runs against the finding. Asserting that selection explains a gap without backing out the counterfactual is how people get the sign wrong.

They size a gap against its own standard error before calling it a finding. Pravara's day-7 return rate fell 1.6 points; on 2,024 and 2,208 depositors that carries a standard error of 1.51 points, a z of 1.06. The tell is a senior person saying "and retention dropped too" — which is how a noise reading becomes a narrative.

They check that a denominator moved before blaming it. Composition is the most over-used explanation in product analytics, and the tell is that nobody checked the base. If before and after sit over the same population it explains nothing, and the cause is an inserted funnel step or a definition quietly changed.

They check that the re-measurement instrument existed during the window. Pinaak's slot-map field began on 15 May; splitting March or April by it would apply a category before it existed. The legitimate move is post-stratification: group the 24 wave-two sites by what the field recorded in their own upgrade week, then read their earlier figures under it.

They distrust the round that agrees with them. An interview confirming the hypothesis is research's cheapest output and its most dangerous, because demand characteristics are strongest when the interviewer already knows the answer. The tell is a round with no surprises in it.

7How the loop differs by product and by stage

In consumer products the quantitative half is cheap and the qualitative half is the bottleneck: Pravara runs a test weekly and interviews eleven people a fortnight. In B2B and enterprise the ratio inverts. Pinaak can get two hours with any customer it likes and cannot get power from 41 sites; its loop runs on quasi-experiments and the discipline of saying which comparison group stands in for randomisation. On marketplaces it must be two-sided by construction; in hardware, observational, because the mechanism is in the building.

For AI products the qualitative half becomes an evaluation set: graded outputs, with the rubric as the interview guide. Here the difference is categorical rather than one of degree. Elsewhere it is mostly cost and cadence that change, though B2B's inverted ratio and Pinaak's quasi- experimental loop reach the logic too.

Stage changes the trigger, not the loop. A seed-stage team has no metric stable enough to trigger anything and should run the loop in reverse: interview first, instrument second. A growth-stage team has traffic and no research capacity, and ships significant results it cannot explain. A mature company has both and fails at the seam.

8Three worked cases, one of them a failure

Pravara, and the anchor. Everything above: nineteen days from readout to mechanism to confirmation, one research round and one query, and a decisive number from neither half alone.

Pinaak, and the confound. Isarwal visited four wave-one sites on 11–14 May and spoke to eight shift supervisors. Six of the eight said what had changed their week was not the software but a slotting reorganisation their own operations team ran alongside the upgrade; three of the four sites had done one. That is the whole qualitative yield — enough to put the 7.1 in doubt, nowhere near enough to replace it.

Table 2. Pinaak Systems, picks per operator-hour, unweighted site means. Wave one (17 sites) upgraded 30 March – 3 April, wave two (24) 18 – 22 May.

Sub-rows are site-count weighted into the row above: (15 × 120.5 + 9 × 122.1) / 24 = 121.10 and (15 × 123.8 + 9 × 130.7) / 24 = 126.3875. 126.39 is 126.3875 rounded for display; Figure 3 plots the exact value. The split is by what the slot-map-version field recorded during each site's own May upgrade week — post-stratification, not retrospective coding. P1 cannot be split; no site-level dispersion is recorded.

Over P2→P3, against wave one's own +1.2 drift, the 15 sites that changed only the software gained +2.1 and the 9 that also reslotted gained +7.4; weighted 15:9, +4.09. Read the 5.3 between them as a slotting premium per reslotted site, and wave one's effect becomes 2.1 + 5.3s for a reslotted share s. Ijardar's claim was that slotting was most of the 7.1, which needs 5.3s above 3.55, so s above 0.670 — at least 12 of the 17 sites. The visits found three of four: at s = 0.75 slotting carries 3.98, which is 56 per cent of the 7.1, and that is most. The thin evidence he has points his way. It cannot carry him there: the exact 95 per cent interval on three of four runs from 19.4 to 99.4 per cent, wide enough to cover both the 12 of 17 his claim needs and the 16 of 17 that s = 0.943 — slotting explaining all of it — would need. At wave two's own 9 in 24 the model predicts 4.09 and leaves 3.01 points, 42.4 per cent, unexplained.

Every figure there is a point estimate on unweighted means of 15 and 9 sites. Pinaak records no site-level dispersion, so none can be sized against its own noise; and because each operations team chose for itself whether to reslot, the groups are self-selected rather than assigned. The waves are different seasons and sites besides. What Pinaak can defend is a range, +2.1 to +7.4 — which still contains the 7.1 it started with.

Prarambh AI, and the failure. Bhadrayu Inaniya's document-extraction copilot for accounting firms shipped a model upgrade on Tuesday 14 July 2026. Suggestion accept rate rose from 61.0 to 68.0 per cent, nine interviews the following week confirmed the tool felt more accurate, and the release was called a success. The same commit had raised the confidence threshold from 0.65 to 0.80, so suggestions per document fell from 24.0 to 18.6 and accepted extractions per document from 14.64 to 12.648 — a 13.6 per cent decline in the work the product did, while its headline metric rose seven points. The arm held two changes and was read as one, and the interviews confirmed the error because "does it feel more accurate?" is a question the threshold change guarantees a yes to.

The recovery began when a customer complained about coverage on 1 September. The headline metric became accepted extractions per document; the protocol moved from opinion to observed work, users watched completing real filings between 7 and 18 September with no release mentioned; and the threshold was retuned to 0.72 on 28 September. Over the fortnight to 11 October the product showed 22.4 suggestions per document at a 67.0 per cent accept rate — 15.008 accepted per document, 2.5 per cent above its pre-upgrade level. Eleven weeks from upgrade to fix, for two and a half per cent.

9Failure modes and their early warnings

Research arriving after the decision. Early sign: a quarterly research calendar against weekly readouts. Diagnostic: the median lag between a readout and the first interview it caused. Caught late, you ship on the wrong mechanism and find out at the renewal.

The confirming round. Early sign: no interview last quarter changed anyone's mind. Diagnostic: name the last finding that contradicted the sponsoring team. Prarambh paid eleven weeks and a customer complaint.

Small-n laundering. Early sign: a deck in which "6 of 8" has become "75 per cent of users" between the appendix and the summary slide. Diagnostic: ask for the denominator and when it was measured. Cost: a roadmap sized on a number with a sixty-point interval.

Mechanism without re-measurement. Early sign: well-written insight documents and no follow-up queries. Diagnostic: for the last three insights, what query tested each? Cost: folklore that cannot be falsified.

Instrumenting after the fact. Early sign: an analyst saying "we can backfill that". Diagnostic: when was the field created, and what is the store's retention? Pravara's deposit-event store keeps 90 days, so the 24 March pull reached back to 24 December 2025 — covering February comfortably, and far too late for the November 2025 round that produced the idea. Cost: the question goes unanswerable for a quarter.

10Where experts genuinely disagree

That the qualitative round must always end in a number. Steelman: an organisation that does not re-measure cannot tell a good researcher from a persuasive one, and a counting test is the only defence against folklore. Evidence: the Prarambh failure. It fails if the most valuable findings are systematically the least countable — which is what the complementarity school claims.

That convergence between methods is evidence. Steelman: Campbell and Fiske's argument is sound where the methods fail differently, and two methods agreeing is the strongest signal most teams will ever get. It fails wherever both draw on the same selected population, which in product work they almost always do: the users who answer a survey are the users who accept an interview.

That you should interview before you experiment, always. Steelman: an experiment tests a hypothesis, and a hypothesis generated from a dashboard is a hypothesis about a dashboard. Evidence: the Pravara pre-fill came from a November 2025 round, not from analysis. It fails when a wrong experiment is cheaper than the research — which, for a mature consumer product with abundant traffic, it sometimes is.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in three visible ways. They ask "what would have to be true" before "what do we think", so the interview guide follows the decomposition. They state intervals and denominators unprompted, including for their own qualitative counts, and will not let a count of eleven become a percentage. And they close loops in public: their artefact is not an insight document but a note saying what was believed, what was measured afterwards, and which was wrong. Someone who has merely studied the topic can define triangulation and will still ship on a confirming round.

12What they decided

Indorewala neither shipped the pre-fill nor killed it. She shipped a three-option chooser with no default, reasoning that the 34-point pile-up at ₹500 was a design defect, not an argument against prompting. The ₹335 drop needed no confirming: at a within-arm standard deviation of ₹2,400 it stood 4.5 standard errors clear on the arms she had. What she declined was the test that the chooser lands within ₹92 of control — five per cent of the control's ₹1,840 — which at 80 per cent power and α = 0.05 needs 10,683 depositors per arm, 97,118 assigned users per arm at an 11.00 per cent deposit rate, or roughly twenty-one weeks of traffic. Ijardar went to the 25 June renewal with a range, +2.1 to +7.4 picks per operator-hour, and a commitment to report the clean figure in December. Ishwarani argues that forcing every finding through a counting test will cost Pravara the findings that matter most; Indrodia holds the opposite, and neither has conceded.

  1. Pinaak's wave-two comparison group is 17 sites already running the new release. What does that assume about their post-upgrade drift, and which direction would a violation push the +2.1?
  2. Pravara's interviewees deposited 31.6 per cent more than their arm's mean. Construct the case that this weakens the anchoring finding rather than strengthening it.
  3. Prarambh's loop ran its full ritual — trigger, interviews, decision — and produced the wrong answer. Which of the three obligations in section 2 would you say it actually met, and what would have caught the error in July?

13Going deeper

  • A/B testing fundamentals — supplies the trigger; without a clean "what", the loop has nothing to explain.
  • Interview fundamentals — the mechanism half; narration-before-recognition made Pravara's round work.
  • Writing an experiment hypothesis — one that names a mechanism is already half a research plan.
  • Significance, power, sample size, peeking — when a gap is a finding, and when 97,118 users per arm is the honest answer.
  • When you can't A/B test — Pinaak's situation: staggered rollouts and difference-in-differences.
  • Experimentation culture — decides whether a confirming round is rewarded or questioned.
  • Feature flags and flighting — separates the two changes Prarambh shipped in one commit.
  • Choosing experiment metrics — accept rate versus accepted extractions per document is the Prarambh case in one choice.
case40v1-exp.qual.quant.loop:
Koravi Technologies: The Night the Day-180 Table Arrived

An Indian School of Business teaching case. Figures are those held by the company on 8 November 2026.

1. Sunday night, Bengaluru

The Deepavali break had emptied the fifth floor of Koravi Technologies' office off Bannerghatta Road, and Thejaswi Damodaran had the long table to herself. Two printouts lay on it, both from her own analytics team, both arithmetically correct, and together saying nothing she could carry into a board room.

The first was five months old: the readout for E-412, which found that a daily savings streak raised thirty-day activation from 9.60 per cent of installs to 11.28 per cent, a gain of 1.68 points on an interval nowhere near zero (Exhibit 1). Koravi shipped it to every new install on Thursday 2 July. The second had been pulled that morning, the day after the experiment cohort first had a complete one-hundred-and-eighty-day window: of the users who activated under the streak, 52.0 per cent were still saving in the sixth month against 60.0 per cent in control (Exhibit 3).

On Friday 13 November she had to explain both to a board that had funded the first and never seen the second. On Monday morning she had to tell her team what she had decided — about the streak, about the Dubai contract waiting on it, and about the one researcher whose twenty-six interviews were the nearest thing anybody had to an account of why either number was what it was.

2. Koravi Technologies, 2019 to 2026

Damodaran and Trinayan Dharmadasan founded Koravi in Bengaluru in June 2019 to sell digital gold from ten rupees upward. In August 2020 they added the product that became the company: Koravi Daily, a UPI autopay mandate sweeping ten to five hundred rupees from a bank account every day into a wrapper of digital gold and a recurring deposit with a partner bank. By October 2026 Koravi had 2.14 crore registered users, 41.6 lakh of them transacting in the month, and, at 30 September, ₹1,240 crore of customer savings balances (Exhibit 6).

The decision that constrains November 2026 was taken in March 2022, when Dharmadasan put Koravi's own app and its white-label tenants on one shared event schema and one assignment service. It saved an estimated ₹4.40 crore of build and carried two consequences nobody wrote down. The first was contractual: that month Koravi signed a five-year platform agreement with Tharavad Remit LLC, a Dubai exchange house serving remitters to Kerala and coastal Karnataka, under which any material change to the India onboarding and mandate flow must be mirrored into the Tharavad tenant within ninety days or a variation fee falls due. The second was instrumental: the 2022 schema recorded every event a user performed and nothing about why. A reason-code column was added in November 2025 and the India client was never wired to populate it.

3. The industry

The rails are UPI, which means NPCI's autopay framework and the RBI e-mandate rules: a recurring debit needs a registered mandate, and the customer must receive a pre-debit notification at least twenty-four hours before each debit. That notification is not optional and cannot be suppressed. Koravi competes with Jar and Gullak on micro-gold, with Groww and Zerodha for the user who graduates to funds and equities, and with PhonePe, Google Pay, Paytm and Amazon Pay, any of which can put a savings tile in front of more users than Koravi will reach directly, and bundles from Jio Finance and Tata Neu have worsened channel economics each year.

Digital gold is not a regulated security, and SEBI has told registered investment advisers not to deal in it. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act governs what Koravi may collect and keep, which bears on research directly. Gold demand is seasonal in a way the metrics inherit — Akshaya Tritiya, in the third week of April 2026, sat inside E-412's enrolment window, and Onam and Ganesh Chaturthi inside the August and September cohorts of Exhibit 2. Overseas exposure runs through Tharavad in Dubai and four NRI partner conversations in the United States.

4. What was believed, and what is now on the table

Exhibit 5 sets the sequence out to scale.

14 April to 11 May 2026. E-412 enrolled 4,20,000 new installs over twenty-eight days, 2,10,000 to each arm, randomised at install. Treatment saw a streak counter, a nine-o'clock reminder, and a streak that reset to zero when a day's debit failed or was skipped. The pre-registered primary metric was thirty-day activation: seven or more successful debits within thirty days. No other metric was registered.

18 June 2026. Tapesh Derebail's team in Toronto published the readout (Exhibit 1). Activation per install rose 9.60 to 11.28 per cent. The belief recorded in the readout's first line was that the streak made daily saving habitual.

2 July to 5 August 2026. The streak went to 100 per cent of new installs in India, and was not applied to users who already held a mandate; by 7 November, 8.37 lakh had registered one through it. On 5 August product shipped a weekly mandate — one larger debit instead of seven small — for users asking to reduce debit frequency. It post-dates enrolment and the day-30 window.

21 September to 16 October 2026. Thanmai Devassery, Koravi's only researcher, ran twenty-six depth interviews in Malayalam, Kannada, Hindi and Tamil. Her memo of 19 October reported fourteen participants describing the nine-o'clock reminder as a warning that money was about to leave their account (Exhibit 4). In March she had asked for an interview arm inside E-412 and had not got one.

8 November 2026. Derebail's day-180 table (Exhibit 3) puts retention among activated users at 60.0 per cent in control and 52.0 in treatment. Per install, the same table puts treatment at 5.87 per cent against control's 5.76, a difference of 0.11 points on a 95 per cent interval from −0.04 to +0.25. Both readings come from the same 4,20,000 users.

5. The people

Seven people will be in the room or on the call on Monday; Figure 1 shows the clock they share.

Thejaswi Damodaran, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Decides Monday, defends it Friday to a board that approved a plan to reach EBITDA breakeven in the quarter to 31 March 2028 and has seen activation every month since July. She is not saying that she refused Devassery's March request for an interview arm to protect the enrolment window.

Trinayan Dharmadasan, co-founder and chief technology officer, Pune, nine platform engineers. Position: the schema cannot be split per tenant in the time available. The 2022 decision is his, as is the NPCI update. He is not saying that it needs twelve of the nineteen engineer-weeks booked against it.

Tapesh Derebail, head of data science, Toronto. Position: E-412 is a clean randomised result and the day-180 split is conditioned on activation, a post-randomisation variable. The platform is his and he has six open roles. He is not saying that he cut the weekly-mandate line from the draft board pack on 8 November.

Thanmai Devassery, lead user researcher, Bengaluru, hired July 2025 and still the only one. Position: the mechanism is mandate anxiety, the reminder read against the RBI notification rather than as encouragement. Those interviews are her year's output. She is not saying that she sent a three-researcher job description to a recruiter on 2 November.

Turvika Dasappan, design director, Berlin. Position: withdraw the streak, because a reward that can be taken away is a penalty in a reward's clothes. She presented the flow in September. She is not saying that she walked Tharavad's design team through a streak-free flow on 23 October.

Tarsem Dhareshwar, customer success lead, Singapore, owner of the white-label tenants. Position: mirror the India flow into Tharavad before 27 December; his variable pay turns on the ₹7.20 crore renewal. He is not saying that Tharavad has signalled it will seek a 15 per cent fee reduction on 1 April 2027 whatever Koravi ships.

Torsha Dugganna, head of growth for the NRI corridor, New Jersey. Position: activation is the metric four partner conversations are priced on, and her pipeline closes in the March quarter. She is not saying that two of the four term sheets name the Tharavad integration as reference.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“Fourteen of twenty-six told me the nine-o'clock message is a warning that money is about to leave the account. I cannot tell you what fraction of the users on this flow that is. Nine of my twenty-six came from a support list, and six of those nine are in the fourteen.”

Thanmai Devassery, research memo, Bengaluru, 19 October 2026

“E-412 randomised 4,20,000 installs and balanced on nine covariates. The day-180 split is conditioned on activation, which happens after randomisation. Most of that eight points is composition, not harm. We are overturning a 1.68-point result on twenty-six conversations.”

Tapesh Derebail, Slack #exp-platform, Toronto, 8 November 2026, 09:14 EST — 19:44 IST

“The reason-code column has been in the schema since November 2025, populated on 3.1 per cent of sessions because nobody wired the India client to send it. Splitting it per tenant is fourteen engineer-weeks and I have eight.”

Trinayan Dharmadasan, email to Damodaran, Pune, 5 November 2026

“We built a reward that can be taken away. The RBI notification arrives a day before every debit, so the user gets two messages about money leaving and one of them is ours.”

Turvika Dasappan, design review, Berlin, 4 November 2026, 07:40 CET — 12:10 IST

“Tharavad's window shuts on 27 December and our last release before the freeze is 27 November. Without the mirror I go into a ₹7.20 crore renewal without the thing I promised them.”

Tarsem Dhareshwar, tenant call, Singapore, 6 November 2026, 16:20 SGT — 13:50 IST

“The board bought activation. I sold activation to four partners in the corridor. Nobody in those rooms asked me about day one hundred and eighty.”

Torsha Dugganna, growth call, New Jersey, 6 November 2026, 08:05 EST — 18:35 IST

8. The options as Damodaran sees them

She wrote four lines on the back of the day-180 table. Not one of them takes the streak away from the 8.37 lakh users who registered a mandate under it, and no Tharavad user has been interviewed.

A. Hold and mirror. Keep the streak at 100 per cent in India, mirror it into the Tharavad tenant in the 27 November release, and take Exhibits 1 and 3 to the board with the day-180 rows attached. Cost: six of the eight uncommitted engineer-weeks. Leaves the reason-code column unwired.

B. Withdraw for new installs. Remove the streak counter and the nine-o'clock reminder from installs after 16 November, leaving existing users untouched because no migration path is built. Cost: two engineer-weeks. Forgoes the mirror and returns the extension question to Tharavad.

C. Run it again. Register E-507 for 5 January to 1 February 2027 with day-180 as a primary metric and a consented interview arm of sixty users recruited at enrolment. Day 180 for the last enrollee closes 31 July 2027. Cost: eleven engineer-weeks, which the freeze pushes into January, plus ₹62 lakh of panel and moderation.

D. Build the loop. Wire the reason-code column into the India client, split the event schema per tenant, and fund research at ₹2.76 crore a year. Cost: fourteen engineer-weeks against the eight uncommitted.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets on Friday 13 November and the pack closes on Wednesday. The release freeze runs from Monday 30 November to 31 December, so the last slot before Tharavad's extension expires on 27 December is Friday 27 November. Of the twenty-seven engineer-weeks the Pune team has between 9 and 27 November, nineteen are booked against the NPCI autopay update, which must be built before the freeze and certified to NPCI by 15 December; eight remain. The pre-debit notification is mandatory, so no option takes a daily mandate below one money-is-leaving message a day. Interview recordings are consented for research for ninety days, so quoting them in a board pack needs re-consent or de-identification. Koravi holds ₹268 crore of cash against FY26 EBITDA of −₹38 crore.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 establish, and over what population and window? State the denominator at every step.
  2. Exhibits 1 and 3 describe the same two arms. Using only the figures printed in them, and assuming the users who would have activated in either arm retained at the control rate, what retention rate must the additional treatment activators show for the eight-point conditional gap to be composition alone? What else could produce that gap?
  3. Exhibit 2 shows day-30 activation per install rising from 10.4 per cent in June to 11.9 in September. List everything other than the streak that changed across those months, and say which of them Exhibit 2 lets you rule out.
  4. Exhibit 4 reports counts and no percentages. What would you need to know about the twenty-six before attaching any proportion to the fourteen who read the reminder as a debit warning, and what would you have specified at recruitment?
  5. Devassery's memo and Derebail's day-180 pull both came months after the flow shipped. At what point in E-412's life could a why have been collected that both would have accepted, what would it have cost in Exhibit 6's units, and what would it have delayed?
  6. It is Monday 9 November. Damodaran has four days before the board and eight engineer-weeks before the freeze. What does she do that morning, in what order and with whom — and what does she say on Friday to a board shown a metric 1.68 points up and never shown Exhibit 3?

It was past eleven. Dasappan's message from Berlin was still open on the laptop, Derebail's under it, and under that Devassery's memo with its fourteen and its twenty-six and its refusal to turn either into a percentage. Damodaran pulled the day-180 table back and looked at the two bottom rows: 52.0 against 60.0, and 5.87 against 5.76. Below them were 8.37 lakh people for whom twenty-six had spoken. She turned the sheet over, wrote what did we think we were measuring, and sat until the guard came to ask whether she wanted the lights left on.

A/B Testing Fundamentals

What can an A/B test actually claim, and what can it not?

1. Fourteen days, one number

On Thursday 20 August 2026, Ivanshi Porwal, head of product at Aranyak Fresh, a Bengaluru grocery-delivery app competing with Blinkit and Zepto, had one page of results to defend. For fourteen days, a free-delivery progress bar on the cart screen, telling a shopper how many rupees remained to reach the ₹299 free-delivery line, had been shown to a randomly chosen eighth of the users who opened a cart for the first time during the test, while another eighth saw the old screen. Inderveer Pansari, the analyst, reported that 19.00 per cent of the shoppers who saw the bar ordered within 24 hours of that first cart opening, against 18.00 per cent of those who did not.

Idrees Pithadia, who ran category finance, asked the question the page had to answer: was that one point real, or luck? His own estimate, an assumption and not a measurement, was that the bar's extra delivery subsidy cost ₹0.15 per exposed user and each extra order earned ₹49 of contribution, which puts break-even at about 0.3 points of conversion (₹0.15 ÷ ₹49). Across the 24,000 first-time cart openers a day, a no-effect bar would burn ₹3,600 daily, ₹1.08 lakh a month. A true one-point effect, left unshipped, forfeited ₹8,160 a day net, ₹2.45 lakh a month.

Ivanshi knew that neither error could be avoided by confidence of tone. The figure could be trusted only to the extent that she could say what the method behind it licensed her to claim.

2. The idea

An A/B test is a controlled experiment in which units, here users, are assigned at random to see version A (the control, the current experience) or version B (the treatment, the change), and one pre-chosen outcome is then compared across the two groups. Randomisation is the invention. Without it, shoppers who happened to see the bar might be more engaged to begin with, and any gap would mix the bar's effect with that difference. The problem the method was invented to solve is separating cause from coincidence.

The method came from agriculture. Ronald Fisher, working at the Rothamsted Experimental Station in the 1920s, randomised which plots received which fertiliser so that soil differences could not masquerade as fertiliser effects, and set the logic out in The Design of Experiments (1935). Medicine adopted it in trials such as the 1948 streptomycin study, and web companies, Google among them around 2000, discovered that software could run thousands of such trials cheaply.

The sentence Ivanshi could repeat in a meeting: because we flipped the coin, the only systematic difference between these two groups is the bar, so a gap bigger than chance can produce is the bar's doing.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics are a chain, and the links practitioners leave implicit are the ones that break. First, the unit and eligibility are fixed: the unit is the user, eligible once, at the first cart opening of the test period. Second, the hypothesis and the decision rule are written down before launch. Inderveer's note, signed on 30 July, said the bar would ship only if the 95 per cent confidence interval (the range of lifts the data cannot rule out, defined properly in section 4) lay wholly above 0.3 points, Idrees's break-even.

Third comes assignment. The app hashes each user ID together with the experiment's name (a "salt", so that this test's split is independent of every other test's) into one of 1,000 buckets: buckets 0 to 124 see control, 125 to 249 see the bar, the rest are untouched. That is 12.5 per cent of users in each arm, a quarter in total. Fourth, exposure is logged at the moment the cart screen renders, so analysis can distinguish assigned from shown.

Fifth, the test runs for whole weeks, because shoppers behave differently on Sundays than on Tuesdays and a partial week would over-weight some days. Because the outcome window is 24 hours, orders were counted through Monday 17 August, so that the last enrolled users had their full day. Sixth, before looking at outcomes, the team checks that the arms are the size randomisation promised. Seventh, everyone is analysed in the arm to which they were assigned, whether or not they scrolled to the bar. Eighth, the pre-written rule is applied, not renegotiated.

4. A worked example

Inderveer sized the test first. Needing to detect a lift from 18.00 to 19.00 per cent with a 5 per cent false-alarm rate (two-sided) and 80 per cent power, the chance of detecting a true lift of that size, she used n = (zα/2 + zβ)² × [p₁(1−p₁) + p₂(1−p₂)] ÷ (p₂−p₁)², per arm.

Table 1. Design inputs and the sample size they determine

The 6,000 a day is the quarter of 24,000 first-time cart openers. The smallest lift this size can reliably detect, the minimum detectable effect (MDE), is 0.75 points: 23,665 users per arm would suffice for one point, and 42,000 buy a finer instrument. Plan, power and MDE are one relationship stated three ways, which is why a team that fixes the first two has fixed the third. Actual assignment was 41,880 control and 42,120 treatment.

Pooled rate = 15,541 ÷ 84,000, not a mean of the two rates. Difference: +1.00 pt.

The standard error, the typical size of chance fluctuation in the gap, is √(0.18×0.82÷41,880 + 0.19×0.81÷42,120) = √(3.524×10⁻⁶ + 3.654×10⁻⁶) = 0.00268, or 0.268 points. The gap is 3.73 standard errors from zero, a two-sided p-value of 0.00019, and the 95 per cent interval is 1.00 ± 1.96 × 0.268, which is +0.48 to +1.53 points. The lower end clears Idrees's 0.3, so the pre-written rule says ship. The interval does not say the true lift has a 95 per cent chance of lying in it; it says the procedure, repeated, would capture the true lift 95 times in 100.

Second pass. Change one input, as a counterfactual: suppose Idrees's break-even had been a half-point lift, not 0.3. Then p₂ = 18.5 per cent, the variance term is 0.1476 + 0.150775 = 0.298375, and n = 7.8489 × 0.298375 ÷ 0.005² = 93,677 per arm, 187,354 users, or 31.2 days at 6,000 a day: five whole weeks, not two. Halving the target roughly quadruples the cost, because n varies with the inverse square of the lift. Figure 5 plots that curve, with this test's 42,000 as the dashed line.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

It speaks of averages, not people

Randomisation licenses a claim about the average effect across the eligible population. The one-point lift does not say that every shopper responds; perhaps a fifth respond strongly and the rest not at all. Claims about who is helped need pre-planned subgroup analysis, and a test sized for the whole population is usually too small to find them.

The p-value is not the chance the bar works

A p-value of 0.00019 means that if the bar did nothing, a gap this large would appear about 19 times in 100,000 experiments. It does not mean there is a 99.98 per cent chance the bar works, and it says nothing about size; the interval does that.

Not significant is not no effect

Had the true lift been 0.5 points, this test, with standard error 0.267, would have detected it only 47 per cent of the time. A null result from an underpowered test is silence, not evidence of absence; report the interval.

Assignment unit and analysis unit must match

Randomising users but counting carts, orders or sessions treats correlated observations as independent and makes the standard error too small. Whatever was randomised is what you count, or you correct for clustering.

A lopsided split is a smoke alarm

The assignment, 41,880 against 42,120, deviates from 42,000 each by 120. The check (a chi-square test of observed against promised counts) gives 0.69, p = 0.41: unremarkable. A very small p there signals a sample ratio mismatch, a pipeline fault that invalidates the comparison.

The result is true for those two weeks

Novelty can inflate early effects, and August shoppers are not festive-season shoppers. The test claims what happened to this population in this fortnight; extending it is a judgement, not a result.

The metric defines the question

Order rate was chosen over revenue per user because the latter is noisier. Revenue per exposed user averages ₹74 (18 per cent × ₹411 average order). Assuming a standard deviation of ₹190 per user (an assumption from prior data), 42,000 users per arm detect about ₹3.67 on that ₹74, roughly 5 per cent, against 4.2 per cent for conversion. A vanity metric, such as bar impressions, would "win" while saying nothing about orders.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

Aranyak's setting, a consumer app with tens of thousands of daily users, is the friendly case: independent individuals, fast outcomes, cheap samples. The table shows where that assumption weakens.

Table 3. How the same method bends
SettingPressure on the methodUsual response
ConsumerNovelty, seasonalityWhole weeks; later holdout
B2BFew accounts, users clusteredRandomise accounts; accept large MDE
MarketplaceOne side's treatment moves the other's outcomesRandomise by city or time block

Scale matters as much as setting. An early-stage company with 500 weekly buyers cannot detect a lift smaller than roughly 10.5 points on an 18 per cent base, and is often better served by interviews. A large company can detect 0.1 points, given 2.3 million users per arm, but runs hundreds of simultaneous tests whose interactions need managing.

7. Common mistakes

Table 4. Four failures, their symptoms and cheap checks
MistakeSymptom outsideMisunderstandingCheapest check
Stopping when it turns significantWins shrink after launchDaily looks each carry a false-alarm chanceFix the end date in advance
Analysing only those who saw the changeLift implausibly largeViewers are self-selectedCount by assignment
Ignoring the splitArms differ by more than chanceRandomisation is assumed, not verifiedChi-square on arm sizes
Reading "not significant" as "no effect"Good ideas buriedPower is never computedReport the MDE and interval

The first is the most common because it feels like diligence. Repeated looks at a test with no fixed end give chance many chances to cross the line, which later modules treat in full.

8. What good looks like

Good handling of Ivanshi's decision resembles the one above: a signed plan on 30 July stating metric, MDE and break-even before a single user was assigned; a split check before outcomes; a fixed fortnight; and a report leading with the interval, +0.48 to +1.53 points, rather than with "19 versus 18". The report also names what it does not claim: that the lift will hold in November, or that shoppers' basket sizes are unchanged. The decision follows from a rule written when no one knew the answer.

9. Closing

Ivanshi approved a staged rollout: ship to all users from Monday 24 August, but keep 5 per cent of users on the old screen as a holdout, so that the lift could be re-measured in the festive season. Her reasoning was that the interval's lower bound, 0.48 points, still left roughly ₹2,000 a day net after subsidy, while the holdout converted an extrapolation into a measurement. Next to learn is significance, power and peeking, which formalise sections 4 and 7; then long-term holdouts, which test whether an effect survives.

For you to sit with. First: which decision at your own company is currently justified by a before-and-after comparison, and what would randomising it require? Second: if Ivanshi's interval had run from −0.2 to +2.2 points, what would you want to know before choosing between shipping and extending the test?
