Saksham Commerce Technologies: Twenty-One Days in October

A checkout experiment ran clean, finished on time, and left its sponsor with two defensible readings of the same six lakh sessions.

1. Sunday night, Indiranagar

The rain over Bengaluru had thinned to nothing by nine on the evening of Sunday, 22 November 2026, and Dhaarna Kothari had the flat to herself. Four printouts lay on the dining table in the order she had put them down: a power memo dated 3 September, a week-by-week completion table, a one-page note on order value, and a thirteen-day read from the holdback she had argued for. At half past nine she would open a board call and say what Saksham should do with Checkout v4.

She had sponsored v4 in February. It replaced a four-screen checkout with one pane: saved address at the top, a UPI intent button under it, everything else behind a chevron. The October test had been registered in advance, randomised, left alone three weeks and analysed once. It had returned a result her chief executive called obvious and her data scientist called unanswerable, from the same table.

A message from Dubai had sat unanswered on her phone since Thursday. She had not replied because the honest answer ran to three paragraphs.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2022

Saksham was founded in Bengaluru in 2017 by Dharmil Khetawat, after six years building payment integrations for garment exporters in Tiruppur. The product is an orchestration layer in front of a merchant's own store: it renders the checkout, routes transactions across acquirers, retries failures, and reconciles. By November 2026 it was live on 9,400 storefronts, mostly Indian direct-to-consumer brands doing forty to four hundred orders a day, plus the Gulf estate of Salwa Markets Group in Dubai. Revenue for the year to 31 March 2026 was ₹142 crore, of which ₹96.4 crore was checkout fees on the Indian estate.

In March 2022 the company made a decision that governs everything on Dhaarna's table. Three large merchants, within a fortnight, refused to let Saksham hold any identifier that would recognise the same shopper on two brands' storefronts. Saksham agreed, wrote the refusal into its standard contract, and — a personal data protection Bill then before Parliament — cut device-level records to a thirty-day purge. It kept one shared checkout bundle, with variants set by storefront configuration rather than per shopper.

3. The industry

Indian checkout economics turn on a rule Saksham does not control: the merchant discount rate on UPI is zero. NPCI's rails carry most of Saksham's order volume and earn nothing beyond a flat fee, while cards and netbanking, governed by the Reserve Bank's tokenisation and additional-factor rules, carry a value-based slice. A UPI order therefore earns Saksham the flat fee and nothing else.

The competitive set is crowded: Razorpay, Cashfree, PayU, Juspay and the checkout stacks inside PhonePe and Paytm sell against Saksham, while Shiprocket and the ONDC network pull smaller sellers toward bundled fulfilment. Saksham's merchants compete with Flipkart, Amazon and Meesho on delivery promise and with Zepto and Blinkit on immediacy.

Abroad the exposure is concentrated. Salwa Markets Group runs 61 stores and a grocery app across the UAE and Oman, is integrating the Aani scheme and the Jaywan card, and sits under the UAE's own data law, not the DPDP Act.

4. What happened, and what was believed at the time

14 July 2026. The v4 rollout plan assumed Salwa's 61 storefronts would be inside the test. Since: on 2 October legal confirmed that clause 7.4 requires thirty days' written notice of any checkout change, putting Salwa outside the October window.

3 September 2026. Devanshika Karnani's power memo sized the test at 16,602 sessions per arm against a 1.50 pp minimum detectable effect, treating sessions as independent. Since: her variance decomposition of 6 November put the intra-storefront correlation at 0.025, a design effect of 63.475.

28 September 2026. Checkout completion rate was registered as the single primary metric, with order value a guardrail to be reviewed only if completion moved. Since: the order-value note of 9 November put GMV per checkout session at −5.87 per cent.

9 October 2026. The assignment script drew 120 storefronts into each arm from the 2,180 eligible and logged the draw as balanced. Since: the pre-period table of 12 November showed treatment storefronts running 5 per cent more sessions a day, and 0.40 pp lower completion, before the test began.

18 October 2026. At the end of day seven the dashboard showed a 4.00 pp gap, and Dharmil Khetawat asked twice why the test was still running. Since: weeks two and three came in at 1.50 pp and 1.00 pp, and the test ended on 1 November as registered.

The 48 storefronts held back on 3 November came from the October control arm. The 192 on v4 from that date are the 120 that had carried it since 12 October and the 72 controls switched over on 3 November.

5. The people

Dhaarna Kothari, Senior Director, Product, Bengaluru. Holds that the test answered a narrower question than the board believes. Her January promotion review is written around v4. She has not said she signed off the 28 September metric registration without reading the power memo's appendix.

Dharmil Khetawat, founder and chief executive, Mumbai. Wants v4 on every Indian storefront on 1 December; Series C conversations reopen in January and a conversion number is the slide. He has not told the team that a February 2026 term sheet lapsed unsigned in August.

Divyam Kalaria, VP Engineering, Pune. Holds that v3 and v4 cannot both be carried past 31 January. His squad owns the NPCI tokenisation migration, the work an audit will examine. He has not said the assignment script ran once, on 9 October, and was never re-run or balance-checked.

Devanshika Karnani, Staff Data Scientist, Toronto. Holds that both intervals in Exhibit 1 are arithmetically correct and only one answers the question asked. She wrote the September memo, and her team is funded against experiments delivered. She has not said an April decomposition on FY2026 data already returned a correlation of 0.021.

Dipanshu Kanodia, Head of Customer Success, Asia-Pacific, Singapore. Reports that six of the forty-eight held-back storefronts have opened tickets asking why their checkout looks old. His renewals number is a quarterly target. He has not said that three of the six were told by his own team in October to expect v4 on 1 November.

Dhritika Kacheria, Head of Design, Berlin. Holds that v4 is four changes under one name: saved address, UPI intent promotion, the collapsed chevron, and removal of the coupon field. The design-system budget she owns is approved on v4 shipping whole. She has not filed the defect she found on 11 November in PIN-code-first address entry.

Dhaivat Khandhar, Head of Sales, North America, New Jersey. Holds that the only number his pipeline buys is value per session. He is three deals short of his year. He has not disclosed that two proposals dated 10 November quote v4 as a 2.1-point conversion gain at a p-value below 0.0001.

Darshika Kumbhat, Group Head of Digital, Salwa Markets Group, Dubai. Will not take a checkout change she has no data for on her own estate. Her board measures basket size through the Dubai Shopping Festival. She has not told Saksham that Salwa began evaluating two other orchestration vendors in September.

6. Exhibits

These six exhibits are what the board will see. Exhibits 1 and 2 are the registered analysis; 3 and 5 the notes that followed; Exhibit 4 was pulled on 12 November and Exhibit 6 on 16 November.

7. Voices

“Four points on 1.8 lakh sessions. We are burning a week of a conversion win to satisfy a calendar. Why are we still running this?”

Dharmil Khetawat, Slack #checkout-v4, Sunday 18 October 2026, 21:14 IST

“Because we registered three weeks, and we have 240 storefronts, not six lakh independent draws. Stop on the day the line is highest and the number you ship is the height of the line on that day.”

Devanshika Karnani, same thread, 13:02 EDT / 22:32 IST

“Pre-period gap −0.40 pp, test gap +2.11 pp, difference-in-differences +2.51 pp. Note that this makes the estimate larger, not smaller. It does not make it narrower.”

Devanshika Karnani, memo to Dhaarna Kothari, 12 November 2026

“We keep saying ‘v4’ as though it were a thing. It is four things. The address block and the UPI promotion are not the same experiment, and we never ran either on its own.”

Dhritika Kacheria, email to the product list, Friday 6 November 2026, 10:40 CET / 15:10 IST

“Six tickets already from the held-back merchants, two of them after seeing a competitor's demo. I cannot hold forty-eight storefronts on the old checkout and call it science to their faces.”

Dipanshu Kanodia, Monday 9 November 2026, 08:15 SGT / 05:45 IST

“My brands do not buy conversion, they buy value per session. If that is down six per cent I would rather know now than after signing three logos on it.”

Dhaivat Khandhar, Thursday 12 November 2026, 07:50 EST / 18:20 IST

“You are asking me to take a change tested on 240 Indian storefronts, none of them mine, weeks before our biggest trading season. What is the number for Salwa?”

Darshika Kumbhat, Thursday 19 November 2026, 16:05 GST / 17:35 IST

8. The options as Dhaarna sees them

A. Ship v4 to all 9,400 Indian storefronts on 1 December. Ends the holdback and any further within-platform comparison. Uses two of the eight uncommitted engineer-weeks. Leaves Salwa on v3 and the payment mix in Exhibit 5 to move wherever it moves.

B. Hold at 192 and 48 until 31 January, then read again. Adds ten weeks of dual-running as a maintenance line, 23 November to 31 January: two engineers, 20 engineer-weeks, ₹14.6 lakh. Keeps the six tickets open.

C. Re-run it, storefront-randomised: eight weeks from Monday 4 January 2027, 419 storefronts in each arm, sized on completion at a 1.50 pp detectable effect, with GMV per checkout session registered alongside completion as a co-primary. Defers any Indian rollout to March and carries both flows past 31 January. Uses three engineer-weeks to build the second assignment. Leaves v4 live on 192 storefronts meanwhile, or rolls them back.

D. Ship the saved-address block alone and leave the payment pane on v3. Five of the eight engineer-weeks go to unbundling one release. The UPI promotion, the chevron and the coupon-field removal stay unshipped and unmeasured.

E. Ship v4 everywhere, Salwa included. Serve notice under clause 7.4 on Thursday 17 December for a 16 January go-live, the second of two change orders the contract allows in a year. Puts the change into the Dubai Shopping Festival, on an estate with no test data of its own.

9. The deadline and what cannot move

The board call is at 09:30 IST on Monday, 23 November 2026. Clause 7.4 requires thirty days' written notice of any checkout change on the Salwa estate, and Salwa's change freeze runs 1 December 2026 to 15 January 2027; the contract, worth ₹9.2 crore a year, renews on 31 March 2027. Saksham's deploy freeze runs 21 December to 3 January.

Capacity between the board call and Friday 18 December is four working weeks across six checkout engineers, or 24 engineer-weeks, of which 16 are committed to the NPCI tokenisation migration. A fully loaded Pune engineer costs ₹38 lakh a year, or ₹73,077 an engineer-week. That leaves 8 build weeks; option B's dual-running is a separate maintenance line at the same rate.

Under the 2022 contract language and the DPDP Act, Saksham holds no identifier linking a shopper across storefronts, and purges device-level records at thirty days. Neither is renegotiable before March.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 2 reports a completion rate for each arm in each week. State the unit of randomisation, the unit of analysis, and the population over which each rate is computed.
  2. Panel B of Exhibit 1 reports the same difference under two variance assumptions. Reproduce both standard errors from the cells in Exhibits 1 and 2, and say what would have to be true of the 240 storefronts for each to be right.
  3. Exhibit 3 reports four changes between the arms. Say which of them run the same way as Exhibit 2 and which do not, give at least two mechanisms that would produce that pattern, and say what measurement would separate them.
  4. Exhibit 6 covers thirteen days, 240 storefronts and 2.70 lakh checkout sessions. What range of true effects is it consistent with, and what happens to that range if the holdback runs another thirteen days?
  5. Saksham holds no identifier linking a shopper across storefronts and purges device records at thirty days. Say which claims in this case, if any, those two rules put out of reach, and describe one experiment Saksham could run inside them that it has not run.
  6. What should Dhaarna Kothari recommend at 09:30 on Monday, and what exactly would she tell the board that the October test can and cannot claim?

The table at eleven o'clock

Dhaarna moved the order-value note to the top of the pile, then moved it back. In Toronto, Devanshika was awake and would take a call at any hour. Dubai was an hour and a half behind, and Darshika Kumbhat's question lay unanswered on the phone beside her. The rain started again. She turned the power memo over to its blank side and began, for the fourth time, to write down what she actually knew.

A/B testing fundamentals: what the result can and cannot claim

Randomise, run, measure — and then say exactly, and only, what the randomisation entitles you to say.

1. Two decisions, one question

In Bengaluru on Sunday 18 October 2026, Jwalant Rajgor, vice-president of growth at Buniyad Money, is drafting the minute he reads to the operating committee on Tuesday 20 October, on whether the goal-first onboarding flow ships to every new signup. The test behind it ran from Monday 6 July to Sunday 19 July 2026 — fourteen days, two complete weekly cycles, 9,200 eligible new signups a day split evenly between arms. It returned a 5.34 per cent relative lift in the share of signups starting a systematic investment plan within seven days, at p = 0.00086, and three months of growth reviews have treated that as settled fact.

On Saturday 17 October the last signup in the July window reached day 90, and the query Jaanki Rambhia had left standing returned. Measured ninety days after signup, the share of signups with a funded, uncancelled plan rose from 7.76 per cent to 7.89 per cent — 0.125 percentage points, with a 95 per cent interval running from −0.168 to +0.418 points. The experiment Rajgor ran cannot tell that apart from nothing. His problem on Tuesday is not whether the feature works, but which sentence the fourteen days licence him to speak.

In Pune, Jignasha Raiyani, head of product at Brijpath Systems, asked on Thursday 10 September 2026 whether the rebuilt exception-triage screen could be tested rather than argued about. Brijpath sells warehouse order-operations software to 268 live accounts carrying 9,340 weekly active users and ₹47.2 crore of annual recurring revenue, of which ₹17.9 crore — 37.9 per cent — sits in twelve customers. Jagrut Rachchh, who runs customer success, wants it shipped in November on the strength of nine support calls. By Friday 23 October Raiyani must choose between a cluster-randomised test starting Monday 2 November and ending Sunday 27 December, and shipping on judgement. Both decisions turn on one question: what can an A/B test actually claim?

2. The idea, and the four schools that disagree about it

An A/B test is a randomised controlled experiment on a live product. Each unit has two potential outcomes, what it would do under A and under B, and only one is observed. Random assignment makes the arms exchangeable in expectation, so the difference in observed means estimates the average treatment effect without bias. Four qualifiers carry the burden: average, over the randomised population, during the exposure window, at the assigned exposure share. Drop one and the claim fails.

The line is older than the industry: Peirce and Jastrow randomised and blinded a psychophysics experiment in 1884. Ronald Fisher, in The Design of Experiments (1935), made randomisation the logical basis of inference rather than a precaution. Neyman and Pearson in 1933 added the second kind of error, and with it power and sample size; Wald (1945) showed a horizon need not be fixed; the Medical Research Council's streptomycin trial of 1948 carried concealed allocation into medicine; Rubin (1974) gave the machinery its modern notation. Google ran a live traffic experiment on results-per-page in February 2000; Amazon and Microsoft industrialised it over the next decade.

Four schools share the apparatus and disagree about what it yields. The Fisherian signs “a small p-value is evidence against the sharp null” and refuses “p = 0.03 means a 97 per cent chance B is better”. The Neyman–Pearson school signs “fix α, power and the effect you care about in advance; what you buy is a long-run error rate on a procedure” and refuses “stop when the chart looks convincing”. The Bayesian decision school signs “report the posterior probability of benefit and the expected loss of each action” and refuses “a fixed horizon is necessary”. The estimation school signs “publish the magnitude and the interval; the accept/reject dichotomy throws away most of the information” and refuses “the winner ships”.

3. Mechanics, worked rather than named

Expert practice starts with sizing, because sizing is where the decision about what the test may claim is taken. For two proportions:

n per arm = (zα/2 + zβ)2 × [ pA(1−pA) + pB(1−pB) ] ÷ δ2
≈ 2 p(1−p) (zα/2 + zβ)2 ÷ δ2 when the two rates are close.
At α = 0.05 and 80 per cent power: (1.9600 + 0.8416)2 = 7.8489.
Buniyad's baseline p = 0.110, so 2p(1−p) = 0.1958.
For a 6 per cent relative effect, δ = 0.06 × 0.110 = 0.00660 and δ2 = 0.00004356.
n = 7.8489 × 0.1958 ÷ 0.00004356 = 35,281 per arm.

δ is absolute, and because it is squared, halving the effect you want to catch quadruples the test — which governs what two weeks buys.

Table 1. Buniyad sizing grid: α = 0.05 two-sided, 80 per cent power, baseline 11.0 per cent.
Relative MDEAbsolute MDE (pp)n per armDays at 4,600/arm/day

Buniyad chose fourteen days for a reason unrelated to power: weekly cycles in Indian consumer finance are strong, and a window of part-weeks leaves the arms differing in calendar coverage. Fourteen days at 4,600 per arm daily plans 64,400 per arm: a standard error of √(2 × 0.110 × 0.890 ÷ 64,400) = 0.001744 and an MDE of 2.8016 × 0.001744 = 0.4885 points, 4.44 per cent of baseline.

The step most teams leave implicit comes next: check the allocation before the outcome. Buniyad logged 64,186 control and 64,614 treatment exposures, 128,800 in all, exactly 9,200 a day. Against the 64,400 each a fair coin predicts, χ² = 2 × 214² ÷ 64,400 = 1.42 on one degree of freedom, p = 0.233. Control converted 7,067 of 64,186 signups, or 11.01 per cent; treatment 7,494 of 64,614, or 11.60 per cent. The difference is 0.588 points, standard error √(0.1101×0.8899/64,186 + 0.1160×0.8840/64,614) = 0.001764, z = 3.33, p = 0.00086, interval 0.242 to 0.934 points — 2.20 to 8.48 per cent of control.

4. When the method applies, stated as conditions you can test

Four conditions decide whether an A/B test answers the question in front of you, each checkable before a line of code is written.

One: units can be assigned independently. Buniyad's signups can; one person's onboarding does not touch another's. Brijpath's users cannot, because the pickers in one warehouse share an exception queue, a supervisor and a training session. Assignment moves up to the account, and everything downstream changes with it. Two: the effect you care about is observable inside a window you can afford. Buniyad's seven-day plan start is; its ninety-day funded balance is not, at the precision needed. Three: the arms do not interfere. True at Buniyad, false wherever a shared budget, a shared inventory or a shared model sits between the arms. Four: there are enough units. Brijpath has 268 accounts, and that is the binding number, not the 9,340 users.

The method is actively misleading in two situations. The first is an equilibrium slower to form than the test runs: a pricing change tested for two weeks measures the surprise, not the steady state. The second is when the decision is irreversible and the test observes only a proxy — a fourteen-day read attached to a change that cannot be withdrawn produces a number with a confidence interval and a decision with none.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

Two-sided marketplaces break condition three first. If riders and drivers come from one pool, a treatment that wins riders wins them from control, and the measured effect is a transfer rather than a gain. The answers are switchback designs randomising time slices across the market, budget-split designs giving each arm its own supply, and cluster randomisation over cities, all three costing power several times over on the clustering arithmetic that costs Brijpath 3.031 in section eight. Regulated products break condition one: a change to disclosure or pricing in a sector supervised by SEBI or the RBI may require uniform treatment of customers, so assignment itself is unavailable and only before-and-after or a geographic quasi-experiment remains. Hardware-plus-software breaks reversibility — firmware shipped to a device cannot be rolled back on a dashboard — and AI-native products break stationarity, because a model retrained on both arms has already mixed them.

At the organisational seams the failure is political, not statistical: the growth team's win is the support team's ticket load, and nobody owns the sum. What mature companies actually do, as opposed to what their blog posts describe, is run a permanent guardrail suite on every test, keep a long-term holdback of a few per cent that never receives shipped winners, and periodically remove a shipped feature at full scale. The holdback is what measures whether an accumulated year of fourteen-day wins is worth what the individual tests said.

6. Eight things an expert sees that a competent practitioner does not

Intention-to-treat is not a preference; it is what randomisation protects. Filter to users who experienced the change and the filter is itself caused by treatment, so the arms stop being comparable. The tell-tale is an analysis table whose arms carry different denominators no sample-ratio check ever saw. The obvious reading — only exposed users can be affected — is true of the mechanism, not the inference.

The minimum detectable effect is not the confidence interval's half-width. The MDE multiplies the standard error by zα/2 + zβ = 2.8016, the interval by 1.9600. The ratio is 1.43, so a design that detects 5.4 per cent reports intervals near ±3.8 per cent. The tell-tale is a post-mortem quoting both as one guarantee, then treating a null result as evidence of no effect.

Relative and absolute lift are not interchangeable, and the design is set on the absolute scale. Five per cent of Buniyad's 11.0 per cent baseline is 0.55 points; of a 2.0 per cent baseline, 0.10 points, needing about six times the sample, since n scales as (1−p) ÷ (r²p). The tell-tale is a brief specifying “a 5 per cent lift” without a baseline.

Sample-ratio mismatch is a chi-square on counts, not an eyeball. Buniyad's split gave χ² = 1.42 and p = 0.233. Had it been 50.5/49.5 — “close enough” in a status meeting — the deviation would be 644 per arm, χ² = 12.88, p ≈ 0.0003, and the result uninterpretable. The tell-tale is a platform reporting the split to one decimal place with no test.

Randomisation unit and analysis unit must agree. Assign users and count sessions, and the standard error treats nested sessions as independent. The correction is a clustered variance or the delta method, widening the interval by roughly the square root of the design effect. The tell-tale is a results table whose sample size exceeds the experiment's headcount.

Novelty and primacy need a standard error before they are claims. Buniyad's week-one lift was 0.765 points (3,748 of 32,302 against 3,478 of 32,090) and its week-two lift 0.411 (3,746 of 32,312 against 3,589 of 32,096). The attenuation looks dramatic until divided by its uncertainty: the difference of 0.354 points sits against a standard error of 0.353, exactly one. Note also what the contrast separates. These are signup-week cohorts, each with its own seven-day window, so the comparison is between cohorts and not between early and late exposure — the distinction most novelty readings skip.

A control arm stops being a counterfactual once the arms share a resource. Shared budgets, inventory, auctions and model weights all leak treatment into control. The tell-tale is an effect that shrinks as exposure share rises: invisible at 5 per cent, halving the gap at 50.

The metric you can move in fourteen days is a surrogate, and the test says nothing about whether it is valid. Buniyad's seven-day plan start stands proxy for funded, retained saving; the experiment measures the proxy perfectly and says nothing about the substitution. The tell-tale is a primary metric whose window is shorter than the payback period — nearly always, which is why holdbacks exist.

7. How the practice differs by product type and company stage

Table 2. Where the binding constraint sits, by setting.
SettingUsual unitBinding constraintWhat breaks first
Consumer appUser or deviceLong-horizon outcomes need more traffic than a fortnight suppliesSurrogate metrics and novelty claims
B2B and enterpriseAccount (cluster)Number of accountsPower, and revenue concentration across arms
Platform, marketplaceRegion, time slice, budget poolInterference between armsControl as counterfactual
Hardware and physical goodsShipment batch or storeLead time and reversibilityEffects outlive the window
AI-nativeUser, model held fixedShared state, non-stationarityArm independence, metric drift

The real differences are in the table; the one usually asserted and not real is that enterprise software cannot be tested. It can, at the account level, with the arithmetic of section eight. Stage matters more. Before product-market fit the limiting resource is ideas, not traffic, and a team running four tests a quarter at 20 per cent power learns almost nothing while feeling rigorous. In the middle stage the platform becomes worth building and the constraint moves from traffic to pre-registration. At scale it moves again, to interference and accumulation: a hundred shipped winners a year, each measured over two weeks, sum to a number nobody has measured.

8. Three worked examples

Buniyad Money: a real win whose claim does not extend. Of the 7,067 control starters, 4,982 still held a funded plan at day 90 — 70.50 per cent; of the 7,494 treatment starters, 5,096 did, or 68.00 per cent. Both numerators count plans begun inside the seven-day window, each signup read at its own day 90: this is the seven-day funnel surviving to day 90, not every saver Buniyad holds then. Per signup, 7.76 against 7.89 per cent: 0.125 points, standard error 0.001497, z = 0.84, p = 0.40, interval −0.168 to +0.418. Treatment produced 0.588 extra starters per hundred signups and 0.125 extra retained savers, so the marginal starters retained at 21.3 per cent against the control cohort's 70.50 — an estimate whose numerator spans zero, putting marginal retention between negative and about 71 per cent. The day-90 design could detect only 5.40 per cent relative and saw 1.61.

Baatcheet AI: the failure and the recovery. Jaladhi Rajyaguru's Hyderabad support-AI company tested a retrieval-grounded composer from Monday 11 May to Sunday 24 May 2026 on 120,000 help-centre visitors per arm. In control, 42,000 reached the assistant and 14,280 resolved without a ticket: 35.0 and 34.0 per cent. In treatment, 49,200 reached and 16,236 deflected: 41.0 and 33.0. The team read deflection among reachers, saw a point lost and killed the composer. On the randomised population the same counts give 11.90 against 13.53 per cent — 1.63 points, 13.70 per cent relative, standard error 0.001360, z = 11.99. Conditioning on reaching the assistant conditions on a post-treatment variable, and the arm changed two things at once. The June re-run, the 15th to the 28th, held the entry card at control: reach 35.0 against 35.1 per cent, deflection among reachers 34.0 against 36.2, ITT 11.90 against 12.71 — 0.81 points, 6.81 per cent of control, buried in May.

The reads reconcile. If the June estimates transfer, the 42,120 May visitors who would have reached the assistant anyway deflected at 36.2 per cent, giving 15,247 of the arm's 16,236 resolutions; the 7,080 marginal visitors drawn in by the entry card supplied the other 989, a rate of 13.97 per cent.

Brijpath Systems: arithmetic that decides whether to test at all. The metric is the share of exceptions cleared inside four working hours, baseline 61.5 per cent, and Raiyani wants a 5.0-point move — 8.13 per cent relative. With users independent, n = 7.8489 × 2 × 0.615 × 0.385 ÷ 0.0025 = 1,487 per arm. But assignment is at the account: with mean cluster size 9,340 ÷ 268 = 34.85 and an intra-cluster correlation of 0.06, the design effect is 1 + (34.85 − 1) × 0.06 = 3.031, and 1,487 × 3.031 = 4,507.1, call it 4,508 users or 130 accounts per arm — 260 of her 268. The whole customer base is one barely powered test. A pre-period covariate changes that: successive eight-week windows in Brijpath's history correlate at 0.72 account by account, so with the eight weeks to Sunday 1 November as the covariate, CUPED scales variance by 1 − 0.72² = 0.4816 — 2,171 users or 63 accounts per arm, 126 in all. That is a floor twice over: it assumes the covariate absorbs variance between clusters as well as within, which it rarely does, and a single mean of 34.85 ignores the spread that puts 37.9 per cent of revenue in twelve accounts, which raises the design effect again.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Peeking. Early sign: a nightly dashboard and a channel where someone posts the p-value daily. Diagnostic question: how often was this looked at before it was read? Under independence, five looks at α = 0.05 bound false positives at 1 − 0.955 = 22.6 per cent; successive looks are strongly correlated, so the true figure is lower: the published repeated-significance tables of Armitage, McPherson and Rowe (1969) put five equally spaced looks near 14 per cent and twenty near 25. Caught late it ships a feature with no effect.

Metric and segment hunting. Early sign: a by-segment appendix. Diagnostic question: which metric and which cut were named before the test started? Twenty independent comparisons at 5 per cent give about a 64 per cent chance of at least one false winner, and a roadmap then rests on a subgroup.

Dilution. Early sign: an effect far smaller than the mechanism allows. Diagnostic question: what share of the randomised population could the change have touched? Reaching 20 per cent of users, a true 10 per cent effect shows as 2 per cent overall and is declared flat. Randomise at the trigger point.

The winner's curse. Early sign: shipped effects reliably below the test estimate. Diagnostic question: what was the power, and what is the prior that such a change works? A barely significant result from an underpowered test overstates the effect, because only lucky draws cross the line. Caught late, an annual plan's gains do not sum to the business result.

10. Where competent experts genuinely disagree

Fixed horizons against always-valid inference. The fixed-horizon camp holds that pre-committing n, α and δ is what makes the error rate mean anything, and that sequential schemes pay for flexibility in power. The always-valid camp replies that people peek regardless, and that mixture sequential probability ratio tests and group-sequential boundaries make peeking honest at modest cost. It would be wrong if teams given valid sequential tools stopped early at estimates themselves biased upward: a claim about behaviour, not statistics.

Significance against expected value. One camp ships on significance because a decision rule with a known error rate is auditable across hundreds of tests. The other argues the loss function is asymmetric — a reversible interface change with a positive posterior mean is worth shipping at p = 0.3 — and that significance imports a cost structure nobody chose. The first fails if changes are cheap and reversible; the second fails if organisations cannot hold a prior they did not fit to the answer they wanted.

Experiment everything against experiment selectively. The first holds that intuition about product changes is poor and the discipline is the point. The second holds that most tests are underpowered, that the measurement tax slows coherent design, and that a strong team shipping on judgement and watching guardrails learns faster. The evidence differs: published win rates of 10 to 30 per cent against velocity. The dispute is about whether ideas or traffic is scarcer.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this reports a p-value and a lift. Someone who has internalised it writes the claim sentence before the test runs, with the population, window and exposure share in it, and notices at once when a results document quietly changes one of the three. They compute the MDE before the test and quote it beside every null result, treat a sample-ratio mismatch as a stop condition rather than a footnote, and know without looking it up what a 2 per cent baseline costs against an 11 per cent one. And they are comfortable saying that an expensive, clean, highly significant experiment answered a question adjacent to the one the business asked.

12. The two decisions

Rajgor ships the flow to all signups on Tuesday 20 October and rewrites the minute. It records a 5.34 per cent relative lift in seven-day plan starts over the July window at even exposure, puts the ninety-day funded rate at 1.61 per cent on an interval of −2.17 to +5.39, and commits Buniyad to a 5 per cent holdback from November. Raiyani declines the 260-account design and runs 126 accounts from Monday 2 November, stratified by revenue band so the twelve largest split six and six, covariate pre-registered. She tells Rachchh it can detect an 8.13 per cent relative improvement and nothing smaller.

  1. Write the sentence about the ninety-day result Rajgor is entitled to put in the minute, and the similar one he is not. What distinguishes them?
  2. Brijpath's 126-account design rests on a pre-period correlation of 0.72 at account level. When is 126 the right number, when is it a floor, and what evidence would tell Raiyani which case she is in?
  3. Baatcheet's May and June reads disagree on the sign of the composer's effect. Which estimate would each of section two's four schools call the effect, and what would each require before shipping?

13. Going deeper

  • Writing an experiment hypothesis — this page's claim sentence; unlocks pre-registration.
  • Significance, power, sample size, peeking — section three's machinery; unlocks defensible stopping rules.
  • Experimentation culture — who stops a test and who owns guardrails; unlocks trust at volume.
  • Qual and quant feedback loop — tests say whether, interviews why; unlocks better hypotheses.
  • Feature flags and flighting — what makes exposure share real; unlocks ramps and holdbacks.
  • Price testing — fairness, regulation, equilibrium; unlocks the hardest edge case.
  • Offline versus online evaluation — what a replay stands in for; unlocks cheaper iteration.
  • Long-term holdouts — measuring accumulated effects; unlocks Buniyad's open day-90 question.
  • Evals, A/B tests and when each decides — the AI-native division of labour; unlocks model shipping.
  • When you can't A/B test — section four's conditions failing; unlocks quasi-experimental tools.
  • Choosing experiment metrics — surrogates, guardrails, the overall evaluation criterion; unlocks tests that answer the question.
  • Experiment pitfalls — the catalogue behind section nine; unlocks faster diagnosis.
  • Experimentation platforms — assignment, logging, diagnostics; unlocks automatic SRM checks.
  • Quasi-experiments and causal inference — synthetic controls, instruments; unlocks causal claims without randomisation.
  • Bayesian versus frequentist interpretation — section ten formalised; unlocks critical reading.
case20v1-exp.ab:
Rangrez and the Prepaid Offer

A decision case on what an A/B test can claim

1. Opening

At 7:00 pm on Thursday 15 October 2026, Chhagan Jivrajani closed the door of the glass meeting room above Rangrez's warehouse in Surat and asked four faces on a screen a single question: could the company say, to its lenders and to itself, that a prepaid-payment offer had raised sales?

For fourteen days, from Monday 14 September to Sunday 27 September, half of the shoppers reaching Rangrez's checkout had been offered ₹75 off if they paid by UPI rather than cash on delivery. Conversion in that half had risen. Cyrene Jalundhwala, the data scientist, had joined from Toronto, where it was 9:30 in the morning, and had circulated her readout two days earlier.

The next release left on Monday 19 October. The festive code freeze began on Monday 26 October, less than two weeks before Diwali on Sunday 8 November. Chhagan owed engineering a decision by noon on Friday: the offer for every shopper, for most of them, or for none.

2. Company background

Chhagan founded Rangrez in 2019, after a decade in his family's textile trade on Surat's Ring Road. The company sells sarees, kurta sets, lehengas and chaniya cholis sourced directly from Surat mills, mainly to women in tier-2 and tier-3 cities, through an Android app and a mobile website. In FY2026 it shipped about 2.6 lakh orders at an average of ₹1,450, roughly ₹38 crore of gross merchandise value.

The competition is large. Meesho, Myntra, Ajio, Flipkart and Nykaa Fashion all sell ethnic wear, and most of them can outspend Rangrez on advertising. Rangrez competes on mill-direct prices and festival collections, and it pays for that with a payment mix that tilts toward cash on delivery. Roughly two orders in three are cash on delivery, couriers such as Delhivery take a fee on every parcel, and a refused or returned parcel costs the fee twice. UPI, run by NPCI, was the obvious lever: money in advance, fewer refusals. Checkout payments run through Razorpay.

3. The situation

Cyrene's team had registered the test on Tuesday 8 September, one page long: showing ₹75 off for prepaid payment would raise the share of checkout visitors who place an order. Visitors were assigned by a hashed user ID, fifty-fifty, on first arrival at checkout. The treatment arm saw the same page plus a banner and the discount; nothing else differed. Figure 1 sets the dates out.

Exhibit 1 gives the headline. The split was 41,230 to 40,770 and passed the sample-ratio check. Order conversion rose from 12.00 to 12.79 per cent. The growth team had made that the primary metric; Cyrene had argued for orders that were actually kept, and recorded it as secondary. On the fourth day, Thursday 17 September, Cheenu Jasoliya asked to stop early because the dashboard looked good. Cyrene declined, citing the registered fourteen days.

Exhibit 2 follows each order to its outcome, closed on Sunday 11 October. Kept orders per visitor rose from 9.12 to 9.85 per cent, and the prepaid share of orders rose from 34 to 45 per cent. Cash-on-delivery failures rose as a share of cash orders, which is consistent with the more reliable cash buyers having switched, though the test did not follow individuals.

Calvin Jobalia, who runs finance and operations, priced it in Exhibit 3. Contribution per visitor fell by ₹0.92, with a 95% interval from −₹3.22 to +₹1.38.

The team saw it differently from its cities. Cleo Jotangiya, the designer in Berlin, where it was 3:30 pm, worried that a ₹75 badge on every checkout teaches shoppers to wait for it. The customer-success lead in Singapore noted that diaspora customers shipped outside India were never in the test. The engineers in Bengaluru and Pune confirmed that the flag could serve any percentage of visitors.

4. The people

Chhagan Jivrajani, co-founder and CEO, Surat. Wants a festive plan he can defend to Rangrez's lenders, and no argument on Monday morning about what was decided.

Cheenu Jasoliya, vice-president of growth, Bengaluru. Owns the conversion target. Wants the offer live for everyone on 19 October, because the freeze leaves no second chance before Diwali.

Cyrene Jalundhwala, senior data scientist, Toronto. Wants every claim worded to what randomisation supports, and wants some visitors kept without the offer so that Rangrez can keep measuring.

Calvin Jobalia, head of finance and operations, Surat. Pays for the discounts and for failed parcels. Wants the decision judged in rupees of contribution, not in orders.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Option A: ship to every visitor on 19 October. Everyone sees the ₹75 offer, and no visitor is left without it. The fortnight lifted the prepaid share of orders from 34 to 45 per cent. Cheenu forecasts 61,500 checkout visitors a week, 1.5 times the test fortnight's weekly average of 41,000, for eight weeks to 14 December: 4.92 lakh visitors. If the fortnight's difference of −₹0.92 per visitor carried over, contribution would be ₹4.53 lakh lower, within an interval of −₹15.84 lakh to +₹6.79 lakh.

Option B: ship nothing now. Cleo and Calvin would redesign the offer, with a smaller discount, and test it in January. The festive weeks run with the prepaid share near the control's 34 per cent, and Rangrez learns nothing about festive behaviour. On Exhibit 3's measure nothing changes.

Option C: ship to 90 per cent and hold out 10 per cent until 14 December. The same offer goes to 4.43 lakh visitors, and 49,200 are kept without it. On the same carry-over arithmetic the cost is ₹4.07 lakh, within an interval of −₹14.26 lakh to +₹6.11 lakh. Holdout visitors do not see the offer during the festival.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does the randomisation in Exhibit 1 allow Rangrez to claim about the 0.79-point difference in order conversion, and which of these claims does it support: the offer raised sales in the fortnight; it will raise Diwali sales; it makes customers more loyal?
  2. Cyrene wanted kept orders as the primary metric, and the registered primary was order conversion. Which metric would you have named primary for a decision about shipping this offer, and what does that choice cost in visitors?
  3. Exhibit 3 puts the difference in contribution per visitor at −₹0.92, with a standard deviation of ₹168 per visitor. How many visitors per arm would a test need to detect a difference of that size at 5% significance and 80% power, and what follows for how Rangrez should decide?
  4. Which option, or alternative, would you instruct engineering to build by noon on Friday, and what result in the next eight weeks, written down now, would make you reverse it?

8. A note for the learner

An A/B test answers one narrow question: among the people randomised, over the weeks it ran, how did outcomes differ because of the treatment? Randomisation lets Rangrez say the offer caused the 0.79-point rise in orders and the 0.72-point rise in kept orders, among India-addressed checkout visitors in a non-festive fortnight. It does not reach Diwali shoppers, repeat purchase or contribution. A test settling ₹0.92 at a standard deviation of ₹168 needs about 5.2 lakh visitors per arm, some seventeen weeks at half of festive traffic (30,750 a week per arm), so none will finish before 8 November.

One defensible path is Option C. Circulate the claim in writing: orders and kept orders up in the fortnight, contribution undetermined. Orders placed by 30 November have closed outcomes by 14 December, fourteen days later; the roughly 37,800 holdout visitors in that span can detect a 0.44-point kept-order gap at 80 per cent power, well under the 0.72 observed. Each point of kept conversion is worth ₹4.35 per visitor, so repaying the ₹0.92 needs about 0.21 point more, roughly 0.93 in all, if mix and failure rates hold. The rule, applied on 14 December to those orders: keep the offer only if the holdout comparison shows at least that; otherwise cut the discount. Cyrene owns the readout, Calvin the rupees.
exp40v2-exp.pitfalls:
Experiment pitfalls

Sample ratio mismatch, interference, multiple comparisons and seasonality — why the repair is a design, not a formula.

1. Two rooms, two weeks apart

On Thursday 1 October 2026, Yashanvi Ghadiali had forty minutes to defend a decision she had already lost once. She runs growth at Mazboot Durust, a home-services marketplace in Bengaluru, Jaipur, Pune, Indore, Lucknow and Coimbatore taking about 10,400 job requests a day. Priority Dispatch, the feature in dispute, moves a job to the front of the technician queue. Its user-randomised test of 1 to 14 July 2026 was emphatic: treated customers had 99.0 per cent of jobs filled against control's 81.0, a gap of 18.0 points, which the board paper turned into 1,872 extra jobs a day.

Yaduvir Gondaliya, who built the measurement, had spent August showing it was an accounting identity: technician-hours are fixed on the day, so every job the feature pulls forward is one it pushes back. His six-city switchback of 3 to 16 August put the effect on network fill rate at +0.18 points, 95 per cent interval −0.70 to +1.06. Same feature, two fortnights a month apart, two estimates a hundredfold apart.

On Friday 16 October, Yugank Gokhru faced a quieter version in Pune. Mavisa Systems sells an AI claims-triage copilot to 38 Indian general insurers; its headline metric is the share of motor claims auto-cleared without a human. Clause Match v3, tested on 125,000 claims from Tuesday 8 September to Monday 28 September, lifted that share from 41.90 to 42.52 per cent, p = 0.028. On 29 September Yogasree Ghoghari noticed the arms held 63,158 and 61,842 claims. Nobody had asked why.

2. What a pitfall is

A controlled experiment licenses one inference: that the difference between two observed averages estimates a causal effect, to a stated precision, at a stated error rate. A pitfall is any mechanism that breaks an assumption behind that licence while leaving the output identical.

The assumptions split in two. Identification assumptions concern assignment: units allocated as intended, a unit's outcome depending only on its own assignment, comparisons made inside the strata where randomisation happened. Sample ratio mismatch, interference and pooling reversals live here. Inference assumptions concern the error rate: a rule fixed before the data, a comparison count matching the correction, a variance estimator matching the randomisation unit. Peeking, multiplicity and clustering live there. The first family biases the estimate, the second your confidence.

The history predates the software. Fisher's randomisation argument of 1935 makes a difference in means interpretable at all; Cox named non-interference in 1958, Rubin folded it into SUTVA in 1980. Armitage, McPherson and Rowe priced repeated looks in 1969, Pocock and then O'Brien and Fleming gave boundaries that pay for them, Benjamini and Hochberg replaced family-wise with false-discovery control in 1995. Online experimentation added one new object: the sample ratio alarm, which has no clinical analogue because no trial allocates by cache.

Three schools disagree about the remedy. The trustworthiness school — Kohavi, Fabijan's group at Microsoft — signs "an imbalance invalidates the result" and refuses "we adjusted and the effect held". The always-valid school, after Johari and colleagues, signs "look as often as you like, under the right boundary" and refuses "peeking is malpractice". The design school signs "if your units interfere, randomise something else" and refuses "estimate it and subtract". Yaduvir belongs to the third.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Sample ratio mismatch

An SRM test is a goodness-of-fit test against the intended allocation, whose expected counts here are 62,500 each. Mavisa observed 63,158 and 61,842, a split of 50.53 to 49.47. The chi-square on one degree of freedom, the sum over arms of (observed − expected)²/expected, is 2 × 658² / 62,500 = 13.85, p = 0.0002: half a point of imbalance is a one-in-five-thousand event. Fabijan and colleagues reported in 2019 that of order six per cent of Microsoft's experiments trip the alarm.

The deviation of 658 is also a count. The flag SDK served treatment whenever a tenant's configuration cache missed, and misses are commoner for the four largest tenants, so 658 control claims were served treatment. Those tenants auto-clear 51 per cent of motor claims against a 42 per cent baseline.

Clause Match v3, 8–28 Sep 2026ClaimsAuto-clearedAuto-clear rate (%)
As logged — treatment63,15826,85442.52
As logged — control61,84225,91441.90
Total as logged125,00052,76842.21
Reallocated — treatment62,50026,51842.43
Reallocated — control62,50026,25042.00
Total reallocated125,00052,76842.21

The 658 excess claims return to control at their own 51 per cent clear rate (658 × 0.51 = 336). Claims and cleared claims are conserved; only the split moves. Rate column holds pooled rates, not row means.

As logged the gap is 0.62 points. The pooled rate is 52,768/125,000 = 0.4221, so the standard error is √(0.4221 × 0.5779 × (1/63,158 + 1/61,842)) = 0.00279, giving z = 2.20, p = 0.028. Reallocated, the gap is 0.43 points, z = 1.53, p = 0.125. The reallocation is no repair: it assumes the mechanism was exactly what the engineer guessed, so its conclusion is only that the answer is mechanism-dependent. Hence: discard.

The design parameters are not free

Mavisa's plan said the study was "powered to detect a 1 per cent relative lift". It was not, and held everything needed to disprove itself. For two proportions with n per arm, two-sided α = 0.05 and 80 per cent power, the minimum detectable effect is (z0.975 + z0.80) × √(2p(1−p)/n). With n = 62,500 and p = 0.42 that is (1.960 + 0.842) × √(0.4872/62,500) = 2.802 × 0.00279 = 0.0078, an MDE of 0.78 points, or 1.86 per cent relative. At the claimed 0.42 points, power is Φ(0.0042/0.00279 − 1.960) = Φ(−0.456) = 0.32. Cohort size, baseline rate, α, power and MDE are five quantities bound by one equation — four degrees of freedom, so any four fix the fifth. A plan that states all five is over-determined by exactly one, and here the one that gave was the MDE.

Peeking

Mavisa's team opened the dashboard every morning. The 0.05 rate belongs to one pre-specified comparison; checking repeatedly and stopping on the first crossing is a different procedure with a different rate. Armitage, McPherson and Rowe computed it for equally spaced looks at a normal mean: two looks inflate a nominal two-sided 0.05 to about 0.083, five to 0.142, ten to 0.193. Twenty-one daily looks, by the same calculation, give nearer one in four.

Two repairs exist. A group-sequential boundary spends the budget across a declared number of looks — Pocock's constant for five is a critical z of 2.413, a nominal p of 0.0158 at each. Always-valid inference builds an interval valid at every sample size. Neither licenses stopping when the number looks good.

4. When the warnings apply, and when they mislead

Four conditions are testable on a specific experiment. One: the arms draw on a conserved resource. True at Mazboot Durust, where technician-hours are fixed on the day; false at Mavisa for compute, true for a handler's attention inside a tenant. Two: the randomisation unit contains the interference. False at Mazboot Durust under user randomisation; true at Mavisa once assignment moved to the tenant. Three: realised allocation matches intention inside every stratum pooled over. Failed at Mavisa globally, and at Mazboot Durust inside cities while passing globally. Four: the stopping rule was fixed before the data. Failed at Mavisa, where daily readouts went to a sales team wanting an answer.

They mislead in three situations. An SRM test on a small experiment catches almost nothing: the same half-point imbalance over 2,000 units gives a chi-square of 0.22 and p = 0.64, so a quiet alarm is not evidence of clean assignment. Bonferroni over forty metrics downstream of one funnel is severely conservative, assuming an independence the funnel denies. And a switchback is worse than a user-level test when carryover outlasts the period: if treatment changes which technician a household gets next week, daily alternation measures a contaminated contrast and loses power too.

5. Hard edges and organisational seams

Regulation changes what may be randomised, not how it is analysed. Mavisa cannot randomise a claim decision: under IRDAI's conduct expectations two identical claimants may not be adjudicated differently because of an experiment. It can randomise the suggestion shown to a handler who keeps the decision — which creates interference, because a handler seeing better suggestions on treated claims becomes better on their control claims too. Hence the rerun's move to tenant-level assignment.

Two-sided marketplaces make interference the default. Hardware is worse: firmware cannot be un-shipped, so the holdout is a manufacturing decision taken before production. Multi-product companies share a login funnel, so a test on one product perturbs another's denominators. AI-native products add non-stationarity the classical literature does not cover, because a model's own outputs re-enter its retrieval corpus and the treatment drifts inside the window. At the seam, the flag SDK belongs to one team, the metric store to another and experiment review to a third, and the sample ratio is the quantity none of them owns. Mature programmes answer with an alarm that marks a test invalid. They also keep an exception process they rarely document: eleven of the fifty-three tests Mavisa invalidated in the year to September 2026 shipped anyway.

6. Eight distinctions between expert and competent

An imbalance is a diagnosis, not a correction. The tell is a deck that reports the mismatch and then the adjusted effect on the next line. The chi-square says the assignment mechanism is not what the analysis assumes, so everything downstream carries unknown bias — netting out the direction fails, because direction is a property of the bug.

Seasonality rarely biases a concurrent contrast. Both arms live through the same Tuesday and the same Diwali week, so calendar effects cancel. What they corrupt is extrapolation, switchbacks and ratios whose denominator mix moves. The tell is a paper that annualises a July lift: Priority Dispatch was tested in peak air-conditioner season, when AC work was 38 per cent of volume against 19 per cent over the year, so an AC-concentrated effect annualises at half the July rate.

Find the conserved quantity. Interference is bounded above by whatever the arms share; share nothing and SUTVA holds. The first question on a marketplace test is not whether interference exists but what is finite and how fast it replenishes. Technician-hours replenish daily, so a one-day switchback is coherent; trust in a named technician never does.

Peeking only bites when the stopping rule depends on the data. A team that looks daily, acts on nothing and decides at the declared horizon has inflated nothing; a team that would have stopped on a good result has, whether or not it did. The tell is a counterfactual: had Tuesday's number been significant, would this test still be running?

A clean global ratio can hide a broken stratum. Mazboot Durust's May test gave 20 per cent of Bengaluru and 80 per cent of Jaipur to treatment by design, and the network split came out at exactly half. The global check passed; a per-city check would have shown two deliberate, opposite imbalances, and pooling them produced a reversal. The tell is a denominator that unions separately randomised strata.

The multiplicity correction follows the decision rule, not the dashboard. Forty charts are not forty tests if only one can change the decision; one veto-bearing guardrail checked across twelve segments is twelve tests. Ask how many distinct ways this experiment could have produced a ship. Correcting for everything plotted makes powered tests unshippable.

Novelty and primacy are not symmetric, and the usual fix is expensive. Mavisa's suggestion-interface test ran four equal weeks from Monday 1 June to Sunday 28 June 2026, 24,500 suggestions per arm per week. Control held 31.0 per cent acceptance throughout; treatment ran 40.4, 36.1, 33.8 and 33.6, so lifts of 9.4, 5.1, 2.8 and 2.6 points. Pooled that is +5.0 against +2.7 for the last two weeks, 1.8 times the asymptote. The effects ran opposite ways: tenured handlers, who saw 41 per cent of the suggestions, began at −1.2 and ended at +3.4, newer handlers at +16.8 and +2.1. Reading only the last week removes the bias and discards three quarters of the data.

"Not significant" is not "no effect". The reallocated Clause Match result is 0.43 points, standard error 0.279, a 95 per cent interval of −0.12 to +0.98. That contains zero and also the 0.78-point effect the test was built to detect, so it has not separated the hypotheses that mattered. The tell is a summary saying "no difference" where the interval says "no information".

7. Product type and company stage

Consumer products with millions of independent users come closest to the textbook, so their dominant pitfalls are inference-side: peeking, multiplicity, novelty. Platforms and marketplaces invert this: identification failures dominate and the investment belongs in switchback and cluster infrastructure. B2B faces different arithmetic. Mavisa's 125,000 claims sit inside 38 tenants; once assignment moves to the tenant the design effect is 1 + (m − 1)ρ on an average cluster of 3,289 claims, so (m − 1) = 3,288 and an intraclass correlation of only 0.004 gives 1 + 3,288 × 0.004 = 14.15. The effective sample is 125,000/14.15 = 8,834, about 4,417 an arm, and the MDE moves from 1.86 to 7.0 per cent relative: most enterprise features cannot be validated by experiment at enterprise sizes.

Hardware differs because the holdout is a manufacturing decision, AI products because the treatment drifts. Where the difference is not real, say so: sample ratio mismatch, peeking and multiplicity behave identically everywhere, being properties of the assignment and decision machinery, not of the product. By stage, a company with two hundred daily actives cannot detect anything it would act on, and the honest response is to stop running A/B tests.

8. Three worked examples

A reversal: Verified Photo Quote, 4–18 May 2026

Mazboot Durust tested a photo-based quote step over fifteen days, enrolling 45,000 photo-eligible jobs from each city so the two strata would carry equal weight. Jaipur, the pilot city, ran at 80 per cent treatment; Bengaluru, the revenue base, at 20. Yamunesh Galundia, who runs Jaipur operations, thought that right and still does: a pilot exists to learn fast, and the pooling failure is the analyst's problem.

CityT jobsT doneT rate (%)C jobsC doneC rate (%)

Jaipur36,00021,60060.09,0005,31059.0
Total (pooled)45,00028,98064.445,00034,47076.6

T = treatment, C = control; "done" is completed and paid. Rate columns are pooled over the row's own jobs, not means of city rates.

Treatment wins by 1.0 point in each city and loses by 12.2 pooled, because pooling sets Bengaluru's control against Jaipur's treatment. Weighting each city by its own 45,000 jobs gives 0.5 × 1.0 + 0.5 × 1.0 = +1.0 point, standard error √(0.25 × 0.004547² + 0.25 × 0.005792²) = 0.00368, so z = 2.72, p = 0.007, interval +0.28 to +1.72 points. The global sample ratio was exactly 45,000 to 45,000.

Forty metrics: the readout of 29 September 2026

If all forty were null and independent, the chance of at least one crossing 0.05 is 1 − 0.9540 = 87 per cent, with two false positives expected. Six crossed.

Two survive Benjamini–Hochberg, one Bonferroni, and the headline motor metric at rank four survives neither. Yet six crossings out of forty is informative: under the global null the binomial probability of six or more is 0.014, so the family is unlikely to be noise. Something real is in there, with no statement of which.

The design that failed, and the recovery

Yaduvir's first answer was a city-level test, three cities against three. A power calculation killed it. The between-city standard deviation of fill rate is 6.2 points, so a three-versus-three difference has a standard error of 6.2 × √(2/3) = 5.06, and at 80 per cent power on four degrees of freedom the MDE is (2.776 + 0.941) × 5.06 = 18.8 points — more than the inflated 18.0-point estimate it was built to test. The recovery was a switchback inside each city, and the identity it had to measure around is one day's arithmetic: on Monday 6 July Bengaluru took 3,000 requests against 2,700 job-slots, and Priority Dispatch moved 135 completions from control to treatment.

The switchback ran 3–16 August with daily alternation from a Monday, treatment taking day one, which balances day-of-week exactly, each arm taking one of every weekday. Holidays it did not balance. Saturday 15 August, Independence Day, fell on day thirteen and so on treatment, at a demand index of 126 against an ordinary Saturday's 118, lifting treatment's days to 101.1 against control's 100.0. Dropping it and control's ordinary Saturday returns both arms to 97.0 over six days each. On the surviving 36 city-days an arm, at a within-city residual standard deviation of 1.9 points, the standard error is 1.9 × √(2/36) = 0.448. The estimate is +0.18 points, interval −0.70 to +1.06 — 18.7 extra jobs a day, interval −73 to +110 — and the user-level claim sits 40 standard errors outside. The recovery's own MDE is 1.25 points, so it refutes the board paper without settling whether the effect is zero or one.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Silent fallback in the assignment layer. The early sign is a mismatch appearing in week two of a test clean in week one, usually tracking a deployment. The diagnostic question is whether the exposure and assignment logs agree on counts, not rates. Caught late it costs the whole test: Mavisa lost 21 days.

Pooling across separately randomised strata. The early sign is any stratum whose allocation ratio differs from the headline, visible to anyone printing allocation by segment. The diagnostic question is whether analysis weights match design weights. Caught late it yields a sign error, the most expensive kind, because teams act on it confidently.

Capacity-bound interference. The early sign is movement in a share metric with none in the absolute total. The diagnostic question is simply whether the total moved. At Mazboot Durust it was identical.

Metric proliferation. The early sign is a readout gaining a column every quarter and losing none. The diagnostic question is how many can veto a launch. Caught late it shows up as launches that do not replicate.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether a mismatch should automatically invalidate. The trustworthiness position rests on causes being heterogeneous and the induced bias having been seen to exceed real effects by an order of magnitude; a rule that always discards is cheap and cannot be argued away under deadline. It would be wrong if causes were mostly benign — logging lag, asymmetric bot filtering — in which case a blanket rule throws away good evidence. No clean taxonomy exists, which is why the disagreement survives.

Whether always-valid inference is a fix or a licence. Advocates argue continuous monitoring is an operational requirement, since a harmful test must be stoppable, and that a method valid at every stopping time beats a horizon nobody obeys. Critics answer that the guarantee holds against stopping rules using the test statistic, while real teams stop for a launch date or a board meeting. For the critics to be wrong, selection on those grounds would have to be uncorrelated with the effect, which a sales-driven stop is not.

Whether to answer interference by design or by estimation. Switchbacks and cluster assignment buy unbiasedness at a severe price in power, as Mavisa's move from 1.86 to 7.0 per cent shows. Exposure-weighted estimators keep the power but make the answer depend on a model of the interference. Each side's strongest claim is the other's weakest: an underpowered unbiased test and a precise biased one are both ways of not learning.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently at three moments. Before the test they write down the decision rule and the number of vetoing metrics, and compute the MDE rather than assert it. During the test they check realised allocation by segment before looking at the effect, and can say what is finite in the system and how fast it replenishes. After it they report an interval beside the threshold that would have justified shipping, and treat a diagnosis as a reason to rerun rather than a parameter to adjust.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Yashanvi did not ship Priority Dispatch as a free default. She shipped it as a paid priority tier whose revenue is ring-fenced to fund extra weekend technician capacity: a feature that cannot create supply can at least price the queue and pay for more of it. Yugank discarded Clause Match v3 and reran it tenant-randomised from 1 to 14 October, accepting that a 7.0 per cent relative MDE meant the rerun could not confirm the effect he believed in. He told the board Mavisa must pool tenants across two quarters before any single model change can be validated.

One. The switchback's MDE is 1.25 points. What would Mazboot Durust have to change about that design to separate a true effect of zero from one of one point, and what would it cost?

Two. Had the 658 misrouted claims come from the four smallest tenants instead, what would the reallocated estimate have been, and would your recommendation to Yugank change?

Three. Yamunesh argues the 20/80 allocation was correct and the reversal an analysis error. Under what conditions is he right, and what would Mazboot Durust have to publish alongside such a test for him to stay right?

13. Going deeper

  • Significance, power, sample size, peeking — the machinery assumed here; unlocks computing an MDE, not quoting one.
  • Experiments in marketplaces and networks — where interference stops being an edge case; unlocks switchback design.
  • Experimenting on ranking systems — interference through a shared index and finite positions.
  • Sequential testing and always-valid inference — the formal answer to peeking, and the disagreement above.
  • Reading launch metrics honestly — where novelty and seasonality do their real damage.
  • Writing an experiment hypothesis — the decision rule that fixes how many tests you run.
  • A/B testing fundamentals — the assumptions each pitfall breaks.
  • When you can't A/B test — the regulated and hardware cases.
  • Experimentation culture — why exception processes exist, and healthy ones.
  • Qual + quant feedback loop — the move when the MDE exceeds any worthwhile effect.
  • Feature flags and flighting — the assignment layer, where mismatch is born.
case20v1-exp.pitfalls:
Harivu and the Green Badge

A teaching case on experiment pitfalls

1. Opening

At 7:00 on Wednesday 21 October 2026, a message from Toronto reached Preethika Ambady, head of growth product at Harivu, a quick-commerce company in Bengaluru. It came from the data scientist Pushyami Aravindakshan and ran to four lines. The split of users in the free-delivery test did not match its design. She wanted the readout held. The dashboard badge for the test had been green on four of the nine days so far, including the last three.

By 18:00 on Thursday 22 October, Preethika had to tell the chief executive, Poornesh Ammanath, whether to lower the free-delivery threshold from ₹299 to ₹199 in all three cities before Diwali on Sunday 8 November. Committing the festival rider pool of ₹1.2 crore depended on her answer.

2. Company background

Poornesh Ammanath and a college friend founded Harivu in 2021. It delivers groceries and household essentials in about twenty minutes from 46 dark stores in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune, about 28,000 orders a day at an average basket of ₹420, or roughly ₹430 crore a year, mostly paid by UPI. Its rivals are Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart and BigBasket, and Poornesh believed they were competing hard on delivery thresholds ahead of the festival.

Harivu charges a ₹35 delivery fee on baskets under ₹299. Riders work from the dark stores and take whichever order is next, whichever customer placed it, so every customer in a catchment draws on one pool of riders. Last year the share of orders placed between ₹199 and ₹299 fell from 31% in September to 19% in the fortnight to Diwali, as festival baskets grew.

3. The situation

Pushyami wrote the test design on Friday 9 October. Users were to be assigned by a hash of user ID, half to the current ₹299 threshold and half to ₹199. The measure was the share of exposed users who placed an order. The design asked for about 150,000 users per arm, enough to detect a half-point change from a 39% base with 80% power at a two-sided 5% level. At about 21,800 logged users a day, split evenly, each arm would pass that figure on day 14. One readout was fixed for Monday 26 October, after the test ended on Sunday 25 October.

The test began on Monday 12 October, the day after Navratri began. A user counts as exposed when the home screen finishes drawing the fee banner. The ₹199 banner carries an animated progress bar and weighs about 1.4 MB, against 0.2 MB for the ₹299 banner. The dashboard recomputes at 06:00 IST, which is 20:30 the previous evening in Toronto, and shows green when its p-value is below 0.05. Exhibit 1 gives the nine daily readings, with the first green on Thursday 15 October.

Pushyami's Tuesday night check compared the arms' sizes with the 50:50 design and then split them by device class. Exhibit 2 shows both. Exhibit 3 shows delivery performance, which Parameshwar Anthikad in Hyderabad had been tracking since the first weekend. He said riders were being pulled across arms, and that late deliveries had risen. Poornesh read the badge differently: four green days out of nine was a trend, and Diwali would not wait for a Monday readout.

Pushyami thought the pre-festival window itself was part of the problem, since the arms shared a calendar with Navratri and the weeks before Diwali. Preethika, in Bengaluru, could not tell from the dashboard which of these concerns, if any, mattered, and the dashboard did not display any of them.

4. The people

  • Preethika Ambady, head of growth product, Bengaluru. She joined in 2023, owns the pricing decision, and wants a launch she can defend to the board and to her own data team.
  • Poornesh Ammanath, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. He wants ₹199 live before Diwali and regards a late answer as a lost festival.
  • Parameshwar Anthikad, head of operations, Hyderabad. He needs ten days to onboard riders and wants the pool commitment settled, whichever way it goes.
  • Pushyami Aravindakshan, senior data scientist, Toronto, 9.5 hours behind IST until 1 November. She wants nothing shipped on a result she cannot reproduce, and she wants her design followed.

5. Exhibits
