6. The options

Option A: ship now. Preethika tells Poornesh on Thursday 22 October to move all three cities to ₹199 and commits the ₹1.2 crore rider pool that day. Riders would be on the road from Sunday 1 November, seven days before Diwali. The pool is payable once committed, whatever later readings show. The test would be stopped, and the user counts in Exhibit 2 would stay as they are.

Option B: wait for the planned readout. The test runs to Sunday 25 October and Preethika decides on Monday 26 October using the original design. A commitment that day puts riders on the road from Thursday 5 November, three days before Diwali. Parameshwar estimates that this reaches about three-quarters of the riders a Thursday commitment would. The commitment is the same ₹1.2 crore, made four days later, and the test's logging stays as built.

Option C: stop and rerun. The team discards the current readings, spends two days making the app log each user's arm at the moment of assignment, and starts a new 14-day test on Monday 26 October, reading out on Monday 9 November, the day after Diwali. Nothing about the fee changes for the wider base until then and the rider pool stays uncommitted. Harivu forgoes whatever festival-fortnight gain ₹199 would bring the wider base.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Does the badge on day 9 measure the same thing the design in section 3 was built to measure? Use Exhibit 1 to say what each would have concluded on each day.
  2. What does Exhibit 2 add to Exhibit 1, and what does it show? Do Exhibit 3 and section 2 bear on whether the two arms were independent?
  3. If Preethika had to estimate the effect of ₹199 on the whole customer base, which figures on this page would you rely on, and what would you compute first?
  4. Which option would you take to Poornesh at 18:00 on Thursday, what would you commit and what would you tell him about the risk you are leaving open?

8. A note for the learner

This topic asks one question of any experiment: did the comparison remain a fair one from assignment to readout? Three checks follow from it, each on the numbers already in hand, before any effect is read.

First, the allocation. A 50:50 design that logs 100,400 and 95,600 users has a z of about 10.8 against its own plan, so the arms are not the groups the design describes. Within each device class the gaps are small, and Low-end Android carries 4,200 of the 4,800-user shortfall. Holding the control's class mix fixed gives 38.89% for treatment against 38.69% for control, a gap of 0.20 points with a z near 0.9, in place of the 0.47 points with z 2.12 on the badge.

Second, the looks. Reading a fixed-horizon test every morning is nine looks at one dataset. By our simulation of nine equally spaced looks, a flat 1.96 threshold flags at least once (two-sided) about 19% of the time with no true effect, and a threshold near 2.5 is needed to hold the whole path to 5%. Day 9's 2.12 is below that. The recomputation rests on our own simulation, not a published table.

Third, what the arms shared. Both arms ride one rider pool, so the treatment's extra orders can slow the control's deliveries too. Exhibit 3 cannot separate that from festival demand in the pre-test week. The contrast between arms is protected from the calendar, since both face it together, but it is not protected from a shared pool, and a full rollout would be expected to load that pool further.

One defensible path is Option C, shaped to cost less than it seems. Preethika holds the ₹1.2 crore, fixes the logging, writes the decision rule and the allocation check into the new design before launch, and tells Poornesh that today's evidence cannot support a yes or a no on ₹199. She reads allocation daily and outcomes once, on Monday 9 November. She does not claim the festival gain is forgone for certain, since it has not been measured.
case40v1-exp.pitfalls:
Indian School of Business · Product Management · Case

Izaafa and the Margin Rail

Izaafa Commerce Technologies Private Limited is fictional. The market around it is not.

1. Sunday night

At twenty to eleven on the night of Sunday 11 October 2026, Reshmika Baliga was still at the long table in her flat in Koramangala, Bengaluru, with the monsoon's last rain on the balcony and one sheet of paper in front of her. On it she had written three numbers: 4.10, 3.23, 1.54. Each was a percentage; each was a lift Izaafa's margin rail had produced in the same test, one of them on a subset of the resellers; each had been computed by someone she trusted.

In a little over ten hours she would tell the growth team whether the rail shipped; on Thursday 15 October she would tell the board. On Friday 16 October the festive code freeze closed the repository until 14 November, and the largest sales event of Izaafa's year — nine days from 24 October — would go out on whatever was in the build. Ramneek Beloor's message from Singapore, 7.14 p.m. IST, was unanswered: Need a yes or no tonight for Dubai.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2022

Izaafa was founded in Bengaluru in 2019 to sell fashion, home and kitchen goods through resellers rather than to shoppers directly. A reseller — typically a woman running a household business from a phone — forwards catalogue items to WhatsApp groups at a price she sets, and keeps the difference. In the year ended 31 March 2026 Izaafa recorded gross merchandise value of ₹7,420 crore, revenue of ₹1,180 crore and a net loss of ₹260 crore; September 2026 GMV was ₹760 crore, on 31.4 lakh monthly active resellers, in eleven languages.

In March 2022 Ranjodh Bairy, then the only engineer on platform tooling, declined a vendor quote of about ₹2.6 crore a year for a hosted experimentation service and built one in-house. Three choices he made then still hold. Assignment is keyed on a hash of the device identifier, not the reseller account. It runs inside the catalogue service, and a reseller counts as exposed only when the home feed renders. And because the hash salt rotates with every app release, live assignments are pinned in a table with a thirty-day time to live — also the retention of the assignment log every readout is built from.

3. The industry

Value commerce in India is fought over by Meesho, Flipkart's Shopsy, Amazon and DealShare, and increasingly by quick commerce — Zepto, Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart — whose ten-minute habit competes for the same impulse rupee. Payments run on UPI over NPCI rails through aggregators such as Razorpay and PhonePe under the RBI's authorisation regime, so Izaafa carries almost no payment margin and everything rests on volume and returns. Resellers past the goods registration threshold must register for GST, so anything that lifts turnover lands a tax obligation on them. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 bears on the assignment design, a device identifier held for thirty days being personal data, and Izaafa's data protection officer asked in April 2026 for the move to the account key.

Demand is brutally seasonal: roughly a third of the year's GMV lands in the Navratri-to-Diwali run-up. Outside India, a licence signed on 2 July 2026 with Ibtisaam Retail LLC of Dubai resells the Izaafa stack to the South Asian expatriate market in the GCC. The team is spread — catalogue service in Bengaluru, platform tooling in Pune, data science in Toronto, design in Berlin, partnerships in Singapore — and a Toronto staff data scientist costs ₹1.34 crore a year loaded against ₹39 lakh at that level in Bengaluru, a ratio of 3.4 to 1, which is why Toronto reviews experiments rather than running them.

4. What happened, and what was believed at the time

The margin rail is a strip on each catalogue card: a suggested resale price and a badge with the rupee margin the reseller keeps at it. The brief was approved on 20 July 2026. At the design review of 2 September, Ritambhara Balakrishnan cut a one-line disclaimer — indicative only; your margin depends on your price — because on a five-inch screen it pushed the badge below the fold. The notes record the belief that resellers would read it as an estimate.

Test E-114 ran from Monday 7 September to Sunday 27 September 2026. Enrolment closed after seventy-two hours, on 9 September, and the arms were fixed from then on. The primary metric was the share of enrolled resellers placing at least one order, and the dashboard refreshed every forty-eight hours, giving nine looks. On 9 September Bairy's crash dashboard showed catalogue-service timeouts on handsets under 2 GB of RAM at 2.3 times their usual rate; he filed a P3. The belief recorded then was that a timeout costs a session, not a cohort. The Festive Preview Sale ran 19 to 21 September at 1.8 times normal discount depth. On 23 September a reseller in Thrissur told support the app had promised her ₹180 and she had made ₹60.

Rajorshee Ballal circulated his readout memo on Tuesday 29 September: 4.10 per cent on the primary metric, z = 6.27, two further wins on secondary metrics, ship nationally. The same day Beloor sent Ibtisaam a schedule assuming an October release. On 2 October the BI warehouse took its quarterly snapshot of the assignment log, and at 09.18 IST that morning Revathika Bhattathiri sent the note that started the argument: the arms stood at 105,327 against 102,913. On 7, 8 and 9 October the assignment rows for 7, 8 and 9 September reached the end of their thirty-day life and were deleted. The only surviving record of who sat in which arm is the 2 October snapshot, which holds 1,204 fewer resellers than the platform counted.

5. The people

Reshmika Baliga, 41, chief product officer, Bengaluru. Position: the rail is probably real but the measurement is not. Incentive: a board that has heard three activation wins in eighteen months and seen none in GMV. Not saying: she approved dropping the account-key request in May 2026.

Ranadhir Bantwal, 47, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Position: ship, measure afterwards, put activation in the Series D deck. Incentive: a January 2027 term sheet priced on activation improving. Not saying: he has shown the 4.10 per cent figure to two prospective investors.

Rajorshee Ballal, 34, head of growth, Mumbai. Position: the test ran its planned length, the primary metric cleared the bar widely, and reopening it is motivated reasoning. Incentive: a shipped win funds four of six roles he has asked for. Not saying: his memo states that no platform defect was raised during the test.

Revathika Bhattathiri, 36, staff data scientist, Toronto. Position: the arms are not comparable and the cluster structure makes the reseller the wrong unit. Incentive: her account-keyed rebuild proposal of February 2026 was deferred. Not saying: she ran the cluster analysis four ways and the low-exposure figure moved between them.

Ranjodh Bairy, 39, engineering manager, experimentation platform, Pune. Position: the platform did what it was built to do; the rail's extra catalogue call is what broke. Incentive: the rebuild is his team's biggest project. Not saying: the same timeout was open during two earlier tests whose arms nobody reconciled.

Ritambhara Balakrishnan, 33, design lead, Berlin. Position: the badge is the part resellers act on; the price line alone does nothing. Incentive: the rail is her team's first shipment to the Indian catalogue in a year. Not saying: she knows the five-inch build and the under-2 GB build are the same handsets, and has never put that in a review.

Ramneek Beloor, 44, head of partnerships, Singapore. Position: the rail ships in October or Dubai becomes a renegotiation. Incentive: his variable pay turns on the Ibtisaam tranches. Not saying: Ibtisaam has twice asked him to widen the acceptance wording and he has not replied.

6. Exhibits

Exhibits 1 to 3 come off the platform and are frozen: the rows behind them are gone from the platform log. Exhibit 4 can still be re-run, on a different frame.

7. Voices

"+4.10 on activation, z of 6.27, full twenty-one days, no stops. Ship Thursday?"

Ballal, #growth-wins, 29 September, 11.04 IST

"The arms are 105,327 and 102,913. That is not rounding, it is chi-square 27.98 on one degree of freedom, and Tier C accounts for 2,381 of the 2,414. The treatment arm is short of its weakest handsets. How much of the 4.10 that explains I cannot tell you, and after the ninth the platform will not be able to either."

Bhattathiri, email to the growth and platform leads, 1 October, 23.48 EDT — 09.18 IST on the 2nd

"The spike was on my dashboard on the ninth. It did not occur to me that a timeout was also a sampling instrument."

Bairy, platform review, 2 October, 14.05 IST

"The app said I would make one hundred and eighty rupees. I made sixty. Now my sister-in-law thinks I cheated her."

Support transcript, Malayalam, reseller in Thrissur, 23 September

"Strip the badge and you have shipped a number nobody asked for. The badge is what they screenshot into the group. And yes, I cut the disclaimer — that or the badge below the fold."

Balakrishnan, design review, 6 October, 10.40 CEST — 14.10 IST

"Reshmika, I am not telling the board on Thursday that we ran three weeks on two lakh resellers and learned nothing. Pick a number you can defend."

Bantwal, voice note, 10 October, 21.15 IST

8. The options as Baliga sees them

A. Ship to all resellers on Monday, with a five per cent holdback read at ninety days, costing nothing beyond the release already cut. The holdback would be assigned by the same device-keyed service, and ninety days from 12 October close on 10 January 2027.

B. Ship to Tier A and Tier B handsets, hold Tier C — 83,209 of the control arm's 105,327 resellers, 79.0 per cent of that arm and not of the 31.4 lakh base. Needs a tier gate, four engineer-days.

C. Rebuild assignment on the account key, seventy engineer-days, and re-run cluster-randomised from 7 to 27 January 2027, reading out on 28 January. Ships nothing into the festive season and answers the April data-protection request.

D. Ship the price line without the margin badge, six engineer-days.

Each of the four is a decision about the rail. The ₹4.5 crore tranche in Exhibit 6 is written against the phrase "margin tooling live in the GCC build".

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets on Thursday 15 October. The freeze runs from Friday 16 October to Saturday 14 November, so the first working day after it is Monday 16 November. Of the platform squad's six engineers two are committed to festive capacity until the freeze lifts, and the four working days from 12 to 15 October leave sixteen engineer-days against the seventy the rebuild needs. At six engineers from 16 November it finishes on its twelfth working day, 1 December; with the year-end sale running 18 December to 4 January, the first clean twenty-one-day window after that is January's. Each platform engineer costs ₹49 lakh a year loaded over 220 chargeable days — ₹22,273 an engineer-day, so seventy days is ₹15.6 lakh.

Cash at 30 September 2026 was ₹412 crore against net burn of ₹21.7 crore a month, nineteen months of runway, and Bantwal's Series D conversation assumes an activation story. The ₹4.5 crore acceptance tranche turns on 31 January 2027. The data protection officer's request is six months old. General counsel has asked that any margin figure shown to a reseller carry a disclaimer, citing the representations provisions of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. And the enrolment rows have left the platform log, so whatever is decided on Monday can be checked only against the 207,036 resellers in the snapshot.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. By tier, where and by how much do Exhibit 1's two arms differ? What does that let you say — and not say — about which resellers are not in the comparison?
  2. Ballal's post of 29 September calls the test "full twenty-one days, no stops". From Exhibit 3 and its footnote, what would a readout written at the day-11 look have said, and what does the A/A replay imply about reading any single look?
  3. Reproduce Exhibit 2's pooled and standardised lifts from its cells and reconcile them with its three within-tier lifts. What would have to be true of the 2,414-reseller gap between the arms for either figure to be the rail's causal effect?
  4. In Exhibit 4 the measured lift rises from +1.54 to +6.82 per cent while the control rate falls. Give two mechanisms that would produce that pattern, and say what Izaafa would have had to randomise to tell them apart.
  5. Exhibits 5 and 6 value the same feature differently. List every base, window and population on which they differ, and say which, if either, reconciles with Exhibit 2.
  6. What should Baliga do on Monday morning, 12 October, what would she say to the board on Thursday, and what would she commit to measuring before next September?

At a quarter past eleven Baliga wrote a fourth figure under the three on her sheet — 177, the replays out of a thousand that crossed the line on nothing at all — and drew a box around all four without writing anything inside it. Thursday's deck had a slide headed Reseller activation: September test, and the slide was empty. Outside the rain had stopped, and the first festive hoarding was going up over the junction.
exp20v2-exp.pitfalls:
Experiment pitfalls

How a clean-looking test stops meaning what its p-value says

1. The readout

On Tuesday 29 September 2026, Vanmali Ediwala, head of product at Lokmandi, a neighbourhood-grocery app with 2.4 million monthly users across Ahmedabad, Surat and Vadodara, opened the readout of a two-week test of a “Repeat basket” button on the home screen. The measure was order conversion: the share of users who ordered within 24 hours of their first visit during the test. Control showed 8.00 per cent of 76,900 users; treatment 8.30 per cent of 75,100. The gap, 0.30 points, carried a p-value of 0.033.

On Saturday 19 September, once the 24-hour windows of day five (Friday 18 September) had closed, the dashboard had shown a 0.60-point gap and a p-value of 0.011, and Vrajlal Eswarwala, who ran operations, had asked why the test was still running. Vanmali had waited. Now Varenya Erachwala, the data scientist, had appended a line nobody requested: the arms differed by 1,800 users, which fair assignment should almost never produce. The festive-season merchandising calendar froze on Friday 30 October. A shipped button would take a home-screen slot from the pantry-staples shelf and cost six engineer-weeks; shipped wrongly, both would be spent on nothing.

2. The idea

An experiment pitfall is any way in which a randomised comparison, an A/B test, stops answering the question its p-value appears to answer. A p-value is the probability, if the change did nothing, of seeing a gap at least as large as the one observed; that promise holds only for the exact procedure the arithmetic assumes. Each pitfall is a gap between that procedure and the one actually run.

The families are old. The inequality behind the Bonferroni correction for many simultaneous tests dates to Carlo Bonferroni’s 1936 paper; Peter Armitage and colleagues showed in 1969 that testing accumulating data repeatedly inflates false positives; Edward Simpson described the aggregation reversal in 1951; Donald Rubin formalised the no-interference assumption in 1980. Sample ratio mismatch was named and popularised by online-experimentation teams, notably at Microsoft, in the 2010s. The sentence Vanmali can repeat: “A significant result is only as good as the procedure that produced it, so we audit the procedure before we read the result.”

3. How it works

Fix the rule before the data. Lokmandi’s plan named one primary metric, a baseline of 8.0 per cent and a minimum detectable effect (MDE, the smallest true gap the test is built to catch reliably) of 0.4 points. At a 5 per cent significance level (the false-alarm rate tolerated when nothing is happening) and 80 per cent power (the chance of catching a true 0.4-point gap), that requires about 73,850 users per arm; at roughly 5,400 per arm per day, 14 days.

Then audit assignment before reading any outcome: do arm sizes match the intended 50:50 split? Then read outcomes once, at the pre-set horizon; then account for how many questions were asked; last, examine the effect over time. Two steps practitioners leave implicit are deciding beforehand which result would be ignored, and testing arm sizes against the observed total rather than the planned one. The table applies the final step to Lokmandi’s data.

Days 1–5 and week 1 agree because they share users. Week 2 shows no lift at all. The all-days figure is an average of a real early gap and an absent later one, and it is that average, not either half, that crossed the significance line.

4. A worked example

Begin with arithmetic Vanmali had accepted. Pooled conversion is 12,385 of 152,000, or 8.148 per cent. The standard error of the gap (the typical size of chance fluctuation in it) is the square root of 0.08148 × 0.91852 × (1/76,900 + 1/75,100), which is 0.140 points. The gap of 0.2996 points divided by that is a z-statistic of 2.13, p = 0.033, with a 95 per cent confidence interval from +0.02 to +0.57 points. The estimate, 0.30, sits below the 0.4 the test was built to detect; an estimate that only just clears significance tends to overstate the truth, the winner’s curse.

Now the audit. With 152,000 users and a 50:50 intent, each arm should hold 76,000. The deviations are +900 and −900, so chi-square, a statistic summing squared deviation over expected count, is 900²/76,000 twice: 10.66 + 10.66 = 21.32. With one degree of freedom, p is 0.0000039, about one in 257,000. Assignment used a random hash, so chance did not do this. Vihanika Eksambia, the engineering lead, traced it in an afternoon: the treatment banner image weighed 1.9 MB, the home screen rendered slowly on low-end phones, and exposure was logged only on render, so impatient users vanished from the treatment count.

Second pass, changing one input. Suppose the 1,800 missing treatment users, the shortfall of treatment against control, are restored. The answer depends on how they would have ordered, which nobody knows.

If they ordered like everyone else, the lift survives at 0.30. If they ordered at roughly half that rate, it falls to 0.20 and stops being significant. The mismatch does not say which way the bias runs; it says the licence to read the result has lapsed.

5. Nuances a learner must know

Sample ratio mismatch audits the pipeline, not the product

A 2.3 per cent difference between arms sounds small, yet here it is a one-in-257,000 event. Magnitude is not significance. Because the check runs on every experiment, many teams alarm at p < 0.001 and block the readout until a cause is found.

Peeking is not forbidden; unmanaged peeking is

Peeking means reading results repeatedly and stopping at the first significant one. Figure 2 shows the false-positive rate when nothing is happening and the test stops at the first look beyond z = 1.96, with equally spaced looks (simulated, two million paths per bar). Daily looks over 14 days give 21.9 per cent, not 5. Sequential designs, which spend the 5 per cent across looks, make peeking legitimate.

Many metrics, one chance of a fluke each

Lokmandi’s dashboard shows 20 metrics. If none moved, each still has a 5 per cent chance of crossing p < 0.05, so the chance that at least one does is 1 − 0.9520 = 64.2 per cent, and the expected number of false alarms is 20 × 0.05 = 1.0. A basket-value metric at p = 0.03 would fail the Bonferroni threshold of 0.05/20 = 0.0025. That threshold is conservative when metrics are correlated; Benjamini and Hochberg’s 1995 procedure instead controls the expected share of false discoveries among those declared.

Simpson’s paradox hides in unequal mix

In an earlier banner test, a campaign week fed treatment mostly new installs. Treatment beat control inside both segments yet lost overall, because the arms held different mixes.

Table 3. A reversal on aggregation

Pooled rates: 840/10,000 and 460/10,000. The fix is to check segment mix like arm size, and to analyse within segments.

Interference breaks the independence of users

Interference means one user’s arm changes another’s outcome, violating Rubin’s assumption that each result depends only on that user’s own assignment. Riders are shared. Take an evening hour with 1,150 orders, 575 per arm, and capacity for 1,200 deliveries. Treatment demand rises 10 per cent to 632.5; total demand, 1,207.5, exceeds capacity by 0.6 per cent. Shortfall shared proportionally leaves 628.6 treatment orders against 571.4 control, still a 10.0 per cent lift. Launched to everyone, demand would be 1,265 against capacity 1,200, so orders rise from 1,150 only to 1,200: 4.3 per cent.

Novelty, primacy and seasonality are timing effects

Novelty is a curiosity bump that fades; primacy is the opposite, users resisting change before adapting. Seasonality is a calendar pattern, such as a month-end salary spike. Fourteen days cover two weekly cycles but neither a salary cycle nor a festival. Week 1 versus week 2 differ by 0.60 points with z = 2.15, itself only borderline; one should not over-read either half.

A clean audit proves less than it seems

Passing every check establishes internal validity: the arms are comparable. It does not show the effect lasts, transfers to other cities, or matters commercially. Before relying on a result, ask who counted the users, what the decision rule was before the data, and which results would have been ignored.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

In consumer products traffic is abundant and cycles are short, so the dangerous pitfalls are statistical: peeking, novelty, many metrics. In B2B, with perhaps 60 customer accounts, power is thin, users inside an account influence each other, and one large account can dominate; teams lean on staged rollouts and matched accounts rather than coin-flip tests. In marketplaces, interference dominates, and designs randomise by city or alternate treatment on and off by time block (a switchback).

Size matters too. A start-up with 2,000 users a day needs 147,700 users for the 0.4-point MDE: 74 days. In 14 days, 14,000 per arm, its MDE is 0.93 points (about 11.6 per cent relative). It must either chase bigger effects or accept slower learning. A large company has the opposite trouble: so many concurrent tests that overlap and automated checks matter more than any single analysis.

7. Common mistakes

Declaring victory at the first significant look. Symptom: the lift shrinks in the weeks after launch. Misunderstanding: that a p-value is valid whenever it is read. Diagnostic: replay the daily z-scores and ask how many days would have crossed 1.96 by chance.

Waving through a small mismatch. Symptom: arm sizes differ by two per cent and the note says “close enough”. Misunderstanding: treating a percentage gap as the test of a split. Diagnostic: chi-square on the counts, computed before any outcome is opened.

Quoting a metric the plan never named. Symptom: the launch note celebrates a number absent from the experiment brief. Misunderstanding: that finding a signal and testing a hypothesis are the same. Diagnostic: count the dashboard’s metrics against the brief’s and apply the corrected threshold.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the same decision begins with a written rule and an automated mismatch alarm. The alarm fires on day eight, not day sixteen; the banner image is compressed before the second weekend; the primary read waits for the horizon, or follows a sequential boundary stated in advance. The readout carries an interval, a week-by-week chart, one primary metric and a short list of guardrails, with every other metric labelled exploratory.

9. What Vanmali decided

He did not ship. He asked Vihanika to cut the banner to under 200 KB by Friday 2 October, and restarted the test on Monday 5 October for 21 days: a first week excluded as burn-in with no announcement push, then a read window of Monday 12 to Sunday 25 October, 14 days at 75,600 users per arm against the roughly 73,850 required. Readout would fall on Tuesday 27 October, three days before the freeze. Vrajlal grumbled about the delay and accepted it once Vanmali showed him Table 2.

Learn next how marketplaces and networks handle interference, then sequential testing, which makes early looks legitimate. Two questions to sit with. If the lost users had been the most engaged rather than the least, which way would the bias run, and would you know? And what would you have wanted written down before 14 September that would have made the 19 September dashboard impossible to misuse?
exp20v2-exp.marketplace:
Experiments in Marketplaces and Networks

A case-style explainer on two-sided interference, clusters and switchbacks

1. The Fourteen-Point Result

On Monday 14 September 2026, Paramita Adhya, head of marketplace at Haatkhola, read a two-line message from her data scientist, Pronoy Alam: "Pickup Boost won. Fourteen points." Haatkhola, based in Guwahati, runs a two-sided marketplace: shops post delivery orders on one side, and independent couriers choose which to accept on the other. It handles about 14,000 orders a day across five cities, 2,000 of them in Guwahati.

Pickup Boost attaches a ₹20 bonus to an order, shown to couriers on the offer screen. From Tuesday 1 September to Sunday 6 September, Pronoy had split Guwahati's shops at random, so that half the orders carried the bonus. The metric was the ten-minute pickup rate: the share of orders collected within ten minutes of posting. Treated shops reached 71 per cent; control shops, 57.

The arithmetic looked decisive. Finance valued each extra on-time order at ₹150 in avoided cancellations and repeat purchases, so a ₹20 bonus breaks even at a lift of 13.3 points (20 divided by 150). Fourteen cleared it. On Thursday 24 September the board would decide whether to fund the bonus in all five cities, at ₹2,80,000 a day. If the true gain were much smaller, Haatkhola would lose roughly ₹7 crore a year. An hour later Pronoy wrote again: "I do not trust the fourteen. The couriers are the same people in both groups."

2. The Idea: Interference

A standard A/B test rests on a quiet assumption: each unit's outcome depends only on its own assignment. Donald Rubin's 1980 formulation, the stable unit treatment value assumption, made it explicit, building on David Cox's 1958 book on experimental planning. Interference is its violation: treating one unit changes the outcome of another.

Marketplaces violate it by construction, because both sides draw on shared, scarce resources such as couriers, drivers, listings and advertising budget. When a treated shop's order recruits a courier, that courier is unavailable to a control shop. Researchers at eBay documented the resulting bias in 2014; Cornell and Facebook researchers proposed randomising clusters of a network in 2013; delivery and ride platforms adopted time-based switchbacks in the 2010s, and statisticians formalised them in the early 2020s.

Two designs answer the problem. A cluster design randomises groups of units that interact heavily, such as neighbourhoods, so most interaction stays inside one arm. A switchback design randomises time: the whole market receives treatment in some periods and control in others.

The sentence Paramita could repeat in a meeting: randomise at the level where units share the scarce thing, or you are measuring redistribution, not growth. Figure 1 shows why.

3. How It Works

Pronoy's reasoning ran in six steps, several of which practitioners leave unspoken. First, name the shared resource. Here it is courier attention: a courier handles one order at a time, and a bonus changes which order wins.

Second, decide who can affect whom, which fixes the unit of randomisation. Shops never touch each other directly, but any two shops in an area compete for the same couriers, so the interacting group is the courier pool. Randomising shops splits one market into two arms that still trade with each other. Third, choose the design. Zones form natural clusters, but a sample of 9,000 pickups showed 2,700 (30 per cent) made outside the courier's usual zone, so zone arms would leak. Time is cleaner: Guwahati operates from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., six two-hour blocks a day, and the whole city flips together.

Fourth, set block length against carryover, the lingering effect of one period on the next. Couriers who log on for a bonus stay about an hour, contaminating the start of the following block. Fifth, analyse at the level you randomised: each block yields one pickup rate, and the comparison runs across blocks, not orders. Sixth, fix the decision rule before looking: roll out only if the interval's lower end reaches 13.3 points. One condition sits beneath all six: the treatment must be switchable. A bonus can be turned on and off within seconds; a redesigned app cannot be toggled every two hours without confusing users, so switchbacks suit only reversible changes.

4. Worked Example: Two Passes

First, what the shop-level test measured. Treated shops: 71 per cent of 6,000 orders, 4,260 collected within ten minutes. Control: 57 per cent of 6,000, or 3,420. The gap is 14.0 points. Its standard error is the square root of (0.71 × 0.29 ÷ 6,000 + 0.57 × 0.43 ÷ 6,000), or 0.87 points, giving an interval of 12.3 to 15.7, treating orders as independent, which understates it. The test looked precise. It answered the wrong question.

Now pool the arms: 7,680 of 12,000 orders, 64 per cent, were collected promptly, against a baseline of 60 from the four weeks before 1 September. The bonus lifted treated shops 11 points above baseline and pushed control shops 3 below it, as couriers were drawn away. Half of each is the market effect: (11 − 3) ÷ 2 = +4 points. A full rollout leaves no unbonused orders to steal from, so the gain is nearer 4 than 14. At ₹150 an order, 4 points earns ₹6 against a ₹20 bonus: a loss of ₹14 an order, or ₹1,96,000 a day across 14,000 orders.

Second pass: change one input, carryover. If bonus-attracted couriers linger an hour, the first hour of a control block after a treated one runs 2 points high, adding 1 point to that block; treated blocks after control start half-ramped, losing 1. Half of all blocks follow the other arm, so each arm's mean shifts 0.5 and the untrimmed estimate falls from 4.0 to 3.0 (row D). Trimming the first hour restores 4.0 but leaves about 167 of 333 orders per block, so binomial noise lifts the spread from an assumed 3.0 to about 4.0 points. With 42 blocks per arm, the interval grows from ±1.3 to ±1.7.

5. Seven Nuances

Interference is not confounding

Confounding means treated and control units differ before treatment, and randomisation cures it. Interference means randomisation worked perfectly and the arms still contaminate each other. Pronoy's arms were balanced on every shop attribute and the estimate was still wrong, so a clean balance table offers no reassurance. Start detecting interference by asking what resource both arms touch.

The bias can run either way

Here shops compete for couriers, so the naive gap overstates. Where units are complements, as with a referral reward paid to inviter and invitee, treating some users also helps their untreated friends, and the naive gap understates. Ask whether units compete or cooperate. The arms alone cannot reveal the direction; a pre-period or whole-market comparison can.

Exposure share changes the answer

The treated-versus-control gap depends on the split. With 10 per cent of shops treated, a few boosted orders face many unboosted rivals, and the gap would probably exceed that at 50 per cent. Any result describes one share; a rollout implies 100 per cent. That is why the exposure share belongs in the write-up, beside the sample size.

Pooling is a shortcut, not a test

Averaging the arms recovered +4 only by assuming that 50 per cent exposure behaves like full exposure and that the 60 per cent baseline stayed put. Neither was tested. Treat it as a planning estimate awaiting a design that exposes the whole market. A pre-period baseline also quietly absorbs weather, festivals and payday effects.

Block length trades bias against power

Longer blocks dilute carryover but yield fewer blocks. Two-hour blocks give 84 in two weeks; four-hour blocks give 42, and halving the count multiplies the standard error by about 1.4. Demand also varies by hour, so shuffle within each day. Choose the shortest block whose carryover you can afford to trim.

Clusters trade leakage against count

Bigger clusters contain more interaction but leave fewer units to randomise. Haatkhola's five cities barely leak, yet a two-against-three split leaves one city's quirks, perhaps a festival or a flood, to decide the answer. Pairing similar cities and randomising within pairs helps, but the count remains the limit.

What the design cannot tell you

Two weeks measure the short run. Couriers may change their hours, shops their posting habits, rivals their prices, and equilibrium takes months. Before relying on any estimate, ask what is shared, who competes for it, how long the effect lingers, and at what share you will deploy it. Long-run effects usually need a holdback market left untreated for months.

6. Consumer, B2B and Marketplace

In consumer products with little sharing, such as a checkout redesign, user-level randomisation is sound; interference appears in feeds and referrals. In B2B, users inside one customer account influence each other, so the account is the cluster. Marketplaces are the severe case because the scarce good is shared by design. Scale matters too: a young company with one city cannot cluster and relies on switchbacks or small holdouts, while a large one with dozens of markets can randomise whole cities. Early-stage teams can tolerate a rough answer because errors are cheap; at Haatkhola's scale, ₹7 crore a year justifies two weeks of design.

SettingWhat is sharedUsual unit
ConsumerLittle; feeds, referralsUser

7. Common Mistakes

Trusting a narrow interval. Symptom: an implausibly large lift with a tight interval that vanishes at rollout. Misunderstanding: precision mistaken for validity. Cheapest diagnostic: compare each arm with the pre-period; a control group that fell below baseline signals interference.

Analysing orders from a switchback. Symptom: "significant" after two days. Misunderstanding: orders in one block share a market state and are not independent. Diagnostic: recompute from block means; an honest interval is wider.

Ignoring carryover. Symptom: the estimate grows as blocks lengthen. Misunderstanding: assuming a bonus stops mattering when the flag turns off. Diagnostic: plot the estimate against minutes since the block began; a ramp reveals the lingering effect.

Reading the pooled mean as proof. Symptom: a launch memo quoting 4 points with no interval. Misunderstanding: treating an assumption-laden shortcut as a measurement. Diagnostic: ask which design exposed the whole market; if none did, the figure is a forecast.

8. What Good Looks Like

Paramita's target is a test she can defend. It names the shared resource, randomises at the market level, fixes block length and trimming, and pre-commits the rule: roll out only if the interval's lower end reaches 13.3 points. Under that rule even the shop-level result, whose lower end was 12.3, would not have passed. She reads block means, not orders, and reports the interval beside the estimate so the board sees how much of the decision rests on noise. Figure 3 shows the readout she wanted.

9. Closing

On 24 September Paramita withdrew the five-city proposal and asked the board for a 14-day Guwahati switchback from Monday 28 September to Sunday 11 October. Treated blocks cover 14,000 orders, so the bonus costs ₹2,80,000, against about ₹7 crore a year on the pooled estimate. She chose it because the courier pool is the thing being shared, and time is the only unit inside one city that does not split it. The rule travels with the request: she will recommend rollout only if the interval's lower end reaches 13.3 points, and she told the board she expects it will not.

Next, study variance reduction and power, since switchbacks are noisy and the interval, not the estimate, will decide. Two questions to sit with: if Haatkhola's couriers also work for a rival, what is the market? What evidence would make you trust a pooled estimate over a randomised one?
exp40v2-exp.marketplace:
Experiments in marketplaces and networks

Why two-sided experiments contaminate themselves, and how to design around it: interference, cluster randomisation, switchbacks, and the estimand you actually needed.

1. Two desks, one broken assumption

On Monday 30 March 2026, Rupanjali Bhowmick, vice-president of marketplace science at Ithaka Freight Exchange in Pune, read a memo saying her company had found ₹106.6 lakh a month lying on the floor. Ithaka matches shippers to road-fleet operators on eighteen trunk corridors. A new bid-ranking model had been tested on carriers over the twenty-eight days from 2 to 29 March: 2,100 treated carriers won 15,840 loads and 2,100 control carriers 12,960 — a 22.2 per cent lift, 5,760 extra loads a month across 4,200 carriers at ₹1,850 of take rate a load.

She turned to the operations dashboard. Over the same twenty-eight days the marketplace cleared 28,800 loads against 27,720 in February, up 3.9 per cent — and loads cleared are Ithaka's only revenue. If treated carriers won 2,880 more loads than control and the market grew by 1,080, most of the memo's ₹106.6 lakh was the same money moving between trucks. The pricing committee met on 6 April and expected a number.

In Bengaluru that Thursday, 2 April, Riddhiman Bharali had the opposite problem. Ikonta sells an AI-assisted collaboration workspace to enterprises: 240,000 paid seats across 1,200 workspaces. A new thread summariser posts a plain-language digest into a shared channel. Ikonta's launch rule required a 5 per cent lift in weekly active days; the seat-randomised test, also 2 to 29 March, returned 3.36 days a week for treated seats against 3.30 for control — plus 0.06 days, 1.8 per cent. The feature died. Riddhiman's objection was mechanical: the summary posts into the channel, and control seats read it. He had measured not a feature against its absence but writers of summaries against readers of them.

Both desks had struck the same assumption from opposite sides.

2. The idea, and the schools that disagree about it

The formal object is a potential outcome. Write Yi(z) for unit i's outcome when the vector of assignments across all N units is z. A/B testing works only if this collapses to Yi(zi) — my outcome depends on my own assignment and nobody else's. In the Neyman–Rubin tradition that is half of SUTVA, the stable unit treatment value assumption; Cox stated it in 1958 as the condition of no interference between units. Interference is its failure.

The idea was invented for soil. Fisher's randomised blocks answered heterogeneity, and guard rows answered the rest: fertiliser and pests reaching a neighbouring plot and changing its yield, so the plot was the wrong unit and the block became the unit. Vaccine trials inherited the structure through herd immunity, with the same answer — randomise villages, not people. Marketplaces rediscovered it between 2010 and 2018, once software made randomising the wrong thing cheap.

The mechanism fixes the sign of the error, as Figure 1 sets out. Where units compete for a scarce shared resource, treatment wins what control loses and the contrast overstates; where they share information or a graph, treatment's output reaches control and the contrast understates. Ithaka sat in the first world, Ikonta in the second.

Three camps disagree, about estimands rather than technique. The design-first camp moves the randomisation unit until it encloses the interference. It will sign: a user-split estimate of a market-clearing change answers a question nobody asked. It will not sign: you can model your way out afterwards. The model-and-adjust camp keeps the efficient unit and estimates the response-to-exposure curve. It will sign: the global effect is recoverable if exposure is randomised at more than two levels. It will not sign: clusters are cheap. The equilibrium camp holds the counterfactual to be a different equilibrium no short experiment visits. It will sign: estimate primitives, then simulate the clearing. It will not sign: a three-week switchback measures the long run.

3. Mechanics: what the estimand actually is

Expert practice begins with a model of exposure. The workhorse is linear in the treated share: for unit i in market m with treated share pm, let Yi = α + d·zi + s·pm, d being the direct effect of one's own assignment and s the spillover from everyone else's. A within-market split compares units at the same pm, differencing out the spillover to estimate d. A rollout needs the global treatment effect, pm = 1 everywhere against 0, which is d + s.

That reframes the problem. A 50/50 user split is not a biased estimate of the global effect; it is an unbiased estimate of a different quantity, and the gap is s. Clusters and switchbacks work by one trick: make the randomised unit large enough that pm is 1 inside treatment and 0 inside control, so the contrast is d + s — in space or in time.

Riddhiman's three numbers identify both parameters, the step usually left implicit. The workspace-randomised test, 6 April to 3 May, gave 3.48 days a week in treated workspaces against 3.18 in control, so d + s = 0.30. In the seat split every workspace was half treated, so its control level was α + 0.5s = 3.30 against a pure control α = 3.18, giving s = 2 × (3.30 − 3.18) = 0.24 and d = 0.06. Treated seats should then read 3.36, and did. Of the total, 0.24 of 0.30 — 80.0 per cent — was spillover, as Figure 2 sets out.

Precision is the price. Ikonta's seat split carried 120,000 seats an arm at a seat-level standard deviation of 1.60 days: a minimum detectable effect of 0.018 days. The workspace split carried the same seats as 600 workspaces of 200, and an intra-cluster correlation of 0.05 inflates the standard error by the root of the design effect 1 + 199 × 0.05 = 10.95, so 0.0183 × 3.31 = 0.061 days — 3.31 times blunter on identical data, and the only design answering the launch rule's question.

Relative terms mislead: +0.06 is 1.8 per cent of 3.30 and +0.30 is 9.4 per cent of 3.18 — different bases, so the absolute figures are like-for-like.

4. When it applies, stated as testable claims

Three conditions do the work, each checkable before an experiment runs. First, do units compete for a fixed stock inside the measurement window? At Ithaka, definitionally: 36,000 loads were posted in the March window and a load has at most one winner, so the carrier side is near zero-sum. At Ikonta, no: a summary costs nobody a seat. Second, is any unit's output visible to another inside the window? At Ikonta, yes by design; at Ithaka, partly — carriers see each other's winning bids in the corridor feed, an informational channel atop the resource channel. Third, is the decision a global rollout? For both, yes, which is what makes d alone insufficient.

The idea is actively misleading in two situations. One is a decision that ranks variants rather than a go/no-go, where interference common to all arms largely cancels and the cheap split gives the right ordering. The other is a constraint binding on a far longer time-scale than the window: a carrier fleet is fixed in a month but not a year, so a switchback is silent about the entry it would induce — a clean answer to a question not at issue.

5. Hard edge cases

In multi-product companies two teams' clusters rarely coincide. Ithaka's supply team randomises carriers; its pricing team randomises corridors. Run in the same week, each becomes the other's interference. Two-sided designs are the hard case: randomising shippers and carriers independently creates four cells, but a matched load belongs to one shipper and one carrier, so half the cells are mixtures. Most teams abandon the 2×2 and randomise the market.

Regulated settings often forbid the split outright: a lender under an equal-treatment obligation cannot route two identical applicants to different models in the same hour, so a time-based switchback is the only lawful randomisation. Hardware-plus-software fleets inherit a shared physical resource — service-centre queues, depot bays — that software cannot separate, so the depot is the cluster, named or not. In AI-native products the interference moves inside the evaluation harness: arms sharing a retrieval index, a prompt cache or a rater pool are not independent, and a cache warmed by one arm serves the other faster. At the seam, mature companies say they run a central exposure registry. What they run is a lease: one market-level test a corridor-week, traded informally and overridden twice a quarter.

6. Eight things experts see that competent practitioners do not

Interference changes the estimand, not the variance. The tell is vocabulary: someone calls it contamination and proposes a larger sample. More data buys a confident estimate of the wrong quantity. The obvious reading treats it as noise because it arrives as an inconsistency, and inconsistency usually is noise.

The sign of the error is a property of the mechanism. An expert asks what is shared before asking how big the effect is: scarcity inflates, information deflates. The tell is a team that cannot say which way its bias points; if it cannot, it has not named the channel — and an unnamed channel is usually both.

Exposure level is part of the estimand. Under strict linearity a split recovers d at every share; the moment the curve bends, a 1 per cent holdout and a 50 per cent split estimate different local slopes and neither is d + s. The tell is a result quoted without its exposure share. The obvious reading — a small holdout is conservative — has no sign until you know the curvature.

Clusters must enclose the interference, not the org chart. Ithaka clears by corridor and time of day, so a city cluster leaks along every corridor leaving it. The tell is a cluster matching a reporting hierarchy — and accountability boundaries are exactly where markets are permitted to cross.

Block length is set by the carryover half-life. A block must be long enough that behaviour induced in one decays before the next is measured. The tell is a block length equal to a calendar unit — a day, a shift, a week. Short blocks buy sample size, a trade experts make deliberately and novices accidentally.

A switchback's effective sample is not its block count. Adjacent blocks are correlated, and burn-in discarded at each block's head removes real exposure. The tell is a power calculation treating 2,016 blocks as 2,016 independent observations — because blocks look like table rows, and rows invite the assumption.

Two-sided randomisation does not double power. It creates four cells on a population with one join key per transaction, so the cross cells are mixtures and the main effects are not what a one-sided test gives. The tell is a two-sided test reported as two one-sided results.

Interference has a time constant. Reallocation happens in hours; entry, exit and price adjustment take quarters. The tell is a switchback result that decays after rollout, read as novelty. Often it is the slow channel arriving: the design held s at its short-run value and the market never would.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

In consumer social products the graph is the interference and graph cluster randomisation is the answer; the hard part is that a few dense communities dominate, so clusters are badly unbalanced. In B2B and enterprise the cluster is handed to you — the account — which is why Ikonta's fix was obvious once named, and why 1,200 workspaces in two arms is the whole customer base, not a sample. In platforms and marketplaces the resource channel dominates and switchbacks are the default. For hardware and physical goods, inventory is the shared stock and the cluster is geographic because the warehouse is. For AI products only the shared object is new.

Stage changes the arithmetic, not the theory. An early-stage marketplace has too few market-periods for a switchback to have power at any block length, so its teams should switchback to detect catastrophe and judge the rest. At scale the constraint inverts: ample power, and a queue of teams wanting the same market-periods. Where the difference is not real, say so plainly: the estimand problem is identical in a ten-corridor exchange and a ten-thousand-corridor one.

8. Three worked examples

a. Ithaka's carrier split, and an analyst's correction

Exhibit 2 holds the March test. The naive contrast is 15,840 − 12,960 = 2,880 loads on 2,100 treated carriers; scaled to all 4,200 that is 5,760 loads a month, 22.2 per cent against a naive counterfactual market of 2 × 12,960 = 25,920. A junior analyst subtracted the market's growth of 1,080 loads from 5,760 and called 81.3 per cent of it displacement. Rupanjali sent the memo back: the 1,080 was measured while half the carriers were treated, so it is (d + s)/2, not d + s. Doubling it, the full-rollout effect is 2,160 loads, 7.8 per cent on the February base of 27,720 — ₹40.0 lakh a month rather than ₹106.6 lakh — with displacement (5,760 − 2,160) ÷ 5,760 = 62.5 per cent, which Figure 3 lays out. The analyst had priced a half-exposed ramp as fully ramped.

Exhibit 2 — Ithaka carrier split: loads won, 28-day windows
Carrier armPre-period, 1–28 FebTest window, 2–29 MarChange in row
Treatment, 2,100 carriers13,86015,840+14.3%
Control, 2,100 carriers13,86012,960−6.5%
Total, 4,200 carriers27,72028,800+3.9%

Onboarding was frozen on 19 January, so the population is closed: every cleared load is won in one arm. Posted loads were flat at 36,000 in each window, so clearance rose 77.0 to 80.0 per cent and the +1,080 is clearance, not demand. The 7.8 per cent assumes February's clearance is a valid counterfactual; a seasonal term moves it, and the 62.5 per cent with it. A point estimate, not a bound.

b. Ikonta's workspace split, and the vanity-metric problem

Exhibit 1 records the fix: the same seats re-randomised by workspace, returning 0.30 days a week against an MDE of 0.061 — five times the seat-split estimate, and well powered. The second finding was about the rule. Weekly active days is near a vanity metric for a summariser meant to let people stop reading threads: a tool that works should plausibly reduce visits. Ikonta's 5 per cent bar had been calibrated on seat splits, each measuring d alone.

c. The switchback that failed, and what recovery cost

Ithaka's answer was a switchback: 18 corridors × four six-hour blocks × 28 days = 2,016 market-periods from 6 April to 3 May, each handed wholly to one arm, 1,008 an arm. Power looked free. At a mean of 14.29 loads a market-period and a standard deviation of 5.60, the MDE is 2.80 × 5.60 × √(2 ÷ 1,008) = 0.70 loads, inflated to 0.83 by a 1.19 carryover factor — 5.8 per cent of the mean, roughly matching the carrier split: SD 4.40 over 2,100 carriers an arm gives 2.80 × 4.40 × √(2 ÷ 2,100) = 0.38 on its February base of 6.60. The window cleared 29,484 loads, a mean of 14.625, treatment blocks at 15.05 against control at 14.20: +0.85, 6.0 per cent.

Each corridor runs 112 blocks and its first has no predecessor, so the cells cover 18 × 111 = 1,998 of the 2,016 periods. Weighting them back gives 14.20 for control and 15.05 for treatment, and (15.05 + 14.20) ÷ 2 = 14.625, the window mean, the arms being equal.

The failure is in Exhibit 3 and Figure 4. Control blocks following a treatment block cleared 14.60 loads against 13.81 for control blocks following control: 0.79 loads of contamination inside the control arm. The ranking had taught carriers a price anchor they carried forward, so carryover outlasted the block. The clean same-arm-preceded contrast is 15.23 − 13.81 = 1.42 loads, 10.3 per cent on 13.81. The naive 0.85 was 59.9 per cent of it: carryover attenuated the estimate by 40.1 per cent. It also sits above the market reading's 7.8 per cent, which the redesign was meant to settle.

Recovery was a redesign, not a reanalysis. Blocks went from six hours to forty-eight, the first twelve hours of each block discarded as burn-in, and the window from 28 days to 84: 18 corridors × 42 blocks = 756 market-periods, 378 an arm, 11 May to 2 August. The outcome became the clearance rate, whose standard deviation falls from 0.150 at six-hour granularity to 0.090 at forty-eight, so the MDE is 2.80 × 0.090 × √(2 ÷ 378) = 0.0183 — 1.83 points on a 0.800 base, 2.3 per cent relative, against 2.8 for the six-hour design carrying its 1.19 factor. Burn-in removes the carryover, so the redesign cost calendar time, three months instead of one, and bought precision rather than spending it.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Treating interference as noise. Early sign: experiment and dashboard disagree, and the remedy proposed is a longer run. Diagnostic: what would this estimate equal at full rollout, and which term in it did we measure? Late, the cost is a roadmap whose forecasts exceed actual growth.

Clustering at the wrong boundary. Early sign: the cluster is named after an organisational unit. Diagnostic: draw the shared object; is any instance touched by both arms? Late, it yields a test underpowered and still biased.

Carryover longer than the block. Early sign: Exhibit 3's signature — control-after-treatment above control-after-control. Diagnostic: split both arms by the preceding block's arm and compare same-arm cells. Late, it attenuates toward zero, so the features it kills leave no incident, only an absence.

Contaminated guardrails. Early sign: a user-split test reports market-level guardrails as neutral — which a within-market split cannot move in expectation. Diagnostic: is this guardrail defined over the randomisation unit or the market? Late, a feature clears on a guardrail incapable of flagging it.

Experiment collision. Early sign: two market-level tests share a corridor-week. Diagnostic: who else is randomising this market, at what unit? Late, both results are unusable and the loss is a quarter of calendar time.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether the global effect is the right target. The decision-sufficiency position is stronger than it sounds: most decisions are relative, interference is common to all arms, and a split test reliably delivers the sign. Its evidence is the large class of ranking changes where cluster and split designs agreed in direction. It fails wherever magnitude decides rather than sign: Ithaka's March test had the right sign and 62.5 per cent displacement. Nobody has a base rate.

Whether switchbacks can be trusted at all. The sceptical position: block length is set by an unobservable carryover half-life, estimating it needs the experiment you are designing, and the diagnostic has low power exactly when carryover is modest. The optimistic reply: long blocks, burn-in and the diagnostic bound the problem, and Ithaka's redesign is the bet. It would be wrong if carryover were multi-week, which for a price anchor it may be.

Whether exposure-curve designs substitute for clusters. Randomising markets to several exposure levels and extrapolating to 100 per cent is efficient and assumes a functional form; the linear model that let Rupanjali double her 50 per cent-exposure figure is that assumption, untested above a 50 per cent share. Proponents note that clusters assume something too: that they do not interfere with each other.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this writes down the estimand before the metric and the exposure share before the sample size. They state the interference channel in a sentence and predict the sign of the error before seeing data. When experiment and dashboard disagree they ask which quantity each estimates, and are rarely surprised to find both right. They price design changes in calendar time, where the cost lands. And they treat the decision rule as apparatus: a bar inherited from the seat-split era is a defect in the instrument.

12. The decisions

On Monday 11 May, Rupanjali declined to roll out. She told the pricing committee the change was worth ₹40.0 lakh a month rather than ₹106.6 lakh, but that the figure rested on February being a valid counterfactual, which she would not defend in a board pack. She bought the 84-day switchback instead, pre-committing to a rule: roll out if the clearance-rate lift exceeds 2.3 per cent, the design's own MDE, with a lower bound above zero. Riddhiman shipped the summariser that day on the 0.30-day workspace estimate, asking that the 5 per cent bar be suspended for any feature travelling through a shared channel.

1. Rupanjali's 7.8 per cent figure doubles a 50 per cent-exposure observation. What would you need before accepting linearity from 50 to 100 per cent, and what would you do if the exchange cannot afford to find out?

2. Ikonta's spillover was 80.0 per cent of the total effect. Does that make the seat split worthless, or the only clean estimate of d the company has?

3. Both fixes were paid for in calendar time. Who should own the budget of market-periods at a company with twelve teams and eighteen corridors?

13. Going deeper

  • Experiment pitfalls — the parent topic; interference is its marketplace member, and sample-ratio mismatch, novelty and selection need different cures.
  • Writing an experiment hypothesis — naming the estimand and the exposure share makes most of this page's errors impossible to commit quietly.
  • A/B testing fundamentals — SUTVA is stated there; this page is what happens when you drop its second half.
  • Significance, power, sample size, peeking — unlocks the design-effect arithmetic that makes a cluster choice a number, not a preference.
  • When you can't A/B test — the regulated and hardware cases lead to synthetic control and interrupted time series.
  • Experimentation culture — the corridor lease is organisational before it is statistical, and this is where its rule gets decided.
  • Qual + quant feedback loop — the fastest way to name a channel is to ask ten carriers what changed; no switchback can.
exp20v2-exp.quasi:
Quasi-Experiments and Causal Inference

A case from Nolen Fresh

1. A rule changed in one city

Nolen Fresh, a grocery delivery app serving Kolkata, Bhubaneswar, Patna, Guwahati and Ranchi, changed one rule on Monday, 1 June 2026. In Kolkata only, orders of ₹249 or more would now ship free; the old threshold was ₹399. Anirban Hossain, the director of product, had approved the change but could not randomise it. Inside one dark-store catchment, two neighbours seeing different fees would screenshot the difference and flood support.

On Tuesday, 4 August, Hossain faced the finance head, Ankur Hore, with a number to defend. Kolkata households were ordering 2.10 times a week, up from 1.80 before the change. Extending the rule to the other four cities was scheduled for 1 September, and Hore valued the forgone fees at ₹9 per household per week. If the rise was caused by the policy, rollout was easy. If part of it was monsoon, Nolen would be paying to subsidise rain. The analyst Arindam Hui, whose first message that morning read "Kolkata is up, but so is everywhere", had one question to answer: what did the policy cause?

2. The idea

The problem these designs solve is that the world rarely waits for analysts: prices, laws and rules arrive for whole populations at once. A causal effect is the difference between what happened and what would have happened without the intervention. The second quantity, the counterfactual, is never observed, so every causal claim leans on a stand-in. A randomised test builds the stand-in by coin toss. A quasi-experiment, from the Latin quasi, "as if", finds the stand-in in the structure of events when a coin toss was unavailable: another city, an earlier period, a cut-off rule.

The vocabulary comes from Donald Campbell and Julian Stanley's 1963 treatment of research designs; Campbell and Donald Thistlethwaite had used a cut-off rule on scholarship scores in 1960. Economists popularised difference-in-differences when David Card and Alan Krueger, in 1994, compared fast-food employment in New Jersey, which raised its minimum wage, with neighbouring Pennsylvania, which did not. Alberto Abadie and co-authors added the synthetic control in 2003 and 2010.

Hossain could say one sentence in the meeting without sounding glib: "We cannot watch Kolkata without the policy, so we borrow the trend of cities that did not get it, and we say how wrong that borrowing could be."

Table 1. Three designs and the stand-in each builds
DesignStand-in for Kolkata without the policyNeeds
Difference-in-differencesKolkata's own past, moved by other cities' changeParallel movement
Synthetic controlWeighted blend of cities matching Kolkata's historyLong history, many candidates
Regression discontinuityBaskets just below the cut-offNo steering across it

3. How it works

Hui worked in five steps, two of which analysts often leave unwritten. First, he fixed the cohort: households that ordered at least once in the eight weeks to 5 April. He tracked them afterwards whether or not they ordered, so that households attracted by cheaper delivery could not alter the denominator. Second, he fixed the outcome as orders per household per week, zero-order weeks included.

Third, he chose comparison cities. Bhubaneswar and Patna had shared no promotions with Kolkata and ordered in similar rhythms; Guwahati and Ranchi had launched in January and were still ramping. Fourth, he inspected the eight weeks before launch, because the design assumes parallel trends: without the policy, Kolkata's gap to the comparison cities would have stayed as it was. That can be made plausible, never proved. The gap averaged 0.29 orders in weeks one to four and 0.31 in weeks five to eight. That already contains a placebo: a launch four weeks early would show +0.02. The cohort is too small to say whether that is noise, yet it equals two-thirds of the 0.03 margin above break-even.

Fifth, he computed each group's change and subtracted. The subtraction removes anything that struck both groups alike, such as the monsoon, and anything permanently different, such as Kolkata's habit of ordering more. What remains is whatever happened in Kolkata alone at that moment. Hui also considered a synthetic Kolkata, but two usable cities and eight weeks of history left too little to weight. Figure 2 draws the logic.

4. The arithmetic, twice

Kolkata rose 0.30; the comparison average rose 0.12, so the shared trend explains two-fifths of the naive figure (0.12 divided by 0.30). The difference-in-differences is 0.30 minus 0.12, or 0.18 extra orders per household per week. Equivalently, the Kolkata gap widened from 0.30 (1.80 minus 1.50) to 0.48 (2.10 minus 1.62).

Hore supplied the economics. Each extra order contributes ₹60 after the waived fee. The lower threshold gives away a ₹29 fee on the 0.31 weekly orders per household that would have fallen in the free band anyway, 0.31 times 29, or about ₹9. Break-even is therefore ₹9 divided by ₹60, or 0.15 extra orders. At 0.18, the net is 0.18 times 60 minus 9, or ₹1.80 per household-week; across 2,00,000 active households in the four other cities, 52 weeks come to about ₹1.87 crore a year.

Now change one input: the comparison. Table 3 shows the verdict moving with the choice, though the data never changed. Neither single-city figure is the truth; each is the pooled estimate with the weights moved, and equal weights were chosen on operating grounds before he saw the cities separately.

5. Nuances that separate users from understanders

The counterfactual is estimated

Nolen saw Kolkata with the policy and never without it. Hossain should say "estimated effect", and treat the spread from 0.15 to 0.21 as a floor on his uncertainty, not as a confidence interval.

Parallel trends concerns change, not level

That Kolkata ordered 0.30 more than the comparison before launch is irrelevant; subtraction removes it. What matters is that the gap would not have drifted. Had Kolkata's lead been growing by 0.02 a week before launch, the same arithmetic would have credited the policy with a trend already under way. A steady pre-period supports this but cannot prove it, and a shock arriving after launch is invisible to any pre-period check.

Quasi, natural and randomised

A natural experiment is a quasi-experiment in which something outside the analysts' control, a lottery, a border, a regulation, assigned treatment. Kolkata was chosen by people expecting it to work, a weaker case: cities picked for treatment may differ in ways that predict the outcome. Randomisation removes this by design; quasi-methods only argue it away.

Choose the design by the data's shape

Difference-in-differences needs a before, an after and an untreated group, and tolerates level gaps. A synthetic control suits one treated unit among many candidates: weights are chosen so the blend tracks the treated unit's history, level included. Its weights are non-negative and sum to one, so the blend cannot stray outside the cities observed. Regression discontinuity needs a rule.

Discontinuities answer a narrower question

Figure 3 shows reorders rising from 33 per cent just below ₹249 to 39 just above, six points. That is the effect of crossing the line for baskets near ₹249, not of the policy overall. Worse, among those July baskets, the band from ₹239 to ₹249 held 2,300 orders and the next held 3,900, about 70 per cent more, which suggests customers top up to qualify. People just above may differ from those just below.

Concurrent events masquerade as effects

Had a rival launched free delivery in Kolkata alone in June, the method would credit Nolen with the rival's doing. Ask what else changed in one group near launch: a competitor, a festival, a tax change, a supply shortage.

What no design can tell you

Eight weeks says nothing about week twenty, when novelty fades. Nor does any design here reveal why households ordered more, whether cheaper baskets, fewer abandoned carts or a rival's loss. And the result belongs to Kolkata; Ranchi may differ.

Questions before relying on it

Who chose the treated group, and why? Is the comparison independent of the treated one? Was the outcome fixed in advance? Does the pre-period look steady, and do placebo dates show nothing?

6. Consumer, business and marketplace settings

Consumer products supply thousands of households and long histories, so city-level comparisons work if seasonality is shared. Business products have few accounts; two accounts compared is an anecdote, so staggered launches across account groups serve better. Marketplaces break the assumption that units are independent: free delivery in Kolkata may pull riders from Patna, contaminating the comparison. An early-stage company often lacks history and comparison units, so a cheap randomised test beats cleverness. A large one has history and markets but also many simultaneous launches, each a candidate confounder.

Table 4. Where each setting is strong and where it breaks
SettingStrengthHazard
ConsumerMany householdsSeasonality
BusinessClear contractsFew units
MarketplaceGeographic splitsSpillover between sides
Early-stageSpeedThin history
LargeMany marketsConcurrent launches

7. Common mistakes

Quoting before-and-after as the effect

The launch deck says "up 0.30" with no comparison. The misunderstanding is that calendar time is neutral. Cheapest diagnostic: ask what the untreated cities did over the same weeks.

Choosing the comparison after seeing results

The deck cites one estimate, never the 0.15 to 0.21 range. The belief is that any control is as good as another. Diagnostic: write the selection rule beforehand and report one estimate per candidate.

Ignoring spillover from treated to untreated

Imagine Patna's ordering drifting up after Kolkata's launch because shared riders were reassigned. The misunderstanding is that cities are sealed. Diagnostic: ask operations whether any resource moved between them.

Trusting a steady pre-period picture

Confidence rests on a chart of the weeks before launch. The misunderstanding is that parallel before means parallel after. Diagnostic: placebo tests at several earlier launch dates, which should show roughly zero.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the team writes its rules on 20 May, before launch: the cohort, the comparison cities, the placebo test, the 0.15 break-even and the instruction to roll out only if the estimate clears it. Hui reports all three estimates in Figure 4, beside what he checked and what he could not check. Hossain then argues from where the evidence sits relative to the line, and the finance head sees the same three points and the same threshold.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

Hossain asked for rollout in Ranchi and Guwahati on 1 September, and for Bhubaneswar and Patna to keep the old threshold for eight more weeks. His reasoning: the estimate sits barely above break-even, the gain at 0.18 is small, and delaying two cities costs little. Holding them back lets the next rollout serve as a second look, but Ranchi and Guwahati are still ramping, so Hui must first check their pre-launch gap to the comparison cities before reading any estimate against 0.15. If it holds, the case for the other two strengthens; if not, Nolen has spent eight weeks and a small subsidy, not a year.

He also asked Hui to run placebos at several earlier cut dates and attach them to the rollout memo, so Hore could see the drift the assumption allows.

Next, study geo experiments and incrementality measurement. They design the comparison on purpose instead of discovering it afterwards.

Two questions to sit with

First, suppose a rival launched free delivery in Kolkata on 15 June: what would you do with the 0.18, and what data would you request? Second, what is the cheapest randomised test Nolen could run in Guwahati to check it, and what would that test cost that this study did not?

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Experimentation & Causal Inference

Quasi-experiments and causal inference

Difference-in-differences, synthetic controls and regression discontinuity, worked through on two live decisions — and the uncomfortable fact that the design choice, not the data, usually sets the answer.

1. Two decisions, one missing randomiser

On Thursday 11 June 2026, Barnali Ishtiaque had a number she did not believe. Padatik Mobility, the two-wheeler taxi and courier network where she ran growth, had launched a ₹99-a-month ride pass in Indore on Monday 6 April; pass holders got 35 per cent off every fare. Over the eight weeks that followed, Indore averaged 214,600 completed rides a week against 182,400 in the eight weeks before — a lift of 17.7 per cent. The investment committee met in a fortnight, and a national roll would discount every pass holder's every ride indefinitely.

Barnali could not run an A/B test. A fare is a public price, filed with the transport authority city by city; randomising riders inside Indore would leak in a day, so whatever she took to the committee would be built on cities, not users. In a March memo she and Bhargabi Inayet, Padatik's staff economist, had fixed the rule in advance: roll nationally at a lift of 8.0 per cent or more, kill below 5.0, extend in between.

On Tuesday 21 July, Binayak Ingtipi faced the mirror image. Parimiti Systems, his Pune employer, sold field-service software to mid-market manufacturers. Its Guided Setup programme attached a solution architect for six weeks to any new account whose implementation-readiness score reached 70, and only to those. Among 270 accounts within fifteen points of the cutoff, 69.2 per cent above the line reached production inside ninety days against 45.3 below — 23.8 points. Six architect-weeks at ₹40,000 cost ₹2.4 lakh an account, so the 120 of those 270 above the line cost ₹288 lakh, and the revenue chief wanted the programme for everybody. Binayak had to price those 23.8 points, knowing no coin had assigned the score.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A quasi-experiment exploits a feature of the world that assigns treatment in a way the analyst did not control but can characterise well enough to argue from. The estimate is never the interesting part; the identifying assumption is. Every method completes one sentence differently: "the untreated units tell us what would have happened to the treated ones, because …".

The lineage predates the vocabulary. John Snow's 1854 comparison of London districts drawing water from Lambeth, which had moved its intake upriver in 1852, with those drawing from Southwark and Vauxhall, which had not, is a difference-in-differences in all but name. Thistlethwaite and Campbell (1960) introduced regression discontinuity; Campbell and Stanley (1963) named the field and catalogued its threats; Ashenfelter (1978) found the pre-treatment dip that carries his name. Card and Krueger (1994) made difference-in-differences standard; Abadie and Gardeazabal (2003), then Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller (2010), built synthetic controls for one treated unit no single control resembles. Goodman-Bacon (2021) and Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) then showed the two-way fixed-effects regression run on staggered rollouts to be a weighted average that could put negative weight on clean comparisons.

Four positions contend, and what each refuses to sign is the more informative half. The design-based school signs "credibility comes from the assignment mechanism, not the model"; refuses "a flexible enough model substitutes for a design". The structural school signs "without a behavioural model you cannot extrapolate past the treated margin"; refuses "the effect at the cutoff is what a decision-maker needs". The algorithmic school signs "weights should come from a stated loss, not judgement"; refuses "more covariates always improve a counterfactual". The decision-theoretic school signs "an estimate without a loss function is not a decision input"; refuses "0.05 is a decision rule". Barnali's thresholds put her in the fourth camp.

3. Mechanics, worked

Padatik operates in twenty-three cities. Six of the twenty-two untreated were disqualified — four in litigation, two running promotions — leaving sixteen eligible controls, of which Bhargabi chose five on pre-period trend fit: standard practice, and the first thing a referee should attack.
