The difference-in-differences estimate is 32.2 − 19.6 = 12.6 thousand rides a week, or 12.6 ÷ 182.4 = 6.9 per cent of Indore's pre-period base, against the naive 17.7. Three-fifths of what her dashboard called an effect was growth the five control cities enjoyed too.

The dashed line exposes the assumption. Before treatment Indore gained 4.7, 4.9 and 5.2 thousand rides per block while the pool gained 5.7, 5.6 and 6.2 — averages of 4.93 against 5.83, a differential of −0.90 per block. Indore was growing slower. Carried two blocks forward, that drift puts the counterfactual change at 19.6 − 1.80 = 17.80 and the trend-adjusted effect at 32.2 − 17.80 = 14.4 thousand, or 7.9 per cent: non-parallel trends deflated this estimate, a direction knowable only by computing it.

A synthetic control replaces the equal-weight pool with weights fitted to reproduce Indore's pre-period: Coimbatore 0.26, Vijayawada 0.24, Rajkot 0.25, Nashik 0.18, Jodhpur 0.07, summing to 1.00. They give a pre-period of 182.5 against 182.4 — a residual of 0.1 — and a post-period of 202.8 against 214.6. The gap is 11.8 thousand; differencing changes rather than levels, removing that bias, gives 11.9. Both round to 6.5 per cent.

Three estimators thus give 6.5, 6.9 and 7.9 per cent. Inference is harder: with one treated unit the honest test is a permutation.

Indore ranks first of six, so the smallest one-sided p-value this design can produce is 1 ÷ 6 = 0.167. That is not a weak result; it is the floor. With all sixteen eligible controls it is 1 ÷ 17 = 0.059, and 0.05 needs nineteen controls Padatik lacks. The largest placebo, Coimbatore's +5.52, is 44 per cent of Indore's on the same leave-one-out basis; an in-time placebo on the P−2/P−1 boundary gives −1.0. Bhargabi's conclusion: real in direction, and not resolvable in magnitude below the 4.6-thousand standard deviation of the five control changes themselves.

4. When it applies, as testable claims

Exhibit 4 — The conditions, each stated so it can fail, applied to both decisions.
ClaimPadatik (DiD / synthetic)Parimiti (RD)

Rows two and three are how a quasi-experiment dies quietly: selection into treatment, contamination of the comparison. Neither appears in a standard error. A fourth claim — enough independent units for a p-value — fails for Padatik and holds for Parimiti.

The idea becomes actively misleading in three situations. First, when the treated unit was chosen because its outcome was already moving — the Ashenfelter dip inverted. Second, when treatment reallocates a fixed resource: Indore's rides rose 17.7 per cent and its driver hours 4.1, so measured rides per driver-hour rose 13.1 per cent (1.177 ÷ 1.041). Most of the naive lift was utilisation, which has a ceiling a national roll would hit. Third, when the estimand is not the quantity needed: Parimiti's discontinuity estimates the effect at a score of 70, while its revenue chief wanted Guided Setup extended to accounts scoring 40.

5. Hard edge cases

In two-sided markets the control group is rarely clean, because supply is mobile in a way demand is not. A courier incentive in one pincode pulls riders off adjacent pincodes, so a within-city geo test understates the treatment and overstates the control. The cure is a unit the spillover cannot cross — a city, a labour market — which is why Padatik has sixteen controls and a floor.

Multi-product companies break parallel trends through their own roadmap: if the treated market also got a new app shell that quarter, the arm holds two treatments and the estimate belongs to the bundle. Regulated settings sometimes hand you a better design than you could build — a rule above a filing threshold, a tariff changing at a state border — while hardware adds a cohort problem, firmware arriving on connectivity's schedule.

AI-native products are the new case: the treatment is a model version, retrained on data its own deployment generated, so the post-period control is itself partly treated. Freezing it makes the comparison stale-model rather than no-feature.

At the organisational seams the failure is political. Marketing owns an attribution vendor reporting one incrementality number, finance owns a geo test reporting another, nobody owns the reconciliation. Mature companies do not pick the better method; they write the design and the rule into the plan before the quarter starts and treat disagreement as a trigger for a holdout.

6. Eight things experts notice

The pre-trend test's power, not its p-value. A test that fails to reject parallel trends across four noisy pre-periods has told you almost nothing. The tell is wide intervals under a confident caption. Ask what drift it could have detected; if that exceeds your expected effect, it is decoration.

A staggered rollout is not one difference-in-differences. Two-way fixed effects on staggered treatment averages every two-by-two comparison, some using already-treated units as controls, sometimes negatively weighted. The tell is an estimate outside the range of every clean two-by-two computed by hand.

The denominator moves with the treatment. Rides per active rider can rise while rides fall, if the treatment churned out light users. The tell is a rate improving while numerator and denominator both decline. State the denominator and its date, and check it moved before blaming composition.

Regression discontinuity estimates a local effect. The quantity is the effect for units at the cutoff, who are by construction marginal; the obvious reading, "the programme works", swaps an average for a boundary. The tell is a deck applying an RD estimate to everyone, as Parimiti's revenue chief proposed.

A good pre-period fit is the objective function, not evidence. Synthetic weights are chosen to minimise pre-period error, so a tight fit is guaranteed, not informative. The tell is near-zero error with forty donors and twelve pre-periods: overfitting with a chart. Fit on earlier pre-periods, check later.

With one treated unit, the permutation floor is one over the number of units. One treated city and seven controls cannot produce a one-sided p-value below 1 ÷ 8 = 0.125, so a reported 0.01 assumed the wrong sampling universe. The tell is an interval on rider-weeks for an effect assigned to cities.

Spillover makes the control a treated group. If the control's own level jumps at the treatment date, it is not a control. The tell is a placebo moving the treatment's way at the same moment. The subtler version is anticipation: the last pre-period becomes the outlier because customers waited.

An effect measured on a ramp is not the effect of the end state. A rollout reaching 35 per cent exposure only in week four spent fewer full-exposure days than its label implies, so dividing the lift by nominal exposure understates the per-user effect. The tell is one exposure figure for a changing window.

7. Where the differences are real

In consumer products the binding constraint is the number of independent units, not of users: Padatik has millions of riders and sixteen usable controls, and the second sets the precision. In B2B the opposite holds — accounts are few but assignment is often rule-based, so thresholds, renewal dates and territory boundaries supply discontinuities consumer products rarely have. Parimiti's readiness score is a better instrument than anything in Padatik's data, and it exists only because somebody wrote a rubric.

Platforms and marketplaces face that spillover and, worse, equilibrium effects: a change raising one seller's conversion may lower another's, so individual effects sum past the market effect. Hardware gets clean geographic and cohort discontinuities — a distribution boundary, a serial number — at the price of long lags. AI products differ in kind, because the counterfactual drifts.

Stage matters less than people claim. A seed-stage company with one market cannot run a geo test and should stop pretending; its honest tools are the discontinuities in its billing and onboarding logic. From roughly ten markets these methods start to pay. What changes with scale is not the method but the standard of proof the organisation tolerates — cultural, not statistical.

8. Three worked cases

Padatik, worked above, is the first. Parimiti, and the heap at 70: Binayak fitted local linear trends either side of the cutoff.

Assigned at 70.0 and above. Below the cutoff, 150 accounts and 68 live, 45.3 per cent; at or above, 120 and 83, 69.2 — the naive 23.8-point gap. The total row, 151 ÷ 270 = 55.9, is pooled, not the 57.2 mean of band rates.

The left fit runs through (62.5, 44.0) and (67.5, 50.0), slope 1.2 per score point, reaching 53.0 at the cutoff; the right through (72.5, 66.0) and (77.5, 70.0), slope 0.8, reaching 64.0. The discontinuity is 11.0 points against the naive 23.8, a ratio of 2.17. All three bands a side, by least squares, give 64.3 − 52.2 = 12.1, so bandwidth moves the answer a tenth.

Then Binayak checked the density. Of the 50 accounts in the 70.0–74.9 band, 19 sat in 70.0–70.9, where a uniform density predicts 50 ÷ 5 = 10 — an excess of 9, or 2.85 Poisson standard deviations (9 ÷ √10). Three of the score's nine inputs are editable by the account executive.

Excluding the heap gives a doughnut estimate. The remaining 31 accounts, now spanning 71.0–74.9 with a midpoint of 72.95, were 58.1 per cent live (18 of 31); against 70.0 at 77.5 that implies a right-side slope of 2.62 and 50.3 at the cutoff — a discontinuity of −2.7 points. He did not report that as the effect — a two-point slope on 31 accounts is not a slope — but the adjacent-band contrast, 58.1 against 50.0 below, or 8.1 points. Those bands lie 5.45 points apart, so 8.1 assumes a flat response; his own left slope of 1.2 implies 6.5 points of trend across them, leaving a slope-matched 1.5. The heap itself went live at 78.9 per cent (15 of 19) against 58.1 for the rest of its band — 20.9 points on a standard error of 12.9, or 1.62 standard errors: suggestive, not established. His range ran −2.7 to 12.1, with 8.1 the figure he defended.

The design choice sets the economics. ₹288 lakh buys 13.2 ninety-day launches at 11.0 points (₹21.8 lakh each) and 9.72 at 8.1 (₹29.6 lakh), but only 1.8 at the slope-matched 1.5 (₹160 lakh). Against the ₹34 lakh of three-year margin Parimiti books on an early launch — itself an unidentified correlation — the first two clear and the third does not.

Pratimaan Instruments, where it failed. Bratin Inghi's company sold connected water-quality sensors to municipal utilities. In October 2025 his team reported a predictive-maintenance module raising first-visit work-order closure by 9.9 points: six treated districts moved 58.0 to 71.6 (+13.6) against eight controls' 61.5 to 65.2 (+3.7), the 9.9 being 17.1 per cent of the treated base. The module had gone to districts that asked.

Two things were wrong. Two of the six treated districts had also received a revised sensor board. Splitting the arm, the four module-only districts moved 59.4 to 68.3 (+8.9) and the two board districts 55.2 to 78.2 (+23.0); weighting four and two reproduces the pooled 13.6, and the clean module-only contrast is 8.9 − 3.7 = 5.2 points, 8.8 per cent of 59.4. Second, the volunteers were already improving faster: over the prior year treated districts gained 3.9 points (54.1 to 58.0) against controls' 2.6 (58.9 to 61.5) — 1.3 a year, or 0.975 over nine months. Subtracting it, assuming the four shared the six's prior trend, leaves 4.2, so selection accounted for 0.975 ÷ 5.2 = 18.8 per cent of the clean effect, not "most of it", as the first review memo asserted without computing anything. An eighteen-month audit closed in August 2026 at 4.6 points; the headline had overstated the module 2.2-fold.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

All six are cheap to catch in advance and expensive afterwards, because by then the organisation has committed to a number. Padatik wrote its diagnostics into the plan; Pratimaan did not, and its recovery cost two quarters and a renegotiated supply contract.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first is whether a bad estimate beats no estimate. The design-based position: a strategy failing its own test should produce no reported number, because organisations anchor on numbers and discard caveats; the evidence is the quasi-experimental findings randomised trials later reversed. The operating position, shared by a strand of decision theory: the alternative is not abstention but somebody's unexamined prior. For the first to be wrong, organisations would have to discount caveated estimates properly; for the second, caveats would have to survive two levels of presentation.

The second is pre-trend testing. One camp holds a passed test weak evidence and an underpowered one none, so parallel trends should be argued from how assignment happened, not tested. The other holds that testing rules out gross violations and that institutional arguments are unfalsifiable. Roth's result that pre-testing distorts the distribution of surviving estimates supports the first; the second replies that the alternative is to stop looking.

The third is fitted weights versus simple averages. Abadie's position is that a stated loss should choose the weights; the sceptics hold that with few pre-periods those weights are noise dressed as method. Padatik is a weak test: 11.8 against 12.6 is 6 per cent on a quantity whose control changes scatter by 4.6 thousand. Out-of-sample tests on many treated units would settle it; the few that exist do not.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this reaches for a method and then looks for data. Someone who has internalised it reaches for the assignment mechanism first, then asks which method it permits. They write the decision rule before the estimate, and state the denominator and its date unprompted. They compute the direction of a bias instead of describing it, as Bhargabi did on finding the pre-trend ran against the treatment. They count independent units before promising precision, and say "the effect at the cutoff" rather than "the effect". And when a correction is inconvenient they run it anyway and report the range — which is why Binayak took −2.7 to 12.1 to a chief who wanted one number.

12. What they decided

Barnali took the three estimates and the permutation floor to the committee a fortnight later. Because 6.5, 6.9 and 7.9 per cent all sat inside the pre-registered band, she asked for an extension, not a national roll: the pass to run in four more cities drawn by lottery from the sixteen eligible controls. Indore is already treated, so the assignments that exist are the lottery's C(16, 4) = 1,820, and the floor falls from 1 ÷ 6 to 1 ÷ 1,820 — the whole argument for a geo experiment over a quasi-experiment. Binayak recommended Guided Setup stay as it is, defended at 8.1, and that the three editable inputs be locked and logged: not to improve the programme, but to make the next two years of data answer what the first two could not.

Discussion questions

  1. Barnali's five controls were selected on pre-period trend fit. What does that do to the placebo distribution in Exhibit 3, and in which direction?
  2. Parimiti's five estimates span −2.7 to 12.1 on the same 270 accounts. Which would you take to the board, and what must you believe about the 19 heaped accounts?
  3. Pratimaan's audit landed at 4.6 points against a corrected 4.2. Does that validate the correction, and what else would you check first?

13. Going deeper

  1. When you can't A/B test — is randomisation unavailable, or merely inconvenient?
  2. Test markets and geo experiments — makes the city a randomisation unit, collapsing the floor.
  3. Incrementality measurement — the same mathematics on spend, holdout deliberate.
  4. Writing an experiment hypothesis — produces the rule that rescued Barnali's meeting.
  5. A/B testing fundamentals — the benchmark these methods approximate.
  6. Significance, power, sample size, peeking — "how many control cities", answered properly.
  7. Experimentation culture — whether a range survives a leadership review.
  8. Qual + quant feedback loop — the only tool left with one market.
  9. Feature flags and flighting — decides which units can be treated separately, so which designs exist.
exp20v2-exp.heterogeneous:
Heterogeneous treatment effects

It won on average. Did it lose for anyone?

1. A green dashboard on a Monday

On Monday 5 October 2026, Kishwar Samanta, head of product analytics at Cairnstone, a grocery-delivery company operating in Kolkata, Bhubaneswar and Guwahati, opened the results of a three-week experiment. The feature, Basket Memory, filled a customer's cart with the items from their recent orders the moment the app opened. Kabeer Sinharoy, the vice president of product, wanted it live for everyone the following Monday, 12 October, ahead of the Puja fortnight, when marketing planned to spend heavily on new customers.

The test had run from 14 September to 4 October on 240,000 users, all enrolled on 14 September and split at random into 120,000 who saw Basket Memory and 120,000 who saw the old app. The share who placed at least one order within 21 days rose from 34.0 to 34.8 per cent. The result was significant, the dashboard was green, and Sinharoy had already drafted the launch note.

At 6.40 that morning, though, Kuhoo Sarbadhikari, the data scientist who built the analysis, had sent a different table: the same result split by whether a user had ordered before the test began. Kishwar read it twice. A feature that helps some customers and quietly hurts others can still win on average, and the gap would surface in retention, not in this week's dashboard. This page follows her reasoning.

2. The idea

A treatment effect is the difference an intervention makes to an outcome, here the change in the chance that a user orders. For any one person it is the gap between what happened to them with the feature and what would have happened without it. We can never observe both, so the individual effect is unobservable. This is what the statistician Donald Rubin, building on Jerzy Neyman's work from 1923, formalised in the 1970s as potential outcomes: each user carries two possible results, and we see only one.

Randomisation gets around this for groups. Because chance decides who is treated, the two arms resemble each other, and the difference between their averages estimates the average treatment effect (ATE). The problem it creates is that an average is a blend. Heterogeneous treatment effects means the effect differs across identifiable kinds of user. The effect inside one such kind is a conditional average treatment effect (CATE), "conditional" because it is conditioned on membership of the group. Researchers such as Susan Athey and Guido Imbens have since built methods to search for such groups systematically.

The sentence Kishwar could repeat in the meeting without sounding glib: "The average tells us what happens to the user base; it does not tell us what happens to any user."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have four steps, plus one that practitioners usually leave unspoken. First, compute the overall effect. Second, define groups using only facts known before randomisation: here, whether the user had at least one order before 14 September. Third, estimate the effect inside each group with its own uncertainty. Fourth, compare the group effects with one another, since the question is whether they differ, not merely whether each is nonzero.

The unspoken part is that the overall effect is a weighted average of the group effects, with weights equal to each group's share of users. Cairnstone's test population was 70 per cent returning and 30 per cent new, so the headline equals 0.7 times the returning effect plus 0.3 times the new effect. The headline is therefore a statement about this mix as much as about the feature.

Figure 1 shows the whole story. The top bar, the overall result, sits right of zero with an interval that clears it. The green and red bars are the components averaged into it. Neither interval comes near zero, and they point in opposite directions. The top bar is small because the two larger effects partly cancel, which is what a blend looks like when a feature helps one group and hurts another.

4. A worked example

Sarbadhikari's counts are in Table 1. Each arm held 84,000 returning and 36,000 new users. In the control arm 33,600 returning users ordered, which is 40.0 per cent of 84,000; in the treatment arm 35,280 did, or 42.0 per cent. Among new users the control rate was 7,200 of 36,000, or 20.0 per cent, and the treatment rate 6,480 of 36,000, or 18.0 per cent.

The pooled row checks out: 33,600 plus 7,200 is 40,800, which is 34.0 per cent of 120,000, and 35,280 plus 6,480 is 41,760, or 34.8 per cent. The overall lift of 0.8 points is 0.7 times 2.0 plus 0.3 times minus 2.0. To judge uncertainty, the standard error (the typical sampling wobble of a difference) for new users is the square root of 0.20 times 0.80 over 36,000 plus 0.18 times 0.82 over 36,000, about 0.29 points. A 95 per cent interval runs 1.96 standard errors either side of the estimate, giving minus 2.57 to minus 1.43. The harm to new users is about seven standard errors from zero. It is not noise.

The test of heterogeneity itself uses the difference between the group lifts, 4.0 points, with a standard error of the square root of 0.240 squared plus 0.292 squared, about 0.38. That is more than ten standard errors. The two groups genuinely differ.

Second pass: change one input. Suppose the Puja campaign lifts the new-user share from 30 to 50 per cent, and assume each group's own effect stays put. The overall effect is then 0.5 times 2.0 plus 0.5 times minus 2.0, which is zero. Table 2 sweeps the share.

Figure 2 draws the warning. The same feature, with unchanged effects on each kind of user, is a clear win on 14 September's mix, a wash at 50 per cent new users, and a loss beyond about 60 per cent. Shipping to returning users only is positive at every share in Table 2. The decision depends on audience composition at least as much as on the feature.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Different size versus different sign

Statisticians call a gap in magnitude with the same sign a quantitative interaction, and a reversal of sign a qualitative one. The first usually still justifies shipping to everyone; the second does not. Cairnstone's is qualitative, which is why the average misleads.

Segments chosen before versus after

A split specified before the test is one hypothesis. Splits discovered afterwards are many. Slicing twenty ways at the 5 per cent level gives a 1 minus 0.95 to the twentieth power, or 64.2 per cent, chance of at least one false "finding". Even a modest six pre-planned cuts need a stricter threshold: dividing 0.05 by six gives 0.0083, about 2.64 standard errors. New users clear that comfortably, at 6.8.

Subgroups are underpowered

Power is the chance a test detects an effect that really exists. A group has fewer users than the whole, so it detects less. For the 36,000 new users per arm at a 20 per cent base rate, the smallest effect detectable with 80 per cent power is about 0.83 points. An insignificant subgroup is therefore not evidence of no effect; it may be a blur.

Segments must precede treatment

Splitting by what users did after exposure, such as "those who tapped the pre-filled basket", destroys the comparison, because treatment changed who falls in the group. Use only characteristics fixed before assignment. "Returning" is safe here because it was recorded before 14 September.

A segment is a proxy, not a mechanism

New versus returning probably stands in for "has an order history to remember". City, device and acquisition channel correlate with it. Before building a rule on the label, ask what the feature actually needs from the user.

What it cannot tell you

A CATE is still an average, now over a smaller group. It does not say who within the new users was harmed, and it holds only for the mix, season and product in which it was measured. Ask what has to stay true for the number to travel.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products; early and late stage

In consumer products, with millions of users and cheap randomisation, heterogeneity is estimable and usually informative; the danger is the opposite one of too many cuts. In B2B, a company may have 200 accounts, and an effect that depends on account size cannot be estimated with any precision. There the practical substitute is a few pre-chosen segments, plus qualitative evidence from customers.

In marketplaces the groups are the two sides: a change that lifts buyer conversion may lower seller earnings, and treated buyers compete with untreated ones for the same supply, so arms are not independent. Early-stage companies rarely have the sample to see subgroups; they should state a prior about who might be hurt and monitor that group after launch. Large companies have the data, and their risk is mining it; they need written segment lists, holdouts, and replication before acting.

7. Common mistakes

Shipping on the headline. The symptom is a green dashboard followed, three weeks later, by weak retention in one cohort. The misunderstanding is treating the average as a property of each user. The cheapest diagnostic is one pre-registered split, new versus existing, plotted with intervals before the launch meeting.

Fishing. The symptom is a vivid story nobody predicted, such as "it hurts Android users in Guwahati on Tuesdays." The misunderstanding is that a search over many cuts yields real findings at the single-test rate. Count the cuts examined, apply the stricter threshold, and test the claim on fresh traffic.

Reading silence as safety. The symptom is "no effect among tier-2 cities". The misunderstanding is that a nonsignificant result is a null. Report the interval and the smallest detectable effect; if the interval still contains a damaging value, the group is unresolved, not safe.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled Monday begins before the test. The team writes down two or three segments and the reason for each, fixes the primary metric and a decision rule: ship to a group only if its interval excludes harm. Results arrive as a single page showing the overall effect, each group's effect with its interval, and the interaction. The meeting then turns on the question "for whom, and by how much?", with the product owner's enthusiasm treated as a hypothesis rather than a verdict.

9. What Kishwar decided

She told Sinharoy that Basket Memory would ship on 12 October to returning customers only. Applied to a 120,000-user population with 84,000 returning, that adds 1,680 ordering users, against 960 if shipped to everyone, because new customers, who would have yielded a net 720 fewer ordering users, stay in the old flow. With the Puja mix shifting toward new customers, the all-user version would add little and might subtract. She also commissioned a separate new-user variant, with a starter basket of popular items, to be tested on its own.

To go further, study multiple comparisons, then uplift modelling and causal forests, which search for heterogeneity at scale while guarding against false discoveries.

Two questions to sit with. If Cairnstone's analysts had examined fifteen segments rather than one, which finding would you trust, and what would you ask for before acting on it? And when a feature helps your most loyal customers but deters your newest ones, whose experience should the product be built around?
exp40v2-exp.heterogeneous:
Heterogeneous treatment effects

It won on average — did it lose for anyone? And how would you tell a group that was hurt from a group that was small?

1. Two rooms, eleven days apart

On Thursday 1 October 2026, Labani Tribedi, vice-president of product at Dhansiri, a Bengaluru savings-and-investing app, had the result of a five-week test. The redesigned auto-invest onboarding, run on 240,000 new users enrolled between 13 July and 16 August, had lifted thirty-day activation — a first recurring deposit — from 18.05 to 19.25 per cent: a 1.20-point gain, 7.5 standard errors from zero. Her growth lead wanted it shipped that afternoon.

Lipin Tokdar, who ran experimentation, had opened the segment view instead. Users on Android handsets with three gigabytes of memory or less — 45 per cent of intake — gained 2.50 points. Better Android hardware gained 0.75. iOS lost 1.50. The iOS cohort was 15 per cent of new users and carried 4.5 times the low-end tier's first-year contribution per activation. The dashboard offered eleven other dimensions, and by the meeting someone had looked at thirty-eight slices. One — older users on low-end Android — showed a 1.50-point loss, exactly the iOS figure, and the room could not say why one number mattered and the other did not.

Eleven days later, on Monday 12 October, Lohitanshu Tantubay faced the mirror image at Dwipantar Systems in Pune, a field-service software vendor. A new scheduling engine had been randomised across the 412 accounts on the release train, 206 an arm. Jobs closed per technician-day rose from 6.35 to 6.71 — 0.36, or 5.7 per cent, significant at p = 0.009 after covariate adjustment. His head of customer success was certain small accounts would suffer: the engine optimises route density, and a nine-technician customer has none. Lalanika Thengari, who ran analytics, had the stratified numbers and said they did not settle it. The question Labani could answer with arithmetic, Lohitanshu could not.

2. The idea, and the three camps

Write a user's outcome under treatment as Y(1) and under control as Y(0); the individual treatment effect is their difference. Neyman's 1923 formulation and Rubin's 1974 extension make that estimand precise; Holland's 1986 statement of the fundamental problem of causal inference makes the difficulty precise too, since for any one user only one of those quantities is ever observed. Randomisation buys an average. Heterogeneous treatment effects are the claim that the distribution of those unobservable individual effects has real spread — that the average conceals groups for whom the sign, not merely the size, differs.

The idea solves a problem its own solution created. Once randomised trials made average effects credible, clinicians asked which patients the average described. Yusuf and colleagues codified the discipline in 1991; the cautionary illustration everyone cites came from ISIS-2, where aspirin after myocardial infarction benefited every astrological birth sign except Gemini and Libra. Twelve subgroups, a 5 per cent test, and chance did the rest. Econometrics arrived from the other direction, through Imbens and Angrist on local average treatment effects and Heckman and Vytlacil on essential heterogeneity. Since 2016 a machine-learning tradition — Athey and Imbens on causal trees, Wager and Athey on causal forests — has tried to estimate the whole conditional effect surface rather than test a few cuts.

Three camps disagree, and what they disagree about is burden of proof. The average-effect camp will sign: ship on the pre-registered primary metric, and treat any subgroup claim as a new hypothesis needing its own power. It will not sign: a nominally significant reversal in one slice is grounds to withhold. The guardrail camp will sign: no identifiable group may be made measurably worse off on a protected metric, and the shipper carries the burden. It will not sign: we must reach 80 per cent power on the interaction before we may act. The effect-function camp will sign: estimate effects conditionally with honest sample splitting and choose the highest-value policy. It will not sign: the right granularity is whatever the dashboard shows.

3. Mechanics, worked

Expert practice has four steps, and the second is usually left implicit. First, pre-register the dimensions: device tier was the only one Dhansiri registered before enrolment, which is why its three cells are evidence and the other thirty-five slices are exploration. Second, compute each difference's standard error before looking at its size — for proportions, SE = √(pc(1−pc)/nc + pt(1−pt)/nt). Third, correct for the number of comparisons. Fourth, shrink.

Exhibit 1 — Dhansiri, thirty-day activation by pre-registered device tier; 240,000 users, 13 July to 16 August 2026, split 50/50.

Run step two on the iOS cell. With pc = 0.250 and pt = 0.235 over 18,000 users an arm, the variance terms 0.1875/18,000 and 0.179775/18,000 sum to 2.040 × 10−5, whose square root is 0.452 points. The 1.50-point loss is 3.32 standard errors, interval −2.39 to −0.61: zero excluded at both ends. Now the slice that looked identical. Older users on low-end Android numbered 2,600 an arm, 15.00 per cent activating under control and 13.50 under treatment. The standard error is 0.969 points, so the same 1.50-point drop is 1.55 standard errors, p = 0.12, interval −3.40 to plus 0.40.

Step three is multiplicity: against thirty-eight looks the Bonferroni threshold is 0.05 / 38 = 0.0013, or |z| > 3.21. The iOS result, at p = 0.0009, clears it; the slice, at p = 0.12, does not. Step four is shrinkage. With τ the between-segment standard deviation of true effects, the empirical-Bayes weight on a segment's own estimate is τ² / (τ² + SE²), and Dhansiri's history of device-tier splits put τ near 1.20 points. For iOS the weight is 1.44 / (1.44 + 0.204) = 0.876, pulling −1.50 to 0.876 × (−1.50) + 0.124 × (+1.20) = −1.16; for the slice it is 1.44 / (1.44 + 0.939) = 0.605, pulling −1.50 to −0.43.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

State the conditions as testable claims. One: the dimension was nominated before the data existed. True for Dhansiri's device tier, and for Dwipantar's account-size strata, registered in the test plan. Two: the subgroup is large enough that a decision-relevant difference would clear its own standard error. True for Dhansiri on all three tiers; false for Dwipantar. Three: the segmenting variable is measured before treatment and cannot be moved by it. True for device tier, captured at install, and for technician headcount at signature. Four: a mechanism predicted the direction in advance. Dhansiri's new flow replaced a four-screen risk questionnaire with one animated allocation preview, which Lipin's engineers expected to help most where the old screens loaded slowest — the low-end tier, as observed. Nothing in it predicts the iOS loss, so claim four half-fails.

The idea actively misleads in three situations: when a segment sits near a ceiling, so a uniform relative improvement reads as heterogeneity on the absolute scale; when the treatment changes who appears in the segment, so the within-segment comparison is no longer randomised; and when the subgroup question is asked because the headline disappointed, which has stopped being inference.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

In a multi-product company the segments are products with different metrics, so no common scale says which lost. On a two-sided marketplace the sides are structurally heterogeneous and, worse, interfere: a change that wins for buyers can reallocate supply away from sellers, so unit-level randomisation violates no-interference and the subgroup effects are not well defined. Market-level randomisation costs an order of magnitude in power, so heterogeneity becomes undetectable where it matters most.

Regulated products invert the question. Lending and insurance are often legally obliged to test for differential impact across protected characteristics and forbidden to use them as a shipping key — you must look and must not act by segmenting; the response is to fix the mechanism. Hardware and firmware fleets cannot be split arbitrarily or rolled back in an afternoon, and their segments are defined by physical environment. AI-native products make heterogeneity the specification rather than a diagnostic: a model whose quality varies by language, accent or domain has an evaluation problem, and the subgroup is the deliverable. At the organisational seam, growth owns the dashboard, data science the interaction test and nobody the decision rule, so the segment acted on has the loudest sponsor. Mature companies answer this with a pre-registration file nobody can edit after enrolment opens.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

The scale artefact

A uniform relative lift mechanically produces unequal absolute gains, and the reverse. Dhansiri's pooled relative lift was 1.20 / 18.05 = 6.65 per cent; applied uniformly it predicts +0.93, +1.33 and +1.66 points, ordered by baseline. The observed +2.50, +0.75, −1.50 is the reverse ordering, so the heterogeneity survives on both scales. The tell-tale sign is an effect column rising monotonically with the baseline rate: arithmetic, not biology.

Segmenting on something the treatment moved

Condition on a post-treatment variable and randomisation stops holding inside the cell; the comparison turns observational without announcing itself. The tell-tale sign is almost never checked — the subgroup's size differs between arms. Randomisation balances a pre-treatment variable in expectation, so a material imbalance shows the variable is not one. The obvious reading, that the treatment moved the outcome, is backwards: it moved the label.

Composition, not causation

A treatment that pulls more low-intent users into a funnel depresses every downstream rate while raising every downstream count, and the table shows harm wherever those users land. Simpson's 1951 reversal is the formal version. The tell-tale sign is a rate falling while its numerator rises; the diagnostic is to fix the denominator at the pre-treatment population.

The arithmetic of looking

Expected false positives are comparisons times threshold: the thirty-five exploratory slices among Dhansiri's thirty-eight looks yield 1.75 at a 5 per cent threshold, while the three registered cells carry the evidence. The tell-tale sign is social rather than statistical — the finding sits in whichever slice the analyst opened last. Gelman and Loken's garden of forking paths describes the mechanism.

Shrinkage as the default

A small segment's own mean is a poor estimate of its effect; a better one is a blend of that mean and the pooled effect, weighted by precision, as Efron and Morris showed. The tell-tale sign of someone who has not internalised it is a ranked list whose extremes are all small segments — that ranking is measuring sample size.

Heterogeneity in the metric versus in value

The experiment measures activations; the business owns rupees. If segments differ in value per unit of the metric, a gain on the metric can be a loss to the business, and the error is not statistical at all. The tell-tale sign is a memo multiplying a net metric gain by one blended value, as Exhibit 3 shows. A blend is rarely close enough when gains and losses sit in different segments.

Time is a segment

Novelty and primacy mean the week-one effect differs from the week-five effect, so a five-week average understates a growing effect and overstates a decaying one. The tell-tale sign is a monotone trend in effect by enrolment cohort. Experts plot effect by cohort week first, because a time trend contaminates every other split.

Shipping two things is not free

The decision is rarely ship-or-not but ship-to-all versus ship-a-policy, and a policy carries a permanent cost — two code paths, two QA matrices — to be subtracted before comparison. Dhansiri costed its second onboarding path at ₹28.00 lakh a year. The tell-tale sign of the merely competent is a segmentation whose carrying cost never reaches the memo.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products sample size is nearly free and value per user small, so heterogeneity is detectable and the binding constraint is multiplicity discipline. In B2B and enterprise the constraint inverts: the unit is an account, there are hundreds not millions, and one large logo can dominate the consequence of a decision no test can resolve. For platforms, interference breaks the estimand before power becomes an issue; for hardware, irreversibility does. In AI products the per-slice evaluation set is the product requirement, the rare category where subgroup analysis is not supplementary.

By stage the difference is real but narrower than usually told. A seed-stage company cannot detect heterogeneity and should stop pretending: its tools are mechanism and qualitative work, and a segment chart at that stage is theatre. At growth stage power arrives and so does multiplicity, and this is where the discipline is built or permanently lost. At scale the question turns infrastructural — pre-registration, holdback cohorts, false-discovery-rate control. What does not change is the arithmetic: a standard error does not care how large the company is, only how large the cell is.

8. Three worked examples

Dhansiri: the value-weighted decision

Dhansiri enrols about 48,000 new users a week, 2,496,000 a year. The tier effects on that intake give +28,080, +7,488 and −5,616 activations, netting 29,952 — also 2,496,000 × 1.20 points. Finance values an activated user at ₹810, making the headline ₹242.61 lakh. Exhibit 3 multiplies tier by tier.

Exhibit 3 — Dhansiri, annual value of shipping to everyone; intake 2,496,000, split 45 / 40 / 15 per cent.

₹810 is the population-share-weighted mean contribution; weighted by control-arm activations it is ₹913, which would make the headline 12.7 per cent larger. The final Δ is pooled.

The true figure is ₹76.38 lakh, 31.5 per cent of the headline. Holding iOS on control is worth 115.13 + 65.15 = ₹180.28 lakh less ₹28.00 lakh of carrying cost, or ₹152.28 lakh — ₹75.90 lakh better. The segmentation is not a precaution; it is the larger number.

Dwipantar: the test that cannot be run

Dwipantar's strata told a tidy story and could not support it.

Final-row means are account-weighted: the weighted difference is 0.3609, printed as +0.36. Before adjustment the residual SD was 2.10, the pooled SE 0.207 and z = 1.74 — variance reduction, not the engine, made the main effect readable.

The gradient is monotone and plausible, which is why everyone believed it. But the quantity in dispute is the interaction. The large-minus-small contrast is 0.85 − 0.18 = 0.67 jobs a day, standard error √(0.182² + 0.388²) = 0.429, so z = 1.56 and p = 0.12. It cannot: the book holds only 92 large accounts, so 46 an arm is the ceiling, the large-stratum standard error cannot go below 1.40 × √(2/46) = 0.292, and z on the 0.67 contrast is capped below 2.30 however the other 1,088 of the 1,180 on its books are randomised. The shortfall is structural.

Deodar Instruments: the segmentation that was not one

Deodar Instruments, maker of connected water purifiers, tested a firmware change to its filter-life algorithm on 12,400 devices, 6,200 an arm. Service calls per device per quarter fell 0.14. Split on the hardness tier each device's sensor reported, hard-water devices looked 0.21 worse and soft-water 0.26 better, so Lipica Tapadar, the product director, held the firmware back from hard-water homes. The algorithm changes flush cycles, flush cycles change the measured dissolved-solids reading, and that reading was the segment key.

Two clues sat in the exhibit. First, the hard-water group held 2,480 of 6,200 treatment devices against 2,108 in control, a 6.0-point gap in share where randomisation guarantees none; the standard error of that gap is 0.87 points, making it a 6.9-standard-error imbalance. Second, the subgroup effects aggregate to −0.14 under no weighting: treatment shares give 0.40 × 0.21 + 0.60 × (−0.26) = −0.072, control shares −0.100. Under the installation-day split the groups balance and both weightings reproduce −0.14. Recovery took eleven months, over which 86,000 hard-water homes were denied 0.09 fewer calls each a quarter — 7,740 a quarter, or 28,380 calls over 11/3 quarters, at ₹520 a call: ₹1.48 crore spent protecting a group from a benefit.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

  • Segment fishing after a flat headline. Early sign: the subgroup request arrives the same hour as a disappointing result. Diagnostic: was this dimension in the test plan? Caught late, a roadmap built on noise.
  • Reading per-segment p-values instead of the interaction. Early sign: three significance stars and no difference-of-differences. Diagnostic: what is the standard error of the gap? Caught late, a policy the data never supported.
  • Hold-back by default. Early sign: a growing list of excluded cohorts nobody revisits. Diagnostic: what is this exclusion's annual carrying cost, and when does it expire? Deodar paid ₹1.48 crore.
  • Segmenting on a variable the treatment moves. Early sign: unequal subgroup sizes across arms. Diagnostic: was this value recorded before assignment? Caught late, every conclusion inverts.
  • Declaring no heterogeneity from an underpowered test. Early sign: "no significant difference by segment" with no minimum detectable effect beside it. Diagnostic: what interaction would we have had power to see? Caught late, a real harm ships unmonitored.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Position one: act only on pre-registered, multiplicity-corrected interactions. Its evidence is the replication record: subgroup findings in medicine replicate poorly, and pre-registration is its standard remedy. It would be wrong if the asymmetry between shipping harm and delaying benefit were steep enough that a p-value of 0.12 on a harm signal justified action, as in safety-adjacent products it often is.

Position two: guardrail segments carry a reversed burden of proof. Its evidence is asymmetry: a 1.50-point loss in the highest-value cohort compounds through retention, while a delayed ship costs one quarter. It would be wrong if guardrail lists grew without expiry, since the carrying cost then exceeds the harm avoided — the Deodar outcome.

Position three: estimate the effect function and optimise policy value. Its evidence is that causal forests with honest sample splitting recover surfaces no hand-chosen segmentation finds. It would be wrong if the estimated surface does not transport, and the unsettled question is how to validate that without running the next experiment first.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this runs the segment report and interprets it. Someone who has internalised it computes the standard error before reading the point estimate, and will not say "heterogeneous" until the interaction has one. They nominate dimensions in writing before enrolment. They ask what the segmenting variable was measured from, and when. They quote shrunk estimates and read a raw segment ranking as a sample-size ranking. They price the harmed segment in money and put an expiry date on every exclusion. And when the sample cannot answer the question, they say so rather than producing a chart that implies it can.

12. The two decisions

Labani shipped to both Android tiers and held iOS on control, with a January 2027 review and a ticket to establish why iOS lost — not on principle but because ₹152.28 lakh beats ₹76.38 lakh and the iOS result cleared a correction for thirty-eight looks. The contrast, not just the cell, carries it: the two Android tiers pooled gain +1.68 points, so iOS against the rest is −3.18 with standard error 0.482 and z = 6.6. She declined to act on the age slice. Lohitanshu shipped to all 412 accounts and then to the book, on mechanism rather than measurement, with a stop rule: roll back if the small-account mean falls more than 0.20 jobs a day below its own eight-week baseline, a shift his 590 small accounts detect at 2.45 standard errors on equal windows. The 5 per cent holdback he had been asked for would have given him 30 accounts and 0.76 standard errors, which is not a guardrail but a gesture.

Discussion questions. (1) Dwipantar's test over-represents large accounts — 52 of 412 eligible accounts, 12.6 per cent, against 92 of 1,180 on the book, 7.8 per cent. What does that do to the +0.36 estimate, and in which direction? (2) Dhansiri's harmed segment is also its most valuable per activation. Does value weighting make the hold-back more defensible or less? (3) Dhansiri took τ, and Dwipantar a stop rule, from prior history rather than from this experiment. What would make either auditable?

13. Going deeper

  • Significance, power, sample size, peeking — where the sample-size penalty on interactions comes from.
  • Segmenting users in analytics — supplies the dimensions, and the after-the-fact habit to resist.
  • Writing an experiment hypothesis — naming segments in advance converts exploration into evidence.
  • A/B testing fundamentals — randomisation makes a subgroup comparison causal; conditioning breaks it.
  • When you can't A/B test — Dwipantar's position: mechanism and stop rules.
  • Experimentation culture — pre-registration survives only where it is institutional.
  • Qual + quant feedback loop — interviews explain why a segment reversed.
  • Feature flags and flighting — makes a segmented ship, and its cost, concrete.
exp20v2-exp.physical:
Testing in Physical Retail

Test markets, store tests and the price of a packet of tea

1. A price rise on one shelf

On 14 October 2026, Sanjukta Choudhury, who ran own-label categories at Joynagar Provisions, a 112-store grocery chain across West Bengal and Assam, had one proposal to defend. Joynagar's 500-gram own-label tea would rise from ₹240 to ₹255, an increase of 6.25 per cent. With unit cost at ₹180, the margin per packet would climb from ₹60 to ₹75. The risk was equally plain: if shoppers crossed to the branded shelf, the extra ₹15 would be paid for in lost volume and in a loyalty the chain had spent a decade building. Tea was a line shoppers bought week after week, so a wrong rollout would show in every store within a month, while a wrong refusal would forgo margin on every packet sold.

No shopper could be randomised. A customer stands at a physical shelf and sees one price tag, and the chain cannot show half of them ₹240. So Saswati Changmai, her analyst, had run a store test: twelve stores charged the new price for six weeks while twelve similar stores kept the old one. The question was how far twelve stores could speak for the other hundred.

ItemFigure
Stores in the chain112
Test stores / matched control stores12 / 12
Price, 500 g own-label tea₹240 to ₹255
Baseline / test period8 weeks / 6 weeks

2. The idea

A store test changes one thing in a subset of physical stores and compares them with similar stores left alone; a test market does the same with whole towns or regions. Both exist because an online A/B test, which assigns each visitor to a version at random, has no shelf equivalent. A price tag is shared by everyone who walks in, so the unit of assignment becomes the store, and a chain has few of those. Fewer units means each store's quirks matter more, which is the problem the rest of this page manages.

Two old ideas fill the gap. Consumer-goods firms ran test towns from the 1950s. The comparison logic is difference-in-differences: measure how much the treated group changed, subtract how much a comparison group changed over the same weeks. It is often traced to John Snow's cholera studies in the 1850s, was given modern form by Orley Ashenfelter in 1978, and became famous through David Card and Alan Krueger's 1994 study of fast-food restaurants in New Jersey and Pennsylvania.

Sanjukta's sentence for the meeting: we are not asking whether the twelve stores sold less, but how much less than they would have sold had the price stayed put, and the matched stores are our best estimate of that.

3. How it works

Step 1 fixes what counts as success. Joynagar's rule was to roll out if profit per store-week at ₹255 beat profit at ₹240. Step 2 builds pairs: Saswati ranked all 112 stores by pre-period tea sales, then paired stores of similar format and catchment income that did not share a town, so that a shopper could not wander between a treated and an untreated shelf. She also froze the shelf plan, so that neither group received a new display, a coupon or a promotion during the fourteen weeks.

Step 3 is the one practitioners skip in speech. Within each pair, a coin decides which store gets the new price. Matching removes differences she could see; the coin guards against differences she could not, such as a manager who would have liked the experiment. Steps 4 and 5 are discipline: confirm the tags changed, hold other promotions equal, and run complete weeks so every weekday appears equally often in both groups. Step 6 is arithmetic, but only because the earlier steps made it fair. The end date is fixed in advance because a manager who watches daily numbers and stops when they look good has quietly turned a test into a search for a flattering result.

4. A worked example

Table 1 gives the averages across stores of weekly packets sold. Test stores sold 150 per week before and 126 during the test, a fall of 24, or 16.0 per cent. Read alone, that would be the answer, and a hurried reader would stop there. But control stores, whose price never moved, also slipped from 148 to 144.

Group8 baseline weeks6 test weeksChange
Test stores (12)150126-24
Control stores (12)148144-4
Difference in differences-20

Table 1. Average packets per store per week.

The control stores say the weeks themselves were 4 packets softer, so without a price change the test stores would have sold about 150 - 4 = 146. They sold 126. The effect is therefore 126 - 146 = -20 packets, or 20 / 146 = 13.7 per cent. Against a price rise of 6.25 per cent, the elasticity, meaning the percentage change in quantity per percentage change in price, is -13.7 / 6.25 = about -2.2.

Now profit. Expected at the old price: 146 x ₹60 = ₹8,760 per store-week. Actual at the new: 126 x ₹75 = ₹9,450. The gain is ₹690. Across 112 stores and 52 weeks, 5,824 store-weeks, that is ₹40,18,560, about ₹40.2 lakh a year.

Second pass, one input changed. Suppose some control stores had benefited from a rival closing, so that instead of falling to 144 the control mean rose from 148 to 152. Expected test sales become 154, the effect becomes -28, or 18.2 per cent, the elasticity -2.9, and the gain falls to 154 x ₹60 = ₹9,240 against ₹9,450, which is ₹210 a store-week and ₹12.2 lakh a year. One input moved the value of the decision by about 70 per cent, from ₹40.2 lakh to ₹12.2 lakh, and nothing about the test stores themselves had changed. The lesson is that the control group carries as much weight as the test group.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Matching is not randomising

Matching equalises only what was measured. Two stores alike on size and income can differ in a manager, a school opening nearby or a car park. The coin flip within pairs is what turns leftover differences into noise rather than bias. Noise can be measured and averaged away; bias cannot, which is why people who only use the vocabulary say "matched" and people who understand it ask who flipped the coin.

The parallel-trends assumption

The method assumes the two groups would have moved together. Test it on history: across the eight baseline weeks the period averages differ by two packets (150 against 148); the weekly series, not shown here, is what you would plot. If it had drifted, the control would be a poor stand-in. Eight weeks of history is a modest check, not a proof.

Twelve pairs is a small sample

Suppose the twelve pair-level differences had a standard deviation of 14 packets. The standard error is 14 / the square root of 12 = 4.04, and with 11 degrees of freedom the 95 per cent multiplier is 2.20, giving -20 plus or minus 8.9, or -28.9 to -11.1. The standard error measures how much an average of twelve pairs would wobble if the test were repeated; the interval is the range that wobble allows. A wide interval is information, not failure.

Break-even is where 75 x (146 - d) = 8,760, so d = 146 - 116.8 = 29.2, holding the 146 expected sales fixed; the margin is too thin for the invented standard deviation to settle. The interval's bad end lies only 0.3 packets inside it.

Spillover and cannibalisation

Packets lost on own-label tea may reappear as branded tea, which carries a different margin. Judge the category, not the item: a rupee of tea margin that moves to a lower-margin brand is not a rupee saved. The cross-town pairing guards against shoppers moving between treated and untreated stores; it cannot guard against shoppers moving between shelves.

Six weeks is not a habit

The test measures reaction at the shelf, not what shoppers do after months. Festival demand also shifts baselines, which is why control stores must run in the same weeks. Shoppers who stock up before a festival may also buy less afterwards, so a rollout decision made on pre-festival weeks may mislead about the weeks that follow.

Store test, test market, geo experiment

These are routinely confused. A store test varies single stores; a test market varies whole towns, with their own media, distribution and competitors; a geo experiment adds statistical modelling to choose and compare regions. The larger the unit, the more realistic the answer and the fewer the units available.

What it cannot tell you

It cannot reveal how competitors would answer a chain-wide move, whether the other hundred stores resemble the twelve, or why shoppers behaved as they did. Before relying on any store test, ask how stores were chosen, what else changed, and what result would have changed the decision. If no plausible result would have changed it, the test was theatre.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and large

SettingNatural unitMain difficulty
Consumer retailStoreFew units, shared shoppers
B2BAccount or depotAccounts differ hugely
MarketplaceRegion or cityBoth sides react

In consumer retail the store is the natural unit, as here. In B2B, selling through distributors, the unit is a distributor or account, perhaps thirty rather than a hundred and twelve, and one large account can swamp an average. In a marketplace, a change in one city moves sellers and buyers together, so tests use whole regions and treat spillover between them as part of the problem. In all three, the same logic holds: define the unit, build a comparison, subtract the comparison's change.

Size matters too. A three-store start-up cannot match anything; it should compare with its own history, say so, and rely on conversations with shoppers and a rule that decisions are easy to reverse. A chain of a thousand stores can randomise within strata and hold out a standing control group permanently.

7. Common mistakes

SymptomMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Result flips with the calendarThe stores' own past is the counterfactualPlot control stores over the same weeks
Test stores are the keen managers' storesHand-picking is harmlessAsk for the assignment log
Report shows one number, no rangeAn average is a verdictCompute break-even before looking
Own-label up, total tea flatThe item is the unit of profitCheck branded tea in test stores

Each row is observable from outside the analysis. The common root is treating a store test as a measurement of the stores, when it is an estimate of an unobserved alternative. The cheapest diagnostics all ask the same thing: where did the comparison come from, and could it have told a different story?

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the rule is written before 31 August, the pairs and coin flips are logged, and the readout shows the estimate, its interval, the break-even and the branded-tea effect on one page. Nobody argues about method on 14 October because it was agreed in July. The finance director sees the same numbers the analyst saw, in the units the decision will be judged by.

9. The decision, and what to carry forward

Sanjukta approved the rise for 90 stores from 19 October. She kept 10 at ₹240 for eight weeks, to 14 December, because the interval's bad end sat almost on break-even and festival demand would soon distort baselines. The 12 test stores stayed at ₹255. Her reasoning was asymmetric: a rise reversed after eight weeks costs little, while a rise unmonitored through the Puja season could hide a slide in loyalty for months. Next, study geo experiments, which extend this logic to whole regions, and synthetic controls built from many weighted stores. Both address the thin stand-in a handful of matched stores provides.

Two questions to sit with. If the lower bound had been -35, what exactly would you have asked for? And what would you want to know about the ten held-back stores before trusting them as a control?

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Experimentation & Causal Inference

Testing in physical retail: test markets and store tests

Matched-store tests, regional launches and price tests on shelf: learning where you cannot randomise the shopper.

1. Two decisions, three weeks apart

On Thursday 15 January 2026 the quarterly audit read reached Tandra Deka, category director for condiments at Kolaba Foods, a Pune packaged-foods firm. Her reformulated, repriced 200 g pickle range had run as a test market in Nagpur and Indore for the thirteen weeks to Sunday 14 December 2025. Kolaba's value share there moved from 11.4 to 13.3 per cent. The rollout she was to approve on Monday 2 March 2026 carried an ₹18.4 crore commitment, almost none of it recoverable.

Tamonash Doley, Kolaba's analytics head, had a narrower question: how much of the 1.9 points belonged to the proposition, and how much to the twenty-three points of distribution those cities also gained because the sales team, paid on shipments, treated the test as a launch.

Within the month, on Monday 9 February 2026, Tazeen Deuri faced the opposite problem. Deuri heads pricing at Kanthari Stores, a 268-store supermarket chain. Kanthari owns its shelves, so it had done what Kolaba could not: taken 240 eligible stores, matched them into 120 pairs on thirteen weeks of pre-period sales, and randomised one of each pair to a 6 per cent price increase on staples for the thirteen weeks to Sunday 4 January 2026. The category read came back at plus 12.4 per cent on gross profit. Annualised across all 268 stores, the slide said ₹11.7 crore.

Both readings were honest arithmetic. Both were about to be used for something the data could not support: Deka's number has an unknown cause, Deuri's a wrong base.

2. The idea, and the three schools that disagree about it

A store test is an experiment whose unit of assignment is a retail outlet rather than a shopper, because the intervention — a shelf price, a facing, a pack, a planogram — is attached to a place. A test market is the same idea at city or regional level, run by a manufacturer that does not control the shelf and reads its result from a retail audit panel, not its own tills. Both share coarse randomisation: tens or hundreds of units, each a correlated bundle of shoppers.

The lineage runs through agriculture. Fisher's field trials of the 1920s solved this problem — treatment attached to a plot, few plots, large plot-to-plot variation — with blocking and matched plots. Packaged goods inherited it through measurement: Nielsen's retail index from 1933, then Information Resources Inc.'s BehaviorScan in 1979. The econometric layer came later: difference-in-differences after Ashenfelter and Card (1985), synthetic control after Abadie and Gardeazabal (2003), geo experiments after Vaver and Koehler (2011).

Three positions coexist; the quickest separation is what each will sign. The design school signs: a test market without a matched control is a time series, not an experiment; randomise stores, and where you cannot, randomise time. It will not sign that model-based adjustment substitutes for a control group. The model school signs: with forty heterogeneous stores a good model beats a design, because the variance of a design-based contrast at that size exceeds the model's bias. It will not sign an unadjusted comparison of forty stores. The dress-rehearsal school signs: a test market exists to learn whether the trade and the field force can execute at all. It will not sign that a test-market share figure forecasts a national launch.

3. Mechanics in depth

Begin with the measure: a price change moves revenue and gross profit in opposite directions. At an elasticity of −1.3 from Kanthari's prior tests, a 6 per cent increase gives a volume index of 0.922. Revenue per baseline unit becomes 1.06 and cost stays at 0.78, so margin per unit rises from 0.22 to 0.28 and the margin rate from 22.0 to 26.4 per cent. Category gross profit therefore moves by 0.922 × 0.28 ÷ 0.22, or plus 17.3 per cent, while category revenue falls 2.3 per cent. A test powered on revenue would have been powered on the wrong sign.

Exhibit 1 — Kanthari Stores: pre-period economics, per store per week (₹ lakh)
LineRevenueGross margin (%)Gross profit

Rest of basket19.8018.03.564

Thirteen-week pre-period means across the 240 eligible stores. The total-row margin is pooled (4.048 ÷ 22.00 = 18.4 per cent), not the mean of the rates above it (20.0). The category is 10.0 per cent of store revenue (2.20 ÷ 22.00).

Then the sample. Of 268 stores, 28 were set aside — 12 remodelled inside the pre-period, 9 in another price zone, 7 trading under thirteen weeks — leaving 240, matched into 120 pairs on pre-period level, trend and festive shape, then randomised within pair. Power follows from minimum detectable effect = 2.80 × σ × √(2/n), where 2.80 = 1.96 + 0.84 for 5 per cent two-sided significance and 80 per cent power. With n = 120 per arm and a cross-store standard deviation of 0.17 on each store's ratio of post-period to pre-period category gross profit, the detectable effect is 6.1 per cent against an expected 17.3.

The step usually left implicit is the second readout. The category gain is ₹0.08395 lakh per store per week — 0.56795 less 0.484 — which is 2.07 per cent of the store's ₹4.048 lakh of total gross profit and 2.36 per cent of the ₹3.564 lakh the rest of the basket contributes. A 2.36 per cent fall in the rest of the basket erases the whole category gain; on the store's own base that harm and that gain are the same 2.07 per cent. The decision therefore needs a store-total readout: at a cross-store standard deviation of 0.045 its detectable effect is 1.63 per cent. The guardrail can see a 2.07 per cent harm, but not if that 0.045 is really 0.058. It cannot confirm the gain as read, 0.484 × 0.124 ÷ 4.048 = 1.48 per cent. A guardrail needs power against the harm, not the gain.

Figure 1 — the two readouts of one test, each on its own scale. The category panel has room to spare; the guardrail panel does not.

Two further steps matter. Kanthari photographed shelf tags in week 2 and found the new price displayed in 86 of the 120 test stores, a compliance rate of 71.7 per cent; the intention-to-treat read of plus 12.4 per cent therefore implies, if week-2 compliance held and non-compliers got none, a treated-store effect of 12.4 ÷ 0.717 = 17.3 per cent, the elasticity-based prediction. That agreement exists only because someone counted tags. The second step is clustering: treating each arm's 1,560 store-weeks as independent, when within-store correlation across thirteen weeks is 0.62, inflates precision by √(1 + 12 × 0.62) = 2.91. The unit of analysis must be the unit of assignment: 120 paired differences.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be stated as testable claims. The intervention is physically bound to the outlet — true for both protagonists. You control assignment — true for Deuri, who owns her shelves; false for Deka, whose shelf belongs to someone else. The unit count makes the detectable effect smaller than the effect that would change the decision — true for Kanthari at 120 pairs, untested for Kolaba, which never computed one. The outcome you decide on is the outcome you measure — false for both as first designed: Kanthari measured a category and decides on a basket, Kolaba measured share and decides on gross profit.

The approach actively misleads in three situations. When the test is also a launch, as in Nagpur and Indore, the treated arm contains two changes and identifies neither. When the intervention is cheap to reverse and expensive to measure, measurement costs more than the mistake it prevents. And when the quantity of interest is long-run, as price always is: a thirteen-week read catches shoppers who still remember the old price and misses the slower re-planning of the weekly shop.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

In multi-product retail the shelf is a fixture of fixed length, so a test that gives the treated product an extra facing takes it from something else: the measured effect is of an assortment change. The honest design holds total facings constant. In quick commerce the assignment unit is a dark-store catchment, but riders, inventory and impressions cross those boundaries, so the control is partly treated and the estimate biased toward zero. In regulated categories the constraint is prior: MRP is printed on the pack under India's packaged-commodities rules, so only a shelf price below MRP is a design option, and scheduled formulations under drug price control cannot be shelf-price-tested at all.

Hardware plus software mismatches the clocks. Firmware can be flighted overnight, but the boxes carrying it sit in channel inventory for weeks, so a store test of a hardware change tests whichever manufacturing vintage is on that shelf. Mature firms make the serial number the unit of assignment and rebuild geography from activation records. AI-native interventions break it differently: an in-store assistant or a vision-based planogram checker runs one shared model, and if it learns from both arms the treatment leaks into the control at an unmonitored rate. The discipline is to freeze the model.

The seams are organisational, and that is where tests die. The field force is paid on shipments, so it over-services the test; finance books test spend to brand while operations books execution to stores; and whoever proposed the test presents its result. Firms say governance handles this. What they do is make measurement report elsewhere and pre-register the decision rule.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Shipments are not sales. The tell is distributor cover rising inside the window: Kolaba's test cities closed holding 4.1 weeks of stock against a 2.6-week norm, so part of the movement was pipeline. The obvious reading, that despatches lag consumption, fails when the test causes the despatch: a pipeline fill never repeats.

Distribution gain dressed as a proposition effect. The tell is share up and rate of sale per stocking outlet down — Exhibit 2's 46 to 69 points of distribution beside a rate-of-sale index of 77.8. The obvious reading credits the proposition; the arithmetic leaves it unsigned.

Power belongs to the deciding measure. The tell is a design document with one detectable effect in it. Most retail decisions carry a primary and a guardrail with different variances and opposite directions, and the design must be powered against the harm, not the hope.

Matching on level while ignoring shape. The tell is a pair whose pre-period means agree to the rupee and whose festive weeks diverge by a fifth. Diwali fell on 20 October 2025, inside both windows; randomisation handled it for Kanthari, but Nagpur and Nashik do not share a festive profile. Run the placebo: the estimator must return zero on the pre-period.

The control group is partly treated. The tell is a control store inside a test store's catchment. The bias has a sign: a shopper diverted into a nearby control store exaggerates the contrast, while exposure the control arm also gets shrinks it.

Compliance is a hidden first stage. The tell is a readout with no photographs. Without a compliance rate an intention-to-treat number cannot be used by a rollout plan, because rollout compliance differs from test compliance, usually downward.

Price effects are asymmetric and they decay. The tell is an elasticity estimated from increases and used to forecast a decrease. Reference-price memory makes the weeks just after an increase the worst, so a short window overstates the damage.

A test market signals competitors. The tell is a rival's regional activity rising inside your window. The obvious reading calls this bad luck; it is endogenous, likelier the better your idea is, and it contaminates your own control arm.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

For consumer packaged goods this is the canonical case and the whole apparatus applies. For B2B and enterprise it mostly does not: there is no shelf, and the honest analogue is a holdout of sales territories for a pricing change, with the same small-n arithmetic and worse contamination. Platforms and marketplaces have the richest version of the problem, geo experiments with known interference. Hardware carries an inventory clock no design removes. AI products differ in one way: the intervention is a model, models are shared, and sharing is a spillover channel retail did not have.

Stage changes what is feasible rather than what is true, and the arithmetic is blunt. A twelve-store chain randomising six against six has a detectable effect of 2.80 × 0.17 × √(2/6) = 27.5 per cent on category gross profit. No commercially interesting effect is that large, so a cross-sectional store test at that size is theatre. The alternative is to randomise time: a switchback over sixteen two-week periods gives 192 store-periods, 96 of them treated, and with a within-store period-level standard deviation of 0.11 the detectable effect falls to 2.80 × 0.11 × √(2/96) = 4.4 per cent.

Figure 2 — randomising time rather than stores converts 27.5 per cent into 4.4, at the price of carryover.

The switchback buys variance with bias: a shopper who saw last fortnight's price carries it into this one. For a shelf tag that carryover is small; for a price it dominates.

8. Three worked examples

Kanthari Stores, the clean test. The ₹11.7 crore on Deuri's slide was ₹0.08395 lakh × 268 stores × 52 weeks: every store, a full year, at full effect from day one and full tag compliance. Her plan excluded the 40 holdout stores and moved the remaining 228 in three tranches of 76 at weeks 1, 5 and 9, giving 76 × (52 + 48 + 44) = 10,944 exposed store-weeks rather than 228 × 52 = 11,856. First-year gross profit is therefore ₹9.2 crore, not the ₹10.0 crore the unramped 228-store figure gives and not the ₹11.7 crore ceiling. The ramp alone costs ₹0.8 crore.

Kolaba Foods, the confounded test market. Deka's plus 1.9 points shrinks twice. Against matched control cities it is plus 1.5. The question is how to charge the seventeen points of excess distribution. Kolaba's cross-city regression over 38 audited cities gives 0.055 share points per distribution point, so 17 × 0.055 = 0.935 points, leaving plus 0.565 (plotted as +0.57) — a 3.4-fold reduction. But the regression's 0.055 is a cross-city average, not a slope for this test's new outlets. Proportional scaling instead predicts 11.4 × 69 ÷ 46 = 17.1 per cent share in the test cities against 13.3 observed, a shortfall of 3.80 points, versus 11.1 × 50 ÷ 44 = 12.61 against 11.5 in control, a shortfall of 1.11; the difference-in-differences on that basis is minus 2.69 points. That method holds rate of sale at its pre-period level, so it over-credits distribution — incremental outlets are weaker — while the regression slope is a plausible but unproven other end. The bracket is assumed, not derived, and it spans zero.

Kuteera Personal Care, the failure. Kuteera ran a sixteen-week test market for a sachet-to-bottle migration from Monday 1 July to Sunday 20 October 2024, and read plus 31 per cent on volume. The national rollout in early 2025 delivered plus 4 per cent. Trade spend in the test ran at ₹4,800 per outlet per month against a national rate card of ₹1,500, a factor of 3.2.
