The recovery is the instructive part. Thaneswar Dinda, who had run the test market, proposed a smaller clean one: 180 outlets, 90 per arm. At a per-outlet volume-ratio standard deviation of 0.34 that detects 2.80 × 0.34 × √(2/90) = 14.2 per cent, useless for a 5-point question. Reaching 5 points by adding outlets needs 2 × (2.80 × 0.34 ÷ 0.05)² = 726 per arm, or 1,452 outlets. Kuteera instead reduced variance: pre-period covariate adjustment on each outlet's prior twelve weeks cut the standard deviation to 0.21, bringing the requirement to 277 per arm, or 554 outlets.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Each has a sign visible before the readout, a question that catches it, and a cost if caught late.

Reading despatches as consumption. Sign: distributor cover rising. Question: what is the rate of sale per stocking outlet? Cost: a plan sized on a pipeline fill. An unmatched control. Sign: pre-period lines not parallel. Question: does the estimator return zero on the pre-period? Cost: the whole effect is the mismatch. Over-servicing the test. Sign: per-outlet spend above the rate card. Question: divide test spend by outlets. Cost: Kuteera's 27 points. Unmeasured compliance. Sign: no shelf photographs. Question: in what share of test stores was the change live in week 2? Cost: a rollout short by the compliance gap. Peeking. Sign: a weekly tracker with a decision attached. Question: what was the pre-registered stopping rule? Cost: a false-positive rate far above 5 per cent. No guardrail. Sign: one measure on the slide. Question: what would have to fall for this gain to be illusory? Cost: a category win and a basket loss.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Design versus model at small n. The randomisers rest on a paired design's bias being zero by construction; the modellers rest on synthetic-control reconstructions that track holdout periods closely with few treated units. The randomisers would be wrong if donor-pool methods recovered known effects under adversarial pre-period selection; the modellers would be wrong if specification search drove their fit.

Whether a test market forecasts a launch at all. The dress-rehearsal school has the better data. Of Kolaba's 14 test markets in ten years, 9 read positive, 6 were rolled out, and 2 landed within 20 per cent of the test read. The opposing position is that this indicts execution rather than method, and it would be vindicated if properly designed matched-market tests predicted better. Nobody has assembled that comparison.

Whether price should be tested at all. One camp holds price to be the highest-return experiment available. The other holds that in retail price is a positioning promise, the shopper's reference price an asset built over years, and a thirteen-week test blind to the asset it is spending. The first camp would be wrong if long-horizon holdouts showed material trip-frequency decay that short tests missed; the second would be wrong if they did not.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four ways. They write the decision rule and both detectable effects before the test is fielded. They ask what else changed in the treated arm before asking how large the effect was, and treat an unexpectedly large effect as a defect report. They know the arithmetic of their own base — which stores, over what period, at what ramp — and volunteer the smaller figure. And they can say that a completed, expensive test cannot answer the question it was run to answer.

12. What the two protagonists decided

Deka did not approve the rollout on 2 March 2026. The business case had valued plus 1.9 share points at ₹21.5 crore of incremental revenue — 1.9 per cent of the ₹1,130 crore category in Kolaba's footprint — and ₹7.3 crore of first-year gross profit at the range's 34 per cent margin. At plus 0.57 points the same arithmetic gives ₹6.4 crore and ₹2.19 crore; at minus 2.69 points, a loss. She commissioned a matched-pair test at national spend, reading on Monday 22 June 2026, and priced the sixteen-week delay at both ends: ₹2.25 crore of deferred gross profit if the business case is right, ₹0.67 crore if the adjusted read is, against an ₹18.4 crore commitment that cannot be unwound.

Deuri rolled, but not as proposed. Prices moved in 228 stores in three tranches, 40 stores were held out for 26 weeks to measure decay, and the first-year figure put to her board was ₹9.2 crore, with the ₹11.7 crore ceiling beside it, labelled the fully-ramped all-store maximum. Her pre-registered rule had been to roll only if category gross profit exceeded 8 per cent and the lower one-sided 80 per cent bound on total store gross profit was at or above zero; both held. What she could not resolve: the guardrail that cleared her increase could never confirm the gain it protected.

  1. Deka's two adjustments bracket the proposition effect between plus 0.57 and minus 2.69 share points. What measurement inside the test window would have narrowed that bracket?
  2. Kanthari's guardrail detects a 2.07 per cent fall in store gross profit but not the 1.48 per cent gain it protected. Is that good design or a hidden bias toward rolling out?
  3. Kuteera's four attribution lines sum exactly to its test read, and its residual equals the national outcome. Why is that agreement weak evidence?

13. Going deeper

  • When you can't A/B test — the parent idea, and the menu store tests come from.
  • Test markets and geo experiments — geography as the randomisation unit.
  • Writing an experiment hypothesis — what makes a pre-registered decision rule writable at all.
  • A/B testing fundamentals — the baseline this departs from, and its cost.
  • Significance, power, sample size, peeking — the source of every detectable effect here.
  • Experimentation culture — why over-serviced test markets persist.
  • Qual + quant feedback loop — why a rate of sale fell.
  • Feature flags and flighting — instant assignment and rollback, which shelves deny.
exp40v2-exp.b2b.experiments:
Experimentation with Few, Large Customers

The constraint is never the number of customers. It is the coarsest unit at which the treatment can be independently assigned, and how much of the outcome's variance lives above that unit.

1. Two decisions, one constraint

On Thursday 15 October 2026, Darpana Khambadkone, head of product at Samanvay Terminal Systems in Navi Mumbai, had to recommend for or against ₹7.6 crore of build. Samanvay sells yard and gate planning software to 34 accounts — container terminals, bulk berths and inland depots around JNPA, Mundra and Kattupalli — for ₹142 crore of annual recurring revenue, a mean of ₹4.18 crore per account; its largest pays ₹19 crore, 13.4 per cent of ARR. Flowcast predicts gate arrivals and issues appointment slots. The same committee had approved a comparable module in 2025 on evidence that evaporated.

Ten days earlier, on Monday 5 October 2026, Devashish Kolwalkar faced the mirror image at Saransh Decisions in Bengaluru. Saransh reads loan files with a document model and proposes credit decisions; its 23 accounts — nine banks, eleven NBFCs, three housing finance companies — produce ₹61 crore of ARR, a mean of ₹2.65 crore each. Dhaarini Kumbhojkar's group had a model that learns from analyst corrections and claimed six percentage points of straight-through rate. Fourteen of the 23 contracts renew by 31 March 2027.

Both had tens of customers, and the standard diagnosis — too few accounts, no power — is nearly useless, naming a quantity neither can change. This page argues for a different question: what is the finest unit at which the change can be switched on and off independently, and how much of the metric's variance sits above it? Darpana could toggle a yard plan weekly; Devashish could not toggle a model that learns. That asymmetry, not the gap between 34 and 23, decided what each could know.

2. The idea, and who disagrees

The assignment unit is the smallest entity that can receive one version while a comparable entity receives another; the unit of analysis must match it, so independent observations number as many as assignment units, never as many as the events they emit. The intra-cluster correlation ρ is the share of outcome variance lying between units rather than within; the design effect is the factor by which clustering inflates a contrast's variance, and the effective sample size the raw count divided by it.

Fisher's 1920s field trials established that the randomised unit is the plot, not the plant; researchers randomising villages and clinics from the 1970s built the arithmetic, Cornfield's 1978 warning that randomisation by cluster demands analysis by cluster being its canonical statement. Stepped-wedge designs, formalised by Hussey and Hughes in 2007, were invented where every unit must eventually be treated and only the order randomised. Switchback designs come from process control; synthetic control from political economy in 2010.

Four schools share the territory. The cluster-randomisation school signs that the unit of analysis must equal the unit of assignment and the design effect must be measured, not assumed; it will not sign that twenty accounts support a precise estimate. The within-unit school signs that an account is its own best control and time variation is free power; it will not sign that carryover can be assumed away. The synthetic-control school signs that with few units one builds a weighted comparison from the donor pool, inferring by permutation; it will not sign a model-based interval on 34 units. The decision-theoretic school signs that the object is whether the posterior moves the optimal action; it will not sign that a null result licenses a claim of no effect.

3. Mechanics: the ladder of assignment units

Samanvay's metric is gate turn time: minutes from a truck's in-gate read to its out-gate read. Its denominator is every visit with both reads recorded: of 82,334 raw visits in an eight-week window, 734 — 0.9 per cent, almost all overnight parking — exceeded 240 minutes and were excluded, leaving 81,600 analysed visits, a mean of 2,400 per terminal across the 34 accounts, range 410 to 9,800. The pre-period mean was 41.0 minutes, the between-terminal SD 9.0 minutes and the within-terminal, truck-to-truck SD 18.0 minutes.

Those components settle almost everything. Total variance is 81 + 324 = 405 min², so ρ = 81/405 = 0.200 and the total SD is √405 = 20.12 minutes. Randomising terminals 17 and 17, the design effect is 1 + (2400 − 1) × 0.200 = 480.8 and the effective sample size per arm is 40,800/480.8 = 84.9 truck-equivalents, against a ceiling as cluster size grows without limit of k/ρ = 17/0.200 = 85.

A two-sided 5 per cent test at 80 per cent power carries, under the normal approximation, a multiplier of 1.960 + 0.842 = 2.802 (on 32 degrees of freedom the t-based figure is 2.890). The standard error of the difference in cluster means is √(81 + 324/2400) × √(2/17) = 9.0075 × 0.3430 = 3.090 minutes, so the minimum detectable effect is 2.802 × 3.090 = 8.66 minutes, 21.1 per cent of the 41.0-minute baseline. The design-effect route agrees: 20.12 × √(2 × 480.8/40,800) = 3.090. It gives 8.93, so the normal approximation used throughout understates MDE by about 3 per cent. Flowcast's prototype suggested about three minutes, so the expert climbs.

To reach 4.12 unadjusted, Samanvay would need 17 × (8.66/4.12)² ≈ 75 terminals per arm, 150 in all. It has 34.

The switchback is a different move. Each terminal's yard plan regenerates weekly, so Flowcast can be on in some weeks and off in others and the terminal becomes its own control — deleting the 81 min² of between-terminal variance outright. What remains is week-to-week variation within a terminal: operational noise of 3.0 minutes plus sampling noise of 18.0/√300 = 1.04, giving √(9 + 1.08) = 3.175 per terminal-week. With four on-weeks and four off, each terminal's contrast has SD √(10.08 × (1/4 + 1/4)) = 2.245 and the mean over 34 terminals has SE 2.245/√34 = 0.385. MDE 1.08 minutes: eight times sharper on identical data.

Then the second-order effect bites. A yard plan built in week 3 shapes container positions still standing in week 4, so part of the effect carries into the next off-week and the contrast is attenuated towards zero by the carried share, measured at 0.345. That turns the top two rungs around: the 4-on/4-off design's nominal MDE of 1.08 recovers only 1 − 0.345 = 0.655 of the true effect, so on the true effect it is 1.08/0.655 = 1.65 minutes against the washout design's 1.25. The margin is not significant, though: the two runs differ by 1.0 minute with SE √(0.385² + 0.445²) = 0.588, 1.7 standard errors from zero, and the carried share itself has a delta-method SE near 0.17. Washout wins on the point estimate only.

4. Conditions, as testable claims

Five claims must hold. One: the treatment can be toggled finer than the account. Samanvay yes, weekly. Saransh no for the learning model, which retains what it absorbed; yes for a frozen one, assignable per application. Two: carryover decays inside one assignment period. Samanvay partly — 0.345 leaks, which washout absorbs. Saransh not at all; contamination is the mechanism. Three: most outcome variance sits below the account. Samanvay yes, 324 of 405 min², 80.0 per cent. Saransh yes; straight-through rate is near-binomial within an account. Four: the product instruments the outcome at the frequency of the assignment unit. Both yes, gate readers and decision logs — but Saransh's economic outcome is 90-day delinquency, nine months late. Five: a decision rule exists that the feasible MDE can trigger. Samanvay yes: 1.25 clears the 2.0-minute service level in eleven contracts. Saransh no: 2.71 points clears the claimed six-point effect but not the two-point threshold its pricing committee needs.

The idea turns actively misleading in two situations. First, when the fast metric is not the valuable one: resolving straight-through rate to a fifth of a point while credit loss is what matters buys precision about the wrong quantity, and precision is persuasive. Second, when short-run and sustained effects differ in sign: a switchback measures alternating exposure, so if controllers trust appointment slots only after six uninterrupted weeks it estimates something smaller than, or opposite to, a permanent rollout.

5. Hard edges

At the organisational seam the statistics are rarely what fails. In Samanvay's 2025 cluster-randomised test, 4 of the 17 terminals assigned to control were switched on early by account managers protecting renewals — a 23.5 per cent crossover, which attenuates an intention-to-treat estimate by roughly that share and surfaced only from the flag audit log, three months late. Mature companies handle this by making the holdout a scheduled wave with a date attached.

Two-sidedness crosses the clusters. Samanvay randomises terminals, but of 4,100 haulier firms with ten or more visits in the window, 1,558 — 38.0 per cent — called at two or more of the 34. Terminal-level outcomes stay clean; haulier-level outcomes are contaminated, and the honest unit for haulier behaviour is the port cluster, of which there are six.

Regulation removes randomisation from the product team: each of Saransh's lenders clears a model change through its own model-risk committee, so wave order is set by whose committee clears first, not by lot, and clearance speed tracks analytics maturity. Hardware is harsher: a firmware toggle needs a maintenance window, and if windows are quarterly the finest unit is the account-quarter. AI-native products break the assumptions by design, since a system that learns from its own deployment violates no-carryover and no-anticipation together, and its usual substitute, offline evaluation on a frozen holdout, changes the estimand rather than costing less.

6. Eight things experts see

The ceiling is k/ρ, and it arrives early. The tell is a deck boasting of observation counts. Samanvay's 40,800 visits per arm bought 84.9 effective observations against a ceiling of 85, because the marginal truck's value falls as the square of the design effect: a terminal's 16th visit adds a sixteenth of what its first adds, its 2,400th about one 231,000th.

Unequal cluster sizes almost never matter in this regime. Samanvay's span 410 to 9,800 visits, a twenty-four-fold range, yet contribute 4.95 and 5.00 effective observations, both sitting at the 1/ρ = 5 ceiling. The tell is a power calculation spending a page on size imbalance and a line on ρ.

ρ belongs to the metric, not the product. Gate turn time has ρ = 0.200 and a ceiling of 85 per arm. Berth productivity, moves per crane-hour, has a between-terminal SD of 4.7 and a within SD of 3.75, so ρ = 22.09/36.15 = 0.611 and the ceiling collapses to 17/0.611 = 27.8. The tell is a team that chose its metric before computing either component.

Carryover and washout trade quantitatively. The tell is a switchback whose first and fourth on-weeks differ systematically: that difference is the attenuation. Samanvay's 1.65 against 1.25 is the whole argument for spending two of eight weeks on nothing.

A within-account design answers a different question. A switchback's estimand is alternating weekly exposure on an unadapted population; an account-level rollout's is the sustained effect after adaptation. They coincide only if adaptation is fast relative to the toggle period. The tell is a readout borrowing switchback precision to justify a permanent decision.

Pre-period adjustment is worth about 1/√(1 − r²), and r disappoints. At r = 0.88 the factor is 2.11 but Table 1's realised gain is 2.10, since the 0.135 min² within-terminal term is untouched; at r = 0.70 both are 1.40. Because r enters squared, a respectable-sounding correlation buys little. The tell is a plan assuming adjustment will rescue an underpowered design without having measured r on last quarter's data.

Permutation inference has a floor set by the unit count. With 23 accounts the smallest attainable p-value is 1/23 = 0.043; with 34 it is 1/34 = 0.029. A pre-registered 0.01 threshold is unreachable below 100 units, whatever the effect. The tell is a stated significance level the design's own permutation distribution cannot produce.

The gain may land on someone else's profit and loss. Samanvay's 2.9-minute saving across the 530,400 visits its 34 terminals handle in a year — 81,600 per eight weeks × 6.5 — is 1,538,160 truck-minutes, or 25,636 truck-hours: at ₹480 per truck-hour, ₹1.23 crore of haulier time a year. Hauliers are not Samanvay's customers; the tell is a value case whose beneficiary never appears on the invoice.

7. Across product types and stages

The differences by product type are differences in where the assignment unit may sit. A consumer product assigns at the person, where ρ is near zero, so thousands of tests a quarter are affordable. An enterprise product assigns at the account by default, which is why it feels powerless; the craft is finding a finer legitimate unit — week, site, queue, document. Platforms and marketplaces have the opposite problem: a finer unit exists but interference invalidates it, so the honest unit coarsens to the region, the count falls to single digits, and permutation and synthetic control are all that is left. Hardware binds the unit to the service calendar; AI products bind it to whether the model is frozen — a product decision disguised as a statistical one.

Stage matters less than is claimed. An eight-customer company cannot run any of this and must rely on design partners and mechanism evidence, discounted for enthusiasm. But 34 accounts and 340 face the same arithmetic, differing by √10 in standard error, about one rung of Table 1. The sharper discontinuity is instrumentation: Samanvay could climb only because it had spent ₹1.1 crore and 14 weeks making the flag switchable per terminal per week.

8. Three worked examples

The failure, and the recovery. In September 2025 Samanvay shipped a berth-planning module to all 34 accounts on a cluster-randomised test read at the truck-visit level: 3.1 minutes with a standard error of 20.12 × √(2/40,800) = 0.141, so t = 22.0. The clustered standard error is 3.090, so t = 3.1/3.090 = 1.00: the design effect, √480.8 = 21.9, was ignored in full. Build cost ₹4.2 crore. By March 2026 nine terminals that had toggled the module off for unrelated reasons gave a retrospective within-terminal contrast of −0.4 minutes, SE 2.245/√9 = 0.748, interval −1.87 to +1.07. Those nine were not randomised and the estimate is not clean; its value was bounding the effect near zero, not three.

The switchback that worked. Run 1 ran the eight weeks from Monday 20 April to Sunday 14 June 2026, four on-weeks and four off per terminal, 17 terminals starting on and 17 off so common week effects cancel in aggregate: −1.9 minutes, SE 0.385, interval −2.65 to −1.15. Run 2 ran from Monday 6 July to Sunday 30 August 2026, a crossover with three on-weeks, three off and two washout weeks: −2.9, SE 0.445, interval −3.77 to −2.03, 7.1 per cent of the 41.0-minute baseline. The runs do not conflict; their ratio is the carryover, since Run 1 measures (1 − φ) of the true effect and φ = 1 − 1.9/2.9 = 0.345, the figure section 3 used. Damodhar Kurdikar, who built both, noted that without Run 2 the earlier interval understates Flowcast by a third.

Saransh, with one treated unit. Account A14, a large NBFC, took the learning model as a design partner from 1 February 2026. Dhaarini built a synthetic A14 from the 22 donors, weights 0.41 on A3, 0.27 on A9, 0.19 on A17 and 0.13 on A22, summing to 1.00; fit over the nine pre-period months to 31 January 2026, from 1 May 2025, had RMSE 0.62 points. Over the six post-period months to 31 July 2026 the gap averaged +4.9 points with an SD of 1.34, reaching 6.8 in the sixth month, where A14 ran at 54.1 per cent against the synthetic's 47.3. The gap RMSE is therefore √(4.9² + 1.34²) = 5.08, a post-to-pre ratio of 8.2. With a placebo on each donor, one of the 22 exceeded 8.2, so A14 ranked second of 23 and the permutation p-value is 2/23 = 0.087: suggestive, and incapable of becoming decisive.

9. Failure modes and their tells

Analysis at the event level. Sign: a t-statistic above 10 from tens of accounts. Diagnostic: how many entities could have received a different version? Late cost: ₹4.2 crore and fourteen months of distrust of Samanvay's own numbers.

Control-arm crossover. Sign: control accounts whose telemetry shows the new surface. Diagnostic: pull the flag audit log, not the plan. Late cost: the estimate is attenuated by the crossover share and later sizing inherits it.

Undetected carryover. Sign: on-week estimates growing across the run, or off-weeks that never return to baseline. Diagnostic: compare the first on-week with the last. Late cost: a real effect understated by a third, a good feature declined.

Proxy drift in AI evaluation. Sign: offline wins on a frozen set that do not reproduce in live straight-through rates. Diagnostic: when was the holdout refreshed, against which decision policy? Late cost: a model shipped on a benchmark that had stopped describing production.

10. Where experts disagree

Randomise accounts, or make each account its own control? The within-unit case is that between-account variance is the dominant noise and deleting it beats extra data; Samanvay's eight-fold gain is the exhibit. The cluster-randomisation case is that this trades a known assumption, exchangeability by lot, for an unknown one — that nothing else moved week to week — which 34 units cannot test. It would fall if secular drift dominated carryover-corrected bias; nobody has shown that at these counts.

Is offline evaluation a substitute or a filter? The substitute position rests on extraction quality being a property of model and document, not deployment: a frozen benchmark measures the thing itself. The filter position rests on straight-through rate depending on analyst trust, which no benchmark contains. It fails if one large account's analysts change their override behaviour, which Saransh has not measured.

Are holdouts legitimate in enterprise at all? One school holds that withholding a paid-for improvement from a named customer under contract is more than the sales relationship can absorb, and that the stepped wedge exists to avoid it. The other holds that shipping unvalidated changes to all 34 accounts is the greater breach. The disagreement is about what a customer is owed; arithmetic does not resolve it.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this asks how many customers are needed. Someone who has internalised it asks what the finest assignable unit is, what fraction of variance sits above it, and what it would cost in engineering to move down one rung — then treats that cost as part of the experiment's budget. They compute ρ before choosing a metric, state the estimand before the estimate rather than after, read the flag audit log first, know their permutation floor, and say early whose profit and loss the gain lands on.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Darpana took Run 2's −2.9 minutes and its interval of −3.77 to −2.03 to the committee on 15 October, with the carryover arithmetic reconciling it to Run 1, and did not ask for the whole ₹7.6 crore. She committed ₹3.1 crore to the eleven accounts whose contracts carry a 2.0-minute gate-turn service level, where the effect clears the threshold at both ends of the interval, and deferred ₹4.5 crore pending a value case addressed to the beneficiary of the ₹1.23 crore of haulier time.

Devashish chose the harder instrument: a stepped wedge of the learning model across all 23 accounts over six months from 1 December 2026, in waves of six, six, six and five, giving 82 treated and 56 control account-months of 138. Parameterised on the six months from 1 March to 31 August 2026 — 158,700 applications reaching extraction, 1,150 per account-month, a 46.0 per cent baseline straight-through rate, month-to-month operational SD of 2.40 points, and a variance inflation factor of 1.44 measured on an A/A test over 11,800 applications in the first fortnight of February, from which A14 is excluded because it switched on then — so the account-month residual SD is √(2.40² + (1.20 × 1.470)²) = 2.978 points. A14's February step is carried by its account fixed effect. Residualising the treatment indicator on account and period gives a sum of squares of 2.875 + 1.875 + 2.006 + 2.722 = 9.478, so the SE is 2.978/√9.478 = 0.967 and the MDE 2.71 points. Randomising applications within accounts on a frozen model would reach 0.84 points on the same applications, 3.22 times sharper, answering a question about a product he will not ship.

Three questions. First: Darpana's eleven accounts were not drawn by lot, so she has applied a population-average effect to a chosen subset — what would you ask before accepting that? Second: when is a precise answer to the wrong question worth more than a coarse answer to the right one? Third: if ₹1.1 crore of flag infrastructure made every later result possible, how should that spend be justified before any of those results exist?

13. Going deeper

When you can't A/B test covers the case where no unit is randomisable, unlocking honest non-experimental reporting. Designing enterprise pilots that convert treats a pilot as an assignment decision with a contract attached, unlocking the wave schedule that replaces a holdout. Writing an experiment hypothesis forces the estimand to be named before the design. A/B testing fundamentals supplies the independent-unit case these designs depart from. Significance, power, sample size, peeking holds the machinery behind the 2.802 multiplier. Experimentation culture stops account managers crossing the control arm. Qual + quant feedback loop carries the weight an interval cannot. Feature flags and flighting sets which rung you stand on.
exp20v2-exp.b2b.experiments:
Experimentation with Few, Large Customers

1. Opening

On Tuesday 13 October 2026, Chiranth Jogalekar, head of product at Rangtaal Systems in Pune, had one slide to show the executive committee. Rangtaal sells reconciliation software to forty large manufacturers and distributors, with annual recurring revenue of ₹96 crore, an average of ₹2.4 crore per account. Its newest feature, Smart Match, pairs incoming payments with open invoices automatically. Engineering wanted ₹3.5 crore to extend it to every customer's accounting system.

Nine contracts, together worth about ₹24 crore a year, came up for renewal by 31 March 2027. Chitkala Jamkhedkar, head of customer success, was certain Smart Match would save them. Chiranth was less sure. A wrong yes would burn ₹3.5 crore; a wrong no might hand rivals the renewals. With forty customers there were no thousands of users to split into test and control. What evidence could he honestly bring?

2. The idea

Experimentation with few, large customers means learning what a change causes when the unit of study is an account, not a person, and there are tens of accounts rather than thousands. It combines three tools: assigning the change by account, comparing before and after against accounts that did not change, and interviewing enough people to explain the mechanism.

The problem is statistical. An ordinary A/B test needs many independent units to separate a real effect from noise. Fisher's agricultural trials of the 1920s randomised plots, and public-health researchers from the 1970s randomised whole villages and clinics (cluster randomisation) because treating individuals within a community was impractical. Difference-in-differences, a before-and-after comparison against a control group, was developed in labour economics in the 1970s, with roots in John Snow's 1854 cholera comparisons.

Two terms recur. A counterfactual is what would have happened to the treated accounts had they not been treated; it can never be observed, only estimated from a comparison group. A decision rule is a threshold agreed in advance that turns a measured result into an action. Together they keep the exercise honest: the first says what the number is compared with, the second says what the number is for.

Chiranth's sentence for the meeting: "With forty customers we cannot detect small effects, so we design for large ones, compare against accounts that did not change, and say in advance what result would change our mind."

3. How it actually works

Step one is to name the unit. Here it is the account, because every user inside an account works under one finance team, one accounting system and one set of rules. Their results move together, so a customer with 900 users is still one observation; across the forty accounts Rangtaal has about 11,000 named users, and none of them is an independent unit. The metric matters as well. Chiranth chose days to close month-end, defined as working days from period end until the controller signs the reconciliation, because it is recorded by the product itself, cannot be flattered by a customer's own reporting, and sits close to the value Smart Match claims to deliver. Revenue or renewal would be more important, but they arrive too late and too rarely to steer a decision this quarter.

Step two is the decision rule, written before any data arrives. Chiranth wrote: extend if Smart Match cuts days-to-close by at least 1.0 day more than the waiting accounts' change, and the interval around that estimate excludes zero. Step three is assignment. Chaaya Jawalkar, the analyst, drew 12 accounts by lot, four from each of three size bands of 10, 14 and 16 accounts, so no band was missed by chance. Sampling fractions differ (40, 29 and 25 per cent) and means are unweighted, so the smallest band is over-represented among treated accounts.

Writing the rule down first is what separates an experiment from a story told afterwards. Step four is measurement. The same metric is recorded in both groups before and after. The June close, finished in early July as the switch was made, and the July close were excluded as transition months. Step five, usually left implicit, is explanation: Chitkala interviewed finance controllers at eight of the twelve treated accounts, because numbers say whether something moved and conversations say why.

4. A worked example

GroupAccountsBefore (days)After (days)Change (days)
Smart Match on129.06.5−2.5
Waiting288.67.8−0.8
Difference in changes−1.7

Cells are account-level mean days to close. Standard deviation of account changes: 1.8 days (treated), 1.5 days (waiting).

Read the table by rows. Each cell is an average over accounts, not over invoices, so a large and a small customer weigh the same. The first two rows give each group's own movement; the last row subtracts one from the other, and only that row is the experimental result.

A naive reading takes the treated group's drop, 2.5 days, as the effect. But the waiting accounts also closed 0.8 days faster, probably because September closes are routinely quicker than April's. Subtracting that drift gives −2.5 − (−0.8) = −1.7 days.

Uncertainty comes from the accounts, not the invoices. The treated mean change has a standard error of 1.8 divided by the square root of 12, which is 0.520. The waiting mean has 1.5 divided by the square root of 28, which is 0.284. Squaring and adding gives 0.270 + 0.080 = 0.350, whose square root, 0.592, is the standard error of the difference. The estimate is 1.7 / 0.592 = 2.9 standard errors from zero; the 95 per cent interval is −1.7 ± 1.96 × 0.592, or −2.9 to −0.5 days. Both conditions of Chiranth's rule are met: 1.7 is at least 1.0, and the interval excludes zero. A caution remains, since the interval's upper end, −0.5, is short of 1.0 day.

Second pass: change one input. Suppose the waiting accounts had improved by 1.6 days instead, say because a tax-filing deadline pushed them. The difference becomes −2.5 − (−1.6) = −0.9 days, the standard error is unchanged at 0.592, the estimate is 1.5 standard errors from zero, and the interval, −0.9 ± 1.16, runs from −2.1 to +0.3 days. The identical treated result now fails the rule. Nothing about Smart Match changed; only the comparison did, which is why the comparison group carries the argument.

Two further points follow from the arithmetic. First, the interval is wide because forty accounts leave little to average: the treated group has twelve, and each one moves the mean by a twelfth of its own change. Second, widening the sample is not available, since Rangtaal cannot conjure sixty more customers. The levers left are a longer window, a less variable metric, and a stronger intervention.

5. Nuances

Randomise accounts, not users. Treating one account's users differently from their colleagues would leave the two groups sharing a finance team. Counting 11,000 users as the sample would make every gap look decisive when only forty independent units exist.

Parallel trends. Subtracting the comparison group's change is valid only if, absent the feature, both groups would have moved alike. Lot-drawing makes that plausible. Hand-picking accounts does not.

Power is thin. With a standard error of 0.592, the smallest effect this design detects reliably, at 80 per cent power and 5 per cent significance, is about 2.8 × 0.592 = 1.7 days. Smaller effects are invisible here, not absent, including the 1.0-day effect the rule treats as success.

Spillover. Controllers at neighbouring companies talk, and shared auditors carry practices between clients. If waiting accounts adopt tricks from treated ones, the estimate shrinks towards zero.

Averages hide giants. One account worth ₹9 crore can dominate a revenue-weighted view while counting as one of forty in an account-weighted view. State which you report, and show both.

Qualitative depth is evidence, not decoration. Six of the eight controllers Chitkala interviewed named part payments, the cases where one cheque settles several invoices, as the place the time was saved. That mechanism predicts which accounts should benefit, a testable claim.

What it cannot tell you. Two closes show a change in speed, not in renewal. Whether faster closes retain customers needs a longer horizon than the contract calendar allows, and the design is silent on it.

Regression to the mean. Accounts selected because their last close was unusually slow will tend to look better next time whatever is done to them. Drawing by lot protects against this, because both groups contain such accounts in equal measure. Choosing the worst performers as pilots does not.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and large

A consumer product runs thousands of randomised tests a quarter and can afford to be wrong in small ways. A B2B product with forty customers cannot, and each exposure has a name and a contract attached; an experiment that disrupts a ₹4 crore account is a commercial event. A marketplace has the opposite difficulty: buyers and sellers interfere with each other, so randomising one side can distort the other, and market-level or region-level comparisons are often the honest unit.

An early-stage company with eight customers cannot run this design at all; it relies on deep qualitative work and design partners, whose enthusiasm must be discounted. A large company with hundreds of accounts can add segment-level comparisons, and eventually ordinary tests inside each account.

The common thread is that the sample size dictates the method. The fewer the units, the more the work moves from statistics to design, to qualitative evidence and to careful reading of what a result does and does not license.

7. Common mistakes

Choosing friendly accounts. Symptom: treated accounts were already outperforming before launch. Misunderstanding: enthusiasm is mistaken for a neutral sample. Cheapest diagnostic: compare the two groups' pre-period figures, and ask who chose them.

Counting users as the sample. Symptom: extremely small p-values from a test across forty customers. Misunderstanding: users in one account are independent. Diagnostic: count the units that could have received a different assignment.

Writing the rule afterwards. Symptom: the success metric changes between kickoff and readout. Misunderstanding: flexibility is rigour. Diagnostic: ask for the dated note that states the metric and threshold.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the slide carries four things: a rule written on 29 June, a draw anyone can re-run, a table that reconciles, and an honest sentence about what the interval excludes. It states the estimate, the interval and the smallest effect detectable. It names the mechanism from the interviews. It notes what remains unknown, namely renewals, and what would be learned next. The committee should leave knowing both what was found and how much weight it bears.

Good also means proportionate. A staged rollout, in which waiting accounts receive the feature in later waves, spares the company the awkwardness of withholding a promising feature from a customer who is about to renew, and gives every account the benefit within a quarter or two. The readout then records not only the result but the cost of waiting, which here is small: the waiting accounts lose perhaps a quarter of delay, against a decision that commits ₹3.5 crore.

9. Closing

Chiranth reported −1.7 days with an interval of −2.9 to −0.5, and noted that the rule was met in full, though the interval's upper end, −0.5, fell short of 1.0 day. He did not commit all ₹3.5 crore. He asked for the part needed to extend Smart Match to the eight waiting accounts nearest renewal, kept the other twenty waiting for the next window, and set the next readout for after the December closes. The reasoning: the evidence was strong that the effect was real and weaker on whether it was large enough to justify the full spend, so he bought information and protected the renewals together.

To learn next, study how enterprise pilots are designed to convert, since a pilot is an experiment with a customer relationship attached, and revisit why too few accounts leave an ordinary test underpowered.

Two questions to sit with. If Chitkala had picked the twelve accounts herself, what single comparison would you ask for before trusting the table? And what result, written down in advance, would have made Chiranth withhold even the partial investment?
exp40v2-exp.bayesian:
What a Posterior Probability Will and Will Not Buy You: Bayesian and Frequentist Readings of the Same Experiment

Is “probability to beat baseline” the same as significance? No — and the argument over which school is right stands in for three questions that are not philosophical: who owns the prior, what a wrong decision costs, and how often the chosen rule fires when nothing is happening.

1. Two readouts, four days apart

On Monday 19 October 2026, Gunashri Mestry, head of product at Vaitarna Health Systems in Pune, opened the readout of experiment ADH‑14. Vaitarna sells a continuous glucose sensor and its app; the variant replaced a five-card onboarding tutorial with a guided placement check. The primary metric was first-sensor completion: the share of new activations wearing sensor one its full fourteen days. Enrolment ran Tuesday 4 August to Monday 14 September 2026, forty-two days at fifty-six activations a day split evenly.

The dashboard said 98 per cent probability to beat baseline, which Mestry did not read as good news. The onboarding flow is part of the device's labelled instructions for use, so changing it needs a submission to Vaitarna's notified body; the next slot closed on Monday 16 November 2026, and the eleven weeks of regulatory work after it would freeze every other onboarding change until Monday 1 February 2027. Gatesh Madkaikar, who runs quality, priced the freeze at the two onboarding experiments it displaces, worth 0.60 points each at the historical average, plus 0.80 points of margin for shrinkage on rollout: a threshold of 1.20 + 0.80 = 2.00 points. The question was never whether the lift was positive.

Four days later, on Friday 23 October 2026, Ganaraj Manerikar took a different readout to the release board at Vachak AI in Bengaluru, whose assistant drafts claim-decision letters for thirty-four general insurers. His team had graded 420 claim scenarios twice, once per prompt, against a rubric. The variant passed 337, the control 311; the dashboard said 99.9 per cent. Gavisha Marchande, the staff analyst, said the honest number was 96.0, and that the difference had nothing to do with Bayes.

2. The idea, and what each school will sign

A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as the observed, under a stated hypothesis — usually that the true difference is exactly zero. What varies is the data; the true effect is a fixed unknown carrying no probability. This is the frequentist reading, formalised by Ronald Fisher in the 1920s and given a decision frame by Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson in 1933.

Probability to beat baseline is P(true lift > 0 | data, prior, model). What varies is the unknown lift; the data are fixed at what was seen. The reading descends from Thomas Bayes's posthumous 1763 essay and Pierre-Simon Laplace, was formalised for science by Harold Jeffreys in 1939, and was defended as coherent belief by Bruno de Finetti and Leonard Savage.

The schools disagree about a narrower proposition than the slogans suggest. Everyone signs: a p-value is not the probability the null is true; a posterior depends on a prior; both are functions of one likelihood. A frequentist will not sign that a parameter has a distribution before data, or that a procedure needs no long-run error guarantee. A Bayesian will not sign that a quantity defined by summing over data never observed can guide one decision, or that the stopping rule changes the inference. Neither signs what mature teams do: decide with a posterior and audit the rule by simulating its frequency properties. Jeffreys and Dennis Lindley showed, in 1939 and 1957, that the readings can be pushed arbitrarily far apart on a point null, and James Berger and Thomas Sellke made the gap concrete in 1987.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Control completed 682 of 1,176 activations, 57.99 per cent; the variant 733 of 1,176, 62.33 per cent, a raw lift of 4.34 points. Both denominators are activations enrolled in that window, counted once, the last fourteen-day outcome landing on Monday 28 September.

With a uniform Beta(1,1) prior per arm the posteriors are Beta(683, 495) and Beta(734, 444). A Beta(a,b) has mean a/(a+b) and variance ab/[(a+b)²(a+b+1)]: 57.98 per cent, SD 1.4375 points; 62.31 per cent, SD 1.4114. Treating the lift as normal, its mean is 4.3294 and its SD √(1.4375² + 1.4114²) = 2.0145, so z = 2.149 and P(lift > 0) = Φ(2.149) = 0.9842.

Two cross-checks. Integrating one Beta against the other's distribution function gives the exact posterior probability, 0.9841. The frequentist route on the same counts has unpooled standard error √(0.5799×0.4201/1,176 + 0.6233×0.3767/1,176) = 2.0170, z = 2.150, two-sided p = 0.0315, 1 − p/2 = 0.9842.

All three agree to three decimals — a coincidence of flat priors and many events, not an identity, and section 6 shows it breaking. The omitted step is turning a posterior into a decision. P(lift > 0) is the wrong input, the threshold being two points: P(lift ≥ 2.00) = 1 − Φ((2.00 − 4.3294)/2.0145) = Φ(1.157) = 0.876. Expected loss from shipping, the mean shortfall if control is better, is σφ(z) − μΦ(−z) = 2.0145×0.03989 − 4.3294×0.01581 = 0.0114 points.

The prior Vaitarna actually had

Mestry's analyst, Gargeya Mulye, objected that Beta(1,1) asserts a falsehood: a 40-point lift as plausible beforehand as a 2-point one. Vaitarna had run 23 completed experiments on the app between April 2024 and July 2026, none of them ADH‑14. Their observed lifts had mean +0.60 points and SD 3.10, median within-test standard error 2.00. Observed variance is true variance plus sampling variance, so τ² = 3.10² − 2.00² = 5.61 and τ = 2.3685 points.

That is an empirical-Bayes prior in Herbert Robbins's 1956 sense: estimated, not asserted. Updating it with this test's likelihood (4.3367 points, SE 2.0170, s² = 4.0683) gives shrinkage B = τ²/(τ² + s²) = 5.61/9.6783 = 0.5796, a posterior mean of 0.60 + 0.5796×(4.3367 − 0.60) = 2.766 points and SD √(0.5796×4.0683) = 1.5356.

4. When the distinction matters, as testable claims

Four conditions decide whether the reading changes anything, each checkable beforehand. One: with a flat prior and hundreds of events per arm, P(lift > 0) and 1 − p/2 agree to within rounding. True at Vaitarna — 0.9842 against 0.9842 — a fact about this dataset, not a theorem. Two: the reading matters when the prior carries weight comparable to the data. True at Vaitarna, where the sceptical prior is worth four times the experiment and the Bayesian reading yields an answer no frequentist test can produce. Three: the reading matters when the decision is asymmetric in cost. True at Vachak; a p-value has no slot for cost, an expected loss does. Four: the reading does not matter when the binding constraint is the model of the data. Also Vachak, and here the argument misleads: a team that spends a month choosing a school while its units are correlated has chosen between two wrong answers.

5. Hard edge cases, and what the clustering did to Vachak

Vachak's 420 scenarios were graded as matched pairs: the same scenario, both prompts. Both arms passed 288, both failed 60, only the variant passed 49, only the control 23 (288 + 60 + 49 + 23 = 420). Control passes are 288 + 23 = 311 and variant 288 + 49 = 337, a paired lift of (49 − 23)/420 = 6.19 points. Only the 72 discordant pairs say which prompt is better.

Put a uniform prior on θ = P(variant wins | pair discordant). The posterior is Beta(50, 24), exact P(θ > 0.5) = 0.9989. McNemar's test on the same pairs gives z = (49 − 23)/√72 = 3.064 and an exact two-sided binomial p = 0.0029, so 1 − p/2 = 0.9985 — agreement again.

Marchande's objection was that the 420 scenarios came from 35 policy templates, twelve per template, and that scenarios from one template pass or fail together. The measured intra-cluster correlation of the pass indicator was 0.18, so the design effect is 1 + (m − 1)ρ = 1 + 11×0.18 = 2.98: 420 nominal pairs are worth 420/2.98 = 141 independent ones, 72 discordant pairs 72/2.98 = 24.2. On effective counts — Beta(17.44, 8.72) — exact P(θ > 0.5) = 0.960, and McNemar's z falls to 3.064/√2.98 = 1.775, p = 0.076. The correlation was measured on the pass indicator and applied to discordance, which assumes the two are equal.

The posterior fell 3.9 points of probability; the p-value rose by a factor of 26. The correction is neither Bayesian nor frequentist — it is a claim about the data-generating process — and it moved the answer far more than the choice of school could, leaving the two on opposite sides of their conventional lines. That is the regime in which teams argue philosophy after the real problem has been solved.

In regulated work the seam is organisational. Vaitarna's clinical group runs genuinely Bayesian trials under the United States Food and Drug Administration's 2010 device-trial guidance, with priors and operating characteristics agreed before enrolment; its product group runs a Bayesian dashboard with neither.

6. Eight things that separate an expert

The threshold is a price, not a convention

Marchande did not pick 0.95. If shipping a non-improvement costs Cs and withholding a real one costs Ch, expected loss is minimised by shipping when (1 − P)Cs < PCh, that is P > Cs/(Cs + Ch). Vachak priced remediating letters already sent at nineteen times a further month on the old prompt: 19/20 = 0.95. The tell: a threshold justified by convention rather than a ratio is decorative.

Direction is not magnitude, and magnitude is what is bought

Vaitarna's dashboard reported 0.984 for P(lift > 0); the number that priced the freeze was 0.691. An expert reads the column matching the decision, treating P(> 0) as a check the experiment ran. The tell is a readout carrying one probability, computed against a threshold of zero nobody faces.

A posterior does not depend on when you looked; a rule does

Both halves are true and teams keep whichever suits. Beta(683, 495) is the same object computed once or thirty-six times; “ship the first day P clears 0.95” is a procedure, and procedures have frequency properties whether their author believes in them or not.

The exaggeration ratio, not the error rate

Vaitarna's raw lift was 4.337 points and its shrunk estimate 2.766, a ratio of 1.57. A company shipping on raw estimates overstates what it shipped by that factor, and its roadmap arithmetic drifts upward though every decision was defensible. The tell is wins that never reach the aggregate metric.

The prior's own uncertainty is usually larger than the prior

τ = 2.3685 came from 23 observed lifts. The standard error of an SD from 23 observations is about SD/√(2×22) = 3.10/6.63 = 0.467, so the SD is 3.10 ± 0.47 and τ² = SD² − 4.00 runs from 2.93 to 8.73. Table 1's second row at those ends gives P(≥2.00) of 0.550 and 0.755, from means of 2.16 and 3.15 points: a band 0.205 wide, a fifth of the probability scale, on one standard error of a nuisance parameter. Two heuristics sit inside it — the median SE² stands in for the mean of SE², and the SE-of-SD formula assumes normality and treats the 2.00 as known.

Conjugacy and the normal approximation fail where events are rare

Vaitarna's secondary metric was sensor-detachment reports in the first fourteen days: 3 of 1,176 in control, 9 of 1,176 in the variant, the primary's denominators. Three readings disagree. The normal approximation to the posterior difference gives P(variant worse) = 0.946; exact integration of Beta(10, 1168) against Beta(4, 1174) gives 0.954; the two-sided test on the pooled rate 12/2,352 gives p = 0.082, so 1 − p/2 = 0.959. Two of three cross a 0.95 trigger. The tell is a binary metric with under ten events in an arm.

The exhibit that cannot be drawn is the one that decides

Nothing in Table 1 or Figure 1 encodes whether completion at fourteen days predicts adherence at twelve months. If it does not, every number here prices the wrong thing and no prior, posterior or p-value detects it. The tell is a metric chosen because it reads out inside the window.

Agreement between the readings is evidence about the data, not the method

At Vaitarna three computations agreed to three decimals; on the rare secondary they spanned 0.013 of probability; at Vachak they agreed before and after a correction that moved the answer 3.9 points. Agreement signals a well-behaved likelihood with many events; divergence asks which approximation broke, never which school is right.

7. Where product type and stage change the answer

In consumer products with millions of events the readings agree numerically and the choice is about communication; the real risks, novelty effects and interference, are shared. In B2B and enterprise, where arms hold tens of accounts, the prior does the work and the honest report is a table like Table 1. Platforms and marketplaces change the unit of randomisation, altering the likelihood for both schools identically; Vachak's design effect of 2.98 is mild beside the eight or ten of a two-sided market. In hardware each arm is partly a manufacturing cohort, so a software effect may be a batch effect. In AI products the pattern is Vachak's: small graded sets, correlated items, a model grading a model, base-model changes that void the corpus.

Stage changes which half binds. An early-stage company has no corpus, cannot build Vaitarna's empirical-Bayes prior, and should say so rather than fake one. A company with Vaitarna's 23 experiments can estimate τ but must publish its uncertainty; one with hundreds can estimate τ by surface and metric.

8. Three worked examples

One: the prior ladder changes the decision, the data do not

Table 1: identical counts, P(≥2.00) of 0.876, 0.691 and 0.230. The question put to Mestry was whether 0.691 bought an eleven-week freeze.

Two: the correction nobody argued about

Vachak's eval. The clustering correction cut effective discordant pairs from 72 to 24.2 and the posterior from 0.9989 to 0.960, still clearing the 0.95 a loss ratio of 19 implies — by 0.010 rather than 0.049.

Three: the prior fitted on the wrong regime

On Thursday 9 July 2026 Vachak held a release its own numbers supported. An eval of a revised assistant had shown an 8.1-point gain, standard error 3.4 points. The team had just adopted an empirical-Bayes prior fitted on its 17 previous evals: τ = 1.60 points, prior mean +0.50. That prior is worth s²/τ² = 11.56/2.56 = 4.52 evals of this size, so B = 0.181, the 8.1 points shrank to 1.88 and P(gain > 0) fell to 0.903, below what the loss ratio demanded. Release was held seven weeks.

The error was that all 17 prior evals were prompt edits on one base model, while the release changed the base model. Manerikar split the corpus: on the five base-model changes alone τ = 5.90 points, a prior worth 11.56/34.81 = 0.33 evals, so B = 0.751, the shrunk gain is 6.21 points and P(gain > 0) = 0.982. The attenuation of 4.3 was not conservatism but the wrong reference class. The recovery was procedural: two corpora, and no shrinking a base-model change against prompt-edit history.

9. Failure modes, and what the measurement showed

Mulye ran the obvious audit. Simulating Vaitarna's traffic — 28 activations per arm per day for 42 days, both arms at 58.0 per cent, a look every day from day 7, so 36 looks — gives Table 2.

Three failure modes sit in that table. Unaudited peeking: the warning sign is a dashboard refreshing daily with no minimum sample; the diagnostic is to ask the rule's A/A ship rate; caught late it leaves a backlog of changes shipped under a rule that fires on noise nearly one time in five. A guard that does not guard: an expected-loss cap added to the 0.95 rule barely moved the A/A rate, because at these sizes the cap is nearly implied by the probability threshold; the minimum sample size does the work, and believing otherwise buys a rule that only looks protected. Blaming the school: the matched frequentist rule, one-sided z ≥ 1.645 on the same 36 days, fired in 18.6 per cent of the same replications, the last row of Table 2. Switching schools does not change the rate.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The error-control position. A decision rule without a measured false-ship rate is a habit, not a method. Only a procedure's frequency properties can be guaranteed in advance, which is why regulators ask for them, and a posterior can say anything through an unaudited prior. This rests on Table 2, and would be wrong if teams faced long runs of exchangeable decisions; they face one at a time.

The coherence position. The only quantity a decision-maker can act on is the probability of the states of the world given what is known. Expected loss has a slot for cost; a p-value does not, which is why Vachak's 0.95 had to be derived. This rests on Savage's and Abraham Wald's decision theory, and would be wrong if priors were arbitrary rather than estimable — Vaitarna's τ was estimable, but one standard error on it moves P(≥2.00) from 0.550 to 0.755.

The position both sides dislike. A posterior calibrated by simulation against the frequency properties of the rule it feeds is what competent teams use. Orthodox frequentists object that the prior is an unaudited input to a procedure claiming error control; orthodox Bayesians, that calibrating a threshold against a sampling distribution reintroduces the dependence on unobserved data the apparatus exists to remove. Both objections are correct; the practice survives because release boards accept it.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this reports a probability and can define it. Someone who has internalised it arrives with the threshold derived from a loss ratio, the prior written with its own standard error, and the rule's A/A rate simulated — then spends the meeting on the model of the data, not the summary. The giveaway is the first question. The competent practitioner asks which number to trust; the expert asks the unit of randomisation, the smallest cell's event count, and the rule's false-ship rate.

12. The two decisions

Mestry did not submit the design change on 16 November. She reported all three rows of Table 1 and the 0.550-to-0.755 band on P(≥2.00), arguing that a freeze displacing two experiments could not be bought with a figure that one standard error on τ moves from 0.550 to 0.755. She reopened enrolment, to read out before the February slot, under a pre-registered rule: threshold 0.990, the prior fixed in writing beforehand, one look. Mulye dissented on the record: a threshold calibrated to a frequency property is not a prior belief and has no Bayesian standing.

Manerikar shipped on 23 October, to eight tenants rather than thirty-four, with the clustered 0.960 in the paper and the 0.9989 struck out. His reasoning: a loss ratio of 19 is itself a judgement, and a staged release lowers the ratio rather than raising the probability.

Three questions. First: Vaitarna's sceptical prior is worth 4.07 experiments against the one run and gives P(≥2.00) = 0.230. Whose prior should bind a decision a regulator will later review, and what would make one of Table 1's rows indefensible rather than conservative? Second: Mestry's pre-registered 0.990, calibrated to a false-ship rate, and Marchande's 0.95, derived from a cost ratio, cannot both be satisfied, and Mulye's dissent is against Mestry rather than Marchande. Which does your organisation need more, and what does it give up? Third: had the clustering correction been found after release, what in Vachak's process would have caught it, and at what cost?

13. Going deeper

Significance, power, sample size, peeking is the prerequisite: Table 2 is a power and error-rate calculation in Bayesian clothes. Writing an experiment hypothesis is where the 2.00-point threshold and the loss ratio of 19 belong, before the data rather than after. A/B testing fundamentals supplies the randomisation unit whose misidentification caused Vachak's problem. When you can't A/B test matters because 56 activations a day puts most of Vaitarna's questions out of reach, when a prior is the asset. Experimentation culture decides whether an A/A rate of 18.6 per cent is a finding or an accusation. Qual + quant feedback loop challenges fourteen-day completion as a proxy for twelve-month adherence. Feature flags and flighting unlocks Manerikar's move: lowering the cost of a wrong ship beats raising the probability of a right one.
exp20v2-exp.bayesian:
Probability to Beat Baseline versus the p-value: Two Answers to Two Different Questions

1. A 92 per cent that nobody could defend

On Tuesday 6 October 2026, Edhavi Lagvankar, a product manager at Tilvara, an Indian grocery-delivery app, opened the readout of a checkout experiment. The variant collapsed the three-screen checkout into one page. It had run on 20,000 sessions that reached the cart, split evenly. Her analyst, Eshaant Lohokare, had put a single line at the top of the dashboard: "Probability variant beats control: 92%."

The finance lead asked whether that meant the result was significant. Lohokare hesitated, because the same data, run through the company's older test calculator, returned a p-value of 0.159 and the word "inconclusive". Tilvara sees about 2.5 million cart sessions a month. A true lift of 0.4 percentage points would be roughly 10,000 extra orders a month; the rollout would cost three weeks of two engineers. Shipping a dud wastes that effort, and shelving a winner forfeits the orders. Lagvankar needed to know which number was telling the truth. The answer is that neither was lying, and that they were not answering the same question.

2. The idea

Two traditions interpret probability differently. The frequentist tradition, built mainly by Ronald Fisher in the 1920s and by Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson in the 1930s, treats probability as the long-run frequency of an outcome across repeated experiments. The true lift is a fixed, unknown number, so it has no probability; only the data do. A p-value is the probability of seeing a difference at least as large as the one observed if the true lift were exactly zero.

The Bayesian tradition descends from Thomas Bayes, whose essay was published posthumously in 1763, and from Pierre-Simon Laplace. It treats probability as a degree of belief and lets the unknown lift carry a probability distribution. A prior is the belief held before the data; the posterior is the belief after updating on it. The sentence Lagvankar could repeat without sounding glib: "The p-value asks how surprising this data would be if nothing worked; the probability to beat baseline asks how likely it is that the variant is better, given this data and what we assumed going in."

3. How it actually works

The Bayesian procedure has four steps, and practitioners often leave the first and last implicit. First, choose a model: each session either orders or does not, with an unknown rate per arm. Second, choose a prior for each rate. Tilvara used a Beta(1, 1), flat between 0 and 100 per cent, which behaves like two imaginary sessions, one order and one non-order. A Beta(a, b) distribution is a shape over rates between 0 and 1 with mean a/(a+b).

Third, update. With x orders in n sessions, a Beta(a, b) prior becomes a Beta(a+x, b+n−x) posterior; no integration is needed. Fourth, and the step usually omitted, convert the posteriors into a decision: compute the probability the variant is better, compare it with a threshold fixed in advance, and weigh the size of the possible loss. No probability tells you what a wrong call costs; the business supplies that. A frequentist test runs a parallel path: assume zero lift, compute how far the observed gap sits from zero in standard errors, and report the tail area.

4. A worked example, line by line

Control: 400 orders in 10,000 sessions (4.00 per cent). Variant: 440 in 10,000 (4.40 per cent). Flat priors give Beta(401, 9,601) for control and Beta(441, 9,561) for the variant. The posterior mean is a/(a+b) and the variance is ab/[(a+b)²(a+b+1)].

  • Control: mean 401/10,002 = 4.009 per cent; standard deviation (SD) 0.196 points.
  • Variant: mean 441/10,002 = 4.409 per cent; SD 0.205 points.
  • Lift = variant − control: mean 0.400 points; SD = √(0.196² + 0.205²) = 0.284 points. This treats the lift as normal, an approximation that is very close at these sample sizes.
  • Probability the lift exceeds 0: z = 0.400 / 0.284 = 1.41, and Φ(1.41) = 0.92, where Φ is the standard normal cumulative probability.
  • 95 per cent credible interval (a range holding the lift with 95 per cent posterior probability): 0.400 ± 1.96 × 0.284, or −0.16 to +0.96 points.
  • Expected loss from shipping (the average shortfall if the control is in fact better) = 0.284 × φ(1.41) − 0.400 × Φ(−1.41) = 0.284 × 0.1476 − 0.400 × 0.0793 = 0.010 points, where φ is the normal density.

The frequentist route: the pooled rate is 840/20,000 = 0.042, so the standard error is √(0.042 × 0.958 × 2/10,000) = 0.00284, giving z = 0.004/0.00284 = 1.41 and a two-sided p of 2 × 0.0793 = 0.159. The Bayesian rule Lagvankar fixed beforehand was: ship if the probability exceeds 0.90 and expected loss is under 0.02 points. Pass 1 meets both.

Now change one input at a time. Pass 2 replaces the flat prior with a sceptical one, Beta(160, 3,840) for both arms, which encodes 4,000 sessions of past experience at 4.0 per cent. Pass 3 keeps the flat prior but doubles the data to 800/20,000 against 880/20,000.

Read across the rows. The sceptical prior pulls the mean lift from 0.400 to 0.286 and drops the probability below the 0.90 threshold, so pass 2 says wait. The sceptical prior is worth about 4,000 imaginary sessions per arm against 10,000 real ones, which is why it moves the answer by a visible but not overwhelming amount. Doubling the data pushes the probability to 0.977 and the p-value to 0.046; the two measures moved together because both are summaries of the same evidence. In pass 1, with a flat prior, the probability (0.92) rounds to one minus half the two-sided p (1 − 0.0793), which is no accident: both numbers reduce to the same z when the prior is flat and both posteriors are near-normal. Pass 2 shows the match failing under an informative prior (1 − 0.159/2 = 0.9205 against 0.885), and with a few dozen accounts per arm it would fail through skew. Their meanings stay apart either way.

5. The nuances

Not the same as significance

A probability of 0.92 and a p of 0.159 are different statements. The first is about the lift; the second is about the data under a hypothesis. Converting between them works only when the prior is flat, both posteriors are near-normal and the p-value is two-sided, as in pass 1; pass 2 breaks the first condition.

The prior is an input, not a detail

Passes 1 and 2 share data and differ only in belief, yet one clears the threshold and one does not. A prior must be written down and defended before the readout. Where data are plentiful the prior washes out; where they are scarce, it decides.

Credible versus confidence intervals

The interval in pass 1 is numerically almost identical to a frequentist 95 per cent confidence interval (−0.156 to 0.956 points unpooled). A credible interval says the lift lies inside with 95 per cent probability. A confidence interval says only that a procedure built this way captures the truth in 95 per cent of repeated experiments.

Direction is not size

Probability to beat baseline counts any positive lift, however tiny. For pass 1, the chance that the lift is at least 0.2 points is 1 − Φ((0.2 − 0.4)/0.284) = Φ(0.70) = 0.76. Ask the question the business cares about, which is usually a size threshold.

Stopping and peeking

The posterior itself does not depend on when you looked. The error rate of a rule such as "ship the first time the probability passes 0.90" does: more looks give more chances to cross by luck. Simulate the rule on data with no true effect before trusting it.

The model carries assumptions

The arithmetic above assumes every session is independent, orders at most once, and was randomly assigned. Repeat visitors, bots, or assignment by city break these assumptions, and no choice of interpretation repairs that.

What neither can tell you

Neither interpretation says whether orders per session was the right metric, whether a novelty effect will fade after week two, or whether a non-randomised comparison is causal. Both are summaries of a model of the data, not of the world.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace; small company, large company

In consumer products with millions of sessions, as at Tilvara, the two methods usually agree and the choice is about communication; a probability and an expected loss are easier for a finance lead than a p-value. In B2B, with perhaps sixty accounts per arm, the data are thin, the prior dominates, and honest reporting shows the posterior under several priors. In marketplaces, buyers and sellers share inventory, so a treated buyer can deplete what a control buyer sees; randomise at a coarser unit, and expect wider uncertainty either way.

An early-stage company has little history and low traffic, so it should use weak priors, accept wide intervals, and favour expected-loss rules for reversible decisions. A large company holds hundreds of past tests, which can justify informative priors for typical lifts. That evidence also shows how often a promising result shrinks on rollout, which a flat prior cannot know.

7. Common mistakes

"92 per cent, so ship"

Symptom: launch decks quote one probability with no threshold, size or cost. Misunderstanding: treating probability of direction as a decision. Cheapest diagnostic: ask for expected loss and the threshold fixed beforehand.

Choosing the prior after the data

Symptom: the prior differs between teams and happens to favour each team's variant. Misunderstanding: a prior as a dial. Diagnostic: rerun with a sceptical prior, as in pass 2, and see if the decision flips.

Reading a posterior probability as a p-value

Symptom: "95 per cent probability, therefore significant at 5 per cent", and stopping at the first crossing. Misunderstanding: the two scales have different meanings and different error properties. Diagnostic: simulate A/A tests, where both arms are identical, under the stopping rule and count false ships.

8. What good looks like

Before launch, Lagvankar's team writes one page: the metric, the minimum lift worth shipping (0.2 points) and the cutoff on the chance of reaching it (judgement, here 0.80), the prior with its source, the ship rule (probability above 0.90, expected loss below 0.02 points), and the sample size at which they will look. At readout they show Table 1's three rows together, the interval, the probability of clearing 0.2 points, and the p-value as a cross-check. Nobody argues about which statistic is correct, because the decision was set before the data arrived.

9. What Lagvankar decided, and what to learn next

Lagvankar did not ship on 6 October. Pass 1 met the rule, but the sceptical prior, which reflected Tilvara's history of shrinking checkout wins, did not, and the 0.76 chance of a lift worth 0.2 points fell short of her 0.80 judgement cutoff against three weeks of engineering. She extended the test to 20,000 sessions per arm, with the same rule, expecting that if the rates held the flat-prior probability would reach 0.977. The reasoning was less "which number is right" than "which evidence is cheap to improve". Learn next how significance, power and sample size work, since the Bayesian reading is a second interpretation of the same data, and how peeking distorts both.

Two questions to sit with. First, if two colleagues hold different priors and the data do not separate them, whose decision rule should the company use, and why? Second, which decision at your own company is cheap enough to reverse that you would accept a 0.88 probability, and which would need far more?
exp40v2-exp.ai.evals.vs.ab:
Shipping on the Score: Evals versus A/B Tests

The arithmetic that decides which changes an eval settles, and which need a live test.

1. Two decisions, four days apart

On Friday 9 October 2026 Bhoomika Imbrekar, product head at Parisar, a Mumbai home-services marketplace, had a model she believed in and no way to prove it. Parisar covers 240 serviceable pin-code clusters and books about 60,000 jobs a week, 71.0 per cent of them ending in a completed, paid visit. Its triage model turns a free-text request into a job specification and a price band, and the candidate scored 3.1 points above the live model on Parisar's offline specification-quality score. Bhaveen Itwarkar, who ran experimentation, had a different number: the cluster-randomised test they would need could not detect the effect they expected.

On Tuesday 13 October, Bhavana Ichalwadkar faced the mirror image. Pranali Health Systems extracts fourteen contracted fields from scanned discharge summaries and hospital bills for 41 insurers and third-party administrators, about 2,40,000 documents a month. Bhushit Indewadkar's candidate, v9, scored 90.0 per cent field accuracy against the live model's 86.0, and Pranali's next quarterly train was Monday 4 January 2027. But it had never run a randomised online test, because the outcome that matters — whether an adjudicator overrides the extraction — is produced by 64 adjudicators at its largest account, and adjudicators learn.

Both asked the question the standard answer handles badly: ship on the eval score, or wait for the A/B? The familiar reply — the eval gates, the test decides — is a special case. An eval is a screening instrument, worth whatever it shifts the odds against the asymmetry between the two ways of being wrong. So read, it is a better veto than a licence.

2. The idea, and the four positions people hold

An eval is a frozen set of inputs, a standard for a good output and a scoring procedure, run without users. An A/B test randomly assigns live units to incumbent or candidate and compares realised behaviour. Each rests on an assumption it cannot check. The eval assumes representativeness: the collection stands in for the population. The test assumes no interference — the stable-unit-treatment-value assumption, that one unit's outcome does not depend on another's assignment. Choosing an instrument is choosing which assumption is safer.

The lineages are separate. Test collections come from the Cranfield experiments in information retrieval under Cyril Cleverdon, whose second study reported in 1966, and were industrialised from 1992 by the TREC programme at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology. Randomised comparison runs from Ronald Fisher's field trials of the 1920s through Jerzy Neyman's 1923 potential-outcome notation to Donald Rubin's 1974 formalisation, where interference is named. The apparatus used here is from a third place: clinical epidemiology's screening statistics and Wald and Raiffa's decision analysis.

Four positions are genuinely held. The test-collection school signs "a frozen collection settles most comparisons at a hundredth of a live test's cost", but not "the collection measures what users will do". The online-arbiter school signs "no offline measure is a stable proxy across release types", but not "test everything", knowing an underpowered test is not evidence. The decision-analytic school signs "an instrument that cannot change the decision is not worth running", but not "the two measure the same quantity". The specification school signs "the eval set is the requirement document: its job is to say what we refuse to ship", but not "an eval gain is a reason to ship".

3. Mechanics: what an eval's number is worth

Indewadkar's eval set was 1,200 claim documents from settlements of April to June 2026, frozen on 1 July 2026 and scored on all fourteen fields: 16,800 extractions per version, identical inputs for both.

The step usually left implicit is that 16,800 is not the sample size: fourteen fields come from one document, and a smudged scan corrupts all of them together. With an intra-document correlation of 0.21 the design effect is 1 + (14 − 1) × 0.21 = 3.73, so the effective sample is 16,800 ÷ 3.73 = 4,504. The naive standard error of the difference — the square root of (0.86 × 0.14 ÷ 16,800 + 0.90 × 0.10 ÷ 16,800) — is 0.354 points; times √3.73 it is 0.683. The interval is 4.0 ± 1.96 × 0.683, or 2.66 to 5.34 points. The naive version claims a precision 1.93 times finer than the data supports.

The eval's ground truth is itself an instrument. Two clinical auditors, Binaifer Inamke and Bhaumita Ilbekar, independently judged 400 extractions: 28 from each of the fourteen fields plus 8 at random.

They agreed on 352 of 400 judgements, 88.0 per cent. Inamke called 344 correct, 86.0 per cent of 400, Ilbekar 340, or 85.0. Chance agreement under Cohen's kappa is 0.86 × 0.85 + 0.14 × 0.15 = 0.752, so kappa is (0.880 − 0.752) ÷ (1 − 0.752) = 0.52. The disagreement rate settles one thing most teams get backwards. If each auditor errs independently with probability e, they disagree with probability 2e(1 − e) = 0.120, so e = 6.4 per cent. Symmetric noise attenuates a measured difference by (1 − 2e) = 0.872, so the observed 4.0 points understates a true gap near 4.6 — conservative, not spurious, provided the noise is independent of which version produced the output, which is what blinding buys.

That supplies an otherwise unobtainable bottom row. Each of the 34 releases from July 2025 to September 2026 carries an eval verdict against a +2.0-point gate and an online verdict.

That asymmetry is the central claim: a pass leaves a coin-flip-and-a-bit, a failure is decisive. The other half is cost. Shipping untested is right when the expected cost of a dud falls below that of waiting, so the predictive value must clear Cdud ÷ (Cdud + Cdelay).
