If so, Cdud shrinks and the threshold falls — which is why Pranali's weekly field audit changes its decision more than a better eval would.

5. Hard edge cases: when the test cannot be run

Itwarkar's objection was arithmetic. A better specification helps a customer by getting a partner to accept sooner, and partners in a locality are a shared, finite pool, so a treated customer's gain is partly a control customer's loss. Randomising by job violates no-interference; randomising by cluster respects it and destroys the sample. Over four weeks each of 120 clusters per arm contributes about 1,000 jobs; with a between-cluster correlation of 0.015 the design effect is 1 + 999 × 0.015 = 15.985, so 120,000 jobs an arm are worth 7,507. At 80 per cent power, two-sided 5 per cent, the detectable effect is 2.80 × √(2 × 0.71 × 0.29 ÷ 7,507) = 2.07 points.

Two readings of Figure 2 separate expert from competent. First, running the cluster test for a year rather than four weeks moves the detectable effect from 2.07 to 2.01 points, because a longer window raises jobs per cluster and the design effect with it. With 120 clusters an arm the floor is 2.80 × √(2 × 0.71 × 0.29 × 0.015 ÷ 120) = 2.01 points however long you wait, and 0.9 points would need 598 clusters an arm against Parisar's 120 an arm, 240 in all. The test is not slow; it is impossible. Second, a switchback re-randomising each cluster weekly gives 960 cluster-weeks an arm over eight weeks, 250 jobs each, a design effect of 1 + 249 × 0.015 = 4.735, an effective 50,686 jobs and a detectable effect of 0.80 points — but only if that 0.015 is a week-to-week disturbance rather than a permanent property of a locality. If it is permanent, the effective sample collapses toward the 120-cluster floor. The decision rests on a variance decomposition nobody had run.

The organisational seam is where this gets expensive. Pranali's fourteen fields are contracted separately, so a release lifting twelve and dropping two is a win to the model team, a breach to the account team. Neither instrument arbitrates: the eval reports an average, no online test is addressed to a clause. Mature firms make exposure reversible and report the worst field.

6. Eight things an expert sees that a competent practitioner does not

An eval is a veto, not a licence.

The tell-tale is a team that quotes its hit rate on passes and never computes what a failure means. Parisar's pass moves the probability 13.8 points, its failure 28.9. The obvious reading — that a predictive instrument exists to approve — is backwards: at 50.0 per cent specificity the gate approves nearly anything.

Raw agreement without marginals means nothing.

The tell-tale is a judge report quoting 88 per cent and no two-by-two. When most items are easy, chance agreement is high and raw agreement nearly uninformative: Table 2's 88.0 per cent is κ = 0.52 or AC1 = 0.84, so an expert asks for cell counts first.

Label noise attenuates differences; it does not manufacture them.

The tell-tale is a reviewer saying the labels are unreliable so the gain may be noise. For symmetric, version-independent noise the arithmetic runs the other way: 4.0 points is a floor on a true 4.6. Unreliable labels make a measured level suspect, not a difference.

An eval's row count is not its sample size.

The tell-tale is an interval that tightens when the team adds fields rather than documents. Pranali's 16,800 extractions are 4,504 independent ones. Twenty-eight fields per document would raise the design effect to 6.67 and buy little; doubling to 2,400 documents halves the variance.

Extending a cluster test buys nothing; widening it is the lever.

The tell-tale is a plan that answers an underpowered cluster test by adding weeks. Thirteen times the window buys Parisar 0.06 points: more data is more power for the unit you randomise, not for observations inside it.

A guardrail finer than your detection floor is a decision already taken.

The tell-tale is a launch note promising to monitor for degradation beside a design that cannot see one point. Parisar's 0.4-point duds are invisible at 2.07 points, the floor of its unbiased design, which is why its Cdud runs 52 weeks rather than to the next review.

A gate's predictive value falls as the team improves.

The tell-tale is a hit rate that declines while the programme visibly improves. Predictive value depends on the base rate of wins in the queue, and a team that pre-filters its own bad ideas removes exactly the candidates the gate was catching. A falling hit rate may mean the opposite.

Product type does not choose the instrument; the cost ratio does.

The tell-tale is an organisation with one experimentation policy. The formula gives Parisar 68.4 per cent and Pranali 84.7 to 88.0 — not because one is a marketplace and the other enterprise software, but because one failure costs ₹32.57 lakh of silent drift and the other a credit.

7. Product type and company stage

In consumer products with independent users, traffic is plentiful and the test is the arbiter, the eval a filter. In B2B and enterprise software the binding constraint is rarely sample size — Pranali has millions of documents — but the mismatch between the unit you can randomise and the unit the outcome lives on, plus contracts that price the worst field. Platforms and marketplaces face interference, so their tests are often underpowered by construction rather than budget. Hardware's lead time makes delay cost dominate, so the threshold rises and offline qualification does the work. AI products differ in one way that is real and one that is not: a candidate can be scored on thousands of inputs for the price of an afternoon, which does not make online tests less necessary.

Stage changes the arithmetic, not the principle. An early-stage company has no release history, cannot estimate a predictive value, and should treat its eval strictly as a veto. A scaled company has the history and has usually not built the table, because that means testing candidates it has rejected.

8. Three worked examples

An eval decided, correctly. Pranali's v8.4, vetoed in July 2026, scored 88.5 per cent on the Table 1 set — better than v8's 86.0 — while its non-payable-items field fell from v8's 79.0 per cent to 71.0 against a contracted floor of 70.0. That field appears in 6.0 per cent of claims; at the pilot account's 6,600 documents a week it occurs 396 times, so the breach would have been a contractual fact long before a statistical one. The eval, the only instrument addressed to that clause, vetoed the release.

A test decided, wrongly. Parisar's February 2026 triage change ran as a job-level A/B for four weeks from Monday 9 February to Sunday 8 March, showed +1.9 points, shipped on Monday 16 March, and was annualised at ₹1.55 crore. A switchback from Monday 1 June to Sunday 26 July put it at +0.4 points. The decomposition is exact: if treatment rose a and control fell b, the job-level read is a + b = 1.9 and the global effect a − b = 0.4, so a = 1.15 and b = 0.75. Over the test, 900 control jobs that would have completed did not, against 1,380 extra in treatment: a net of 480. The forecast had overstated the release by ₹1.22 crore a year, and was not corrected until the switchback read on 26 July, nineteen weeks after shipping.

The recovery was a measurement policy. Before the shadow-test rule of June 2025, Parisar could compute a predictive value and nothing else: with no failing candidates tested online, specificity was unknowable and a +2.0-point gate unauditable. The 11 failures tested since include 2 genuine wins, each worth about ₹73.29 lakh a year at +0.9 points, ₹1.47 crore together. The cost was not a wrong decision but the absence of the only table that could say whether the gate was worth obeying.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Treating the gate as the verdict.

Early sign: a launch note citing an eval delta with no interval and no predictive value. Diagnostic: what share of passing candidates later won online, and how many failing ones did we test? Caught late, the cost is a queue of shipped 0.4-point regressions no monitor can see, at ₹32.57 lakh apiece.

Randomising the convenient unit.

Early sign: the measured effect shrinks as exposure rises from 5 to 50 per cent — the signature of interference, not novelty. Diagnostic: if everyone received this, where would the extra supply come from? Caught late, the cost is a plan built on an effect that does not exist globally.

Judge or rater drift.

Early sign: eval scores that move on a day with no release, or agreement that falls after a rubric edit. Diagnostic: re-score last quarter's frozen candidates and check the numbers reproduce. Caught late, every comparison across the drift point is void, including the history table the gate rests on.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether offline-to-online ratios generalise. The affirmative case is strong where tested: Parisar's fourteen passing winners sat near 0.29 points of completion per point of offline score, which is how Itwarkar forecast 0.9 from 3.1. The objection is that the ratio is estimated only on releases that passed the gate, a selected sample, and that each release type is a new regime. It would be refuted by a ratio holding across deliberately heterogeneous releases.

Whether a cluster correlation is a week-level or a locality-level property. On this hangs the difference between a 0.80-point switchback and a 2.01-point floor. The week-level camp points to rosters, weather and festivals turning over weekly; the locality camp replies that building stock and partner density do not, and that a switchback assumes away what makes clusters clusters. A decomposition of Parisar's cluster-week data would settle it; until then the switchback is a bet.

Whether chance-corrected agreement is the right standard. Kappa's defenders argue that credit for agreeing by accident is no credit. Its critics observe that kappa punishes exactly the skewed marginals a mature product should have, so a team improving its extraction watches its reliability fall. AC1 answers that, at the price of a chance model in which raters guess at the average prevalence. More data cannot settle it: the disagreement is about what "chance" means.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks for the negative predictive value first, because that is where a gate's value sits, and asks what became of the candidates the gate rejected. They arrive with the detectable effect computed, so the argument is whether the design can answer the question, not whether the result looks promising. They refuse to lengthen a cluster test. And when a figure rests on an assumption — that the correlation is weekly, that noise is version-independent, that a dud would go unnoticed for a year — they say it in the same breath as the number, because that is the sentence a reviewer can disagree with.

12. What each of them decided

Imbrekar did not ship. The eval's 60.9 per cent fell short of 68.4; expected cost favoured waiting by ₹3.58 lakh, 0.391 × ₹32.57 lakh against 0.609 × ₹15.03 lakh; and the switchback's 0.80 points was, barely, finer than the 0.9 she expected. She launched it on Monday 19 October 2026 to run eight weeks to Sunday 13 December, rewrote the gate as veto-only, and commissioned the locality-versus-week decomposition.

Ichalwadkar did not wait. No randomised test addressed her question, the quarterly train was a calendar artefact rather than a constraint, and a threshold of 84.7 to 88.0 per cent is unreachable by any eval. So she changed the question from which instrument decides to what the cheapest reversible exposure is: v9 behind a per-account flag at the pilot account from Monday 26 October, with a weekly blinded audit of the two weak fields. At 396 instances a week, three weeks give 1,188 observations and a 95 per cent half-width of 2.1 points on a field at 83.0 per cent, ample to see it fall through a 70.0 per cent floor.

Three questions. First, Parisar's 68.4 per cent threshold assumes a dud runs undetected for 52 weeks: what change to its monitoring would move that threshold most, and would it cost less than the switchback? Second, Pranali's auditors agree on 88.0 per cent of judgements, which is κ = 0.52 and AC1 = 0.84: which figure belongs in a customer-facing accuracy claim? Third, both gates were calibrated on the firm's own history: what would show that a gate's predictive value had decayed rather than its queue improved?

13. Going deeper

Offline vs online evaluation — the split this page prices, and what each pipeline measures. A/B testing fundamentals — randomisation, guardrails and assignment units, which the interference argument needs. Writing an experiment hypothesis — forces the effect size into the open, making a power calculation possible. Significance, power, sample size, peeking — the machinery behind Figure 2. When you can't A/B test — switchbacks, staged rollouts, synthetic controls. Experimentation culture — what makes a shadow-test policy survive a quarter that finds nothing. Qual + quant feedback loop — how production failures become next quarter's eval cases. Feature flags and flighting — what makes exposure reversible, and lowers the threshold in Table 4.

Evals, A/B Tests and When Each Decides

1. A Monday in October

On Monday 12 October 2026, Ankita Hendre, head of product at Nirvahi, a Pune-based bill-payment and credit-reminder app, opened a one-page note from her machine-learning lead, Ambrish Hattikar. Nirvahi's in-app assistant, Nirvahak, answers questions about refunds, failed UPI payments and EMI dates in English, Hindi and Marathi. About 3,000 eligible sessions a day reach it, and 22.0 per cent of them end with the user asking for a human, roughly 660 contacts a day.

Hattikar's candidate, version 7, had been scored on the team's evaluation set: 74.0 per cent of its answers judged correct against 68.0 per cent for the live version. His note ended, "Ready to ship." The chief executive wanted it live before Diwali on 8 November, when sessions would roughly double.

Hendre hesitated for a specific reason. Anjum Hanchate, who ran Nirvahi's experimentation platform, had reminded her of August, when a release that made answers longer scored three points higher on the evaluation and then pushed escalations up. A weaker assistant in Diwali week would mean thousands of anxious users given worse refund guidance. Waiting meant three weeks. The question was the one this page answers: ship on the eval score, or wait for the A/B?

2. The idea

An eval (offline evaluation) is a fixed set of test inputs, a written standard for what a good output is, and a scoring procedure, all run against a candidate system without any real user involved. An A/B test (an online controlled experiment) randomly assigns live users to the current version or the candidate and compares an outcome that is measured in their behaviour.

They were invented for different problems. Held-out test collections go back to the Cranfield experiments in information retrieval, led by Cyril Cleverdon from the late 1950s: build a fixed set of questions with known good answers so that systems can be compared cheaply and repeatably. Scoring open-ended language output with a second model acting as grader, a judge, became common from about 2023. Randomised comparison is older still, from Ronald Fisher's agricultural field trials in the 1920s, and web companies industrialised it in the 2000s because random assignment is the only reliable defence against the question "would those users have done that anyway?"

The sentence Hendre could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: an eval tells us whether the answer is right; an A/B test tells us whether being right changed what people did. Most of the work in this topic is deciding which of those two questions a given change actually raises.

3. How it actually works

Figure 1 shows the sequence. Offline, five steps matter. First, state the claim being tested ("version 7 resolves more queries correctly"). Second, build the set: Hattikar's team drew 800 conversations from earlier traffic and froze them, so that nobody could tune the assistant against them. Third, write the rubric and calibrate the judge: the team had two staff read 100 sampled judgements and found they agreed with the judge on 88. Fourth, run both versions over the same 800 inputs. Fifth, compute the difference and its uncertainty, which practitioners often leave implicit.

Online, the steps are different. Randomise by user, not by session, so one person never sees both versions. Name one primary metric (here, escalation: the user asks for a human in the same session, as in the 22.0 per cent baseline) and a few guardrail metrics that must not worsen. Size the test before launching it. Run whole weeks, because Nirvahi's traffic spikes around salary day and EMI due dates. Look once, at the end.

The step both pipelines share, and most teams skip, is writing the decision rule down before seeing any result. The dashed arrow in Figure 1 closes the loop: sessions that ended badly in production are sampled weekly and become new eval cases, so the eval set keeps tracking what users really ask.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Figure 2 organises the nuances below around two questions asked of any change: is there an answer key, and does the result depend on how people react?

The eval set is a photograph of the past.

Hattikar's 800 conversations were drawn from spring. New products, new failure types and new festivals do not appear in them, so a win means "better on what we already knew to ask."

The judge is an instrument that must be calibrated.

Agreement on 88 of 100 sampled judgements still leaves 12 disputed, and a judge may favour longer answers. Re-check it whenever the rubric or the judge model changes.

Correct is not the same as helpful.

R4's answers were more complete and scored higher. Users read more, trusted less and asked for a human. The eval measured the property engineers could define; the A/B measured the outcome the business wanted.

Eval gains carry noise.

Table 1's six points carry an interval of 1.6 to 10.4. Declaring a winner at +1 on 200 conversations is reading tea leaves.

Reusing an eval set wears it out.

Each time a team tunes against the same 800 conversations, a little of what it learns is about those conversations. This is Goodhart's law, in which a measure used as a target stops measuring.

An A/B tells you whether, never why.

It shows escalations fell; it does not show which change did it. Novelty can inflate the first days, which is another reason for whole weeks.

Some questions neither pipeline answers.

Rare, severe harms, such as one in 10,000 sessions giving dangerous guidance, never accumulate enough in an A/B, and an eval only finds what it was written to look for. Before relying on either, ask: what would this score look like if the change were useless? Who chose the inputs? Is the metric the outcome, or a stand-in for it?

6. Across products, and across company stages

In consumer products, behaviour is noisy and traffic plentiful, so A/B tests are cheap and fast, and evals earn their place as a filter that keeps bad candidates away from users. In B2B products, there may be only 60 customer accounts, so an A/B cannot reach significance; evals built from each customer's own documents carry most of the weight, supplemented by staged rollouts. In marketplaces, a change for buyers can alter what sellers see, so users in the control arm are affected by treated users, and randomising by region or time slot is often needed.

Early-stage companies often cannot afford the traffic for any A/B and should spend their effort on a small, honest eval set. Large companies have the opposite problem: traffic is abundant, and discipline is the scarce good, in the form of a registered decision rule, a guardrail list and a record of which evals have predicted which tests.

7. Common mistakes

Shipping on the eval and calling it proven.

Symptom: the eval chart climbs for three months while support volume stays flat. Misunderstanding: that "correct" is the outcome. Cheapest diagnostic: a table like Table 2 for your own releases; if it is empty, you have never checked.

Stopping the A/B early.

Symptom: a "flat" result announced after three days, or a "win" after two. Misunderstanding: that a test can be read whenever it looks decisive. Diagnostic: write the required sample (11,662 per arm here) in the launch note and refuse to read before it.

A frozen, leaking eval set.

Symptom: the score rises 2 points a month while the online metric stays level. Misunderstanding: that a set stays representative once the team has seen it. Diagnostic: score both versions on 100 fresh conversations from last week; if the gap shrinks, the set has worn out.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Hendre's decision has four visible features. The decision rule exists in writing before the result: "ship if escalation falls by at least 0.8 points and no guardrail worsens." The eval is treated as a gate, not a verdict, and its interval is quoted next to its point estimate. The A/B is sized for a smaller effect than the eval implies. And the team arrives at the meeting with Table 2, so the argument is about evidence from their own history rather than about whose instinct is stronger.

9. What Hendre decided

Hendre did not ship on 12 October, and she did not ignore the eval. She treated version 7's pass as the ticket to a test: a 50/50 split by user starting Monday 19 October, running 14 days to Sunday 1 November, with the decision on Monday 2 November, six days before Diwali. Her written rule was to ship to everyone if escalation fell by at least 0.8 points and no guardrail worsened, hold if the interval spanned zero, and stop if escalation rose. The eval had earned the test, since 1.6 to 10.4 points excludes zero. It could not earn the launch, since R4 had shown that a better eval score can still come with worse behaviour.

To learn next: the mechanics of A/B testing itself (power, guardrails, why peeking inflates false wins), then how offline and online evaluation are calibrated against one another over many releases. Two questions to sit with. If R4 had been the only release in your history, what would you have believed about evals, and what would that have cost you? And which change in your own product would no instrument you currently own be able to settle?
